Musutafu.name: Musutafu
Musutafu.basicInfo: Musutafu is a mid-sized Shizuoka city on Suruga Bay, about 30 kilometers southeast of Mount Fuji's summit, an ordinary working town that happens to sit beneath the country's most famous hero academy. Its center is Musutafu Station, a Tokaido shinkansen stop 45 minutes from Tokyo and two hours from Osaka, ringed by office blocks, two all-night convenience stores at the north exit, a covered hero-merchandise arcade off the south exit, alley bars and the main bus terminal. From the station the city spreads in low layers. Quiet residential blocks of apartments and family houses reach southeast, where Aldera High School and the Midoriya and Bakugo homes sit among ordinary schools and corner shops; the riverside blocks about 4 kilometers east hold Hero Agency Row and its small agencies; Musutafu General Hospital stands about 5 kilometers west; and homes and shops run southwest to the bay, where Kiyashi Shopping Mall sits about 5 kilometers south-southwest of the station and Dagobah Municipal Beach Park lines the shore about 5 kilometers southwest. Above the city to the north and northeast the forested hills climb toward Fuji, and U.A. Academy's walled campus fills them: its Main Gate is about 3 kilometers northeast of the station, ten minutes by city bus up the hill road, and U.A. controls everything inside its wall. Musutafu Police Headquarters stands on the city's northwest edge, about 3.5 kilometers from the station. To the south the Izu Peninsula begins in farms, hot-spring towns and wooded hills. The air is mild and humid, with afternoon sea wind, fog on the foothills and snow on Fuji into early summer; cherry blossoms line the river in April, the rainy season soaks June, summer is hot and sticky, typhoons come off the Pacific from late summer into autumn, and winters are dry and clear, with snow rare in town. Residents are families, office workers and shopkeepers, with anglers and harbor workers along the bay and small farms on the edges. Most get around by local train, city bus or bicycle, taxis wait at the station, and the shinkansen carries business travelers to Tokyo and Osaka. The economy is ordinary city work, offices, shops, the hospital and the bay, plus a steady trade in hero goods, fans and visitors that U.A. brings. Newer buildings have wide doors and reinforced seats for heteromorph bodies; older shopping streets do not. City police at neighborhood police boxes and the small hero agencies patrol the town and handle the everyday calls: bag snatchers, traffic accidents, Quirk scuffles, lost toddlers. Public Quirk use beyond what a body cannot help is illegal and frowned on. U.A. students live on campus and come down on weekends, signed out from their dorms, and a uniform in town still draws stares. A player can work a part-time shift, shop and eat, shadow a patrol, visit a ward or a family home, run the beach at dawn or follow a rumor into the station's back alleys.
Musutafu.hiddenInfo: Since the news that All Might now teaches at U.A., Musutafu has more eyes on it than ever: reporters and fans at the station, sidekicks from bigger agencies taking calls the small local pros counted on, and a few small-time crooks drawn by a famous town. In the station's back alleys, brokers who never give their names have been hiring crooks with fighting Quirks for cash up front, and several have dropped out of sight; the police have only bar talk so far. Most residents believe nothing truly bad can happen this close to the Number One hero.

Greater Tokyo.name: Greater Tokyo
Greater Tokyo.basicInfo: Greater Tokyo is the capital and the heart of the hero business, about 100 kilometers northeast of Musutafu, 45 minutes by shinkansen into Tokyo Station, and it reaches north to the commuter city of Hosu. It spreads across a flat river plain to the head of Tokyo Bay: a dense field of office towers, rail lines, elevated expressways and shopping districts, and around them endless low neighborhoods of apartments, family houses and corner shops, with older wards, canals and factory lots toward the coast. Summers are hot and sticky, June brings the rainy season, late-summer typhoons can stop the trains for a day, and winter is dry and cold under clear skies; in April the parks and rail embankments fill with cherry blossoms. Millions live and work here: office workers, students, shopkeepers, tourists, reporters and fans who chase incidents with their phones raised. The economy is everything at once, government, finance, media, retail and the hero trade itself, and Japan's largest agencies, Endeavor's and Best Jeanist's among them, compete for its cases alongside the police. Scramble crossings sit under giant screens looping hero news and sponsor ads, and billboards of top-ranked heroes hang over the main avenues. Tokyo Station, the national rail hub at the center, sends shinkansen across Japan. Around it the hero world sits close together: the Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarters about 3 kilometers west-southwest in the government district; the Endeavor Hero Agency tower about 6 kilometers west; Central Tokyo Streets, with the scramble crossing, Billboard Avenue and the department stores, about 7 kilometers west-southwest; the Best Jeanist Hero Agency about 6 kilometers south-southwest, with the Tokyo Broadcasting Center about 6 kilometers south of the station and about 2.5 from Jeanist's door; and the Commission's Hero Billboard Chart Hall about 4 kilometers southeast. About 30 kilometers north, half an hour out by express train and about an hour and a half from Musutafu, Hosu runs on the commuter clock: elevated lines cross it on concrete overpasses, Main Street runs north from Hosu Station to a plaza with a police box and a giant news screen, the walled-in lanes of the Back Alleys lie about 4 km southwest of the station, Hosu General Hospital about 4 km north-northwest, and the small, careful Manual Hero Agency keeps a second-floor office about 3 km east-northeast. Hosu has few heroes for its size, and a call from downtown can wait ten minutes or more for a pro. South of the center, past the river mouths, the bay shore runs on toward Kamino and Yokohama. The Metropolitan Police keep order in the capital, with police boxes on busy corners and cameras over the main crossings, and Hosu's own city police work under Chief Kenji Tsuragamae alongside small local agencies, while the pro hero Native walks Hosu's Main Street on foot; heroes cover the districts their agencies have staked out, and public Quirk use without a license is illegal here as everywhere. People get around by subway, commuter rail, bus and taxi; cars crawl, and heroes with movement Quirks take the rooftops. A visitor can shop, work, sightsee, chase a sidekick contract, keep a Commission appointment, sell footage to the networks, intern with a by-the-book pro in Hosu, or ride the elevated lines and watch the city go by below.
Greater Tokyo.hiddenInfo: Under the shine, Greater Tokyo runs on competition and quiet deals. The big agencies fight over case credit in front of the cameras, the Commission settles what would embarrass the system and watches the ranking tallies, and every new Hero Killer attack elsewhere puts the capital's pros on edge. Hosu's real weakness is coverage: heroes are spread thin, police take twenty minutes to reach the older quarters, the Back Alleys have no cameras and the station's cameras cover no rooftops, so anyone who moves by roof or lane can cross the city unseen. Local heroes read every report about the Hero Killer Stain, who watches a city's heroes from its rooftops before he strikes; Hosu is exactly the kind of city he studies, and nobody there would notice him doing it.

Mountain Training Lands.name: Mountain Training Lands
Mountain Training Lands.basicInfo: Remote mountains in the Japanese Alps around the Kiso valley, about 130 kilometers northwest of Musutafu, three to four hours by chartered bus from U.A. Academy. Dense forest of cedar, cypress, beech and oak covers the slopes, cut by gorges, cold streams and waterfalls, and hot springs rise in the valleys. Far down the Kiso valley are small towns of old post-road inns, sawmills and soba shops, with a highway, a rail line and the last convenience store for a long way. Above them, one high valley holds a timber lodge with a training clearing, the only building for kilometers, reached by a single mountain road; northwest of it spreads Beast's Forest, a thick forest the owners use for training, and to the northeast, high on a cliff, is a ledge nobody at the lodge knows about. Wild boar, serow and monkeys roam the slopes, black bears wake hungry in spring, and the trails are marked with bear bells and faded wooden signposts. The weather turns fast: morning mist, sudden rain, cool summer nights and snow on the high ridges well into spring. In April the snowmelt swells every stream, mudslides close trails, and hikers underestimate the cold. Above the valley towns, almost no one lives but the four pro heroes of the Wild Wild Pussycats, Mandalay, Pixie-Bob, Ragdoll and Tiger, who own the land as far as the eye can see and run mountain rescue across these ranges, and Kota Izumi, the small boy Mandalay looks after. The team is the law up here in practice: it answers search-and-rescue calls from the valley police and the regional fire service, warns trespassers off its land and reshapes washed-out trails. The economy below is timber, tourism and inns; up here it is rescue work and U.A.'s summer training camps, which fill the lodge with students every year. Getting around means the one road, then boots; there is no rail above the valley and no phone signal in the gorges, so the team relies on radios. A visitor can hike, soak in the hot springs, train with the team's permission, volunteer as rescue support, or get lost, which is the most common way strangers meet the Pussycats.
Mountain Training Lands.hiddenInfo: The team is busier and poorer than its cheerful act suggests: four heroes cover hundreds of square kilometers, rescue pays little, and summer camp fees and merchandise keep the agency afloat. Spring is the worst season, with snowmelt, mudslides and careless visitors. Grief sits under the lodge's noise: Kota's parents died as heroes, and he hates everything the team stands for. He has a hiding place none of them has found. Right now trespassing video streamers are testing how far they can get into Beast's Forest, and the mountains do not forgive mistakes.

Kyushu.name: Kyushu
Kyushu.basicInfo: Kyushu here is the island's north coast, where the shinkansen line from Tokyo ends. Fukuoka, a big port city on Hakata Bay, fills the coastal plain between the water and a ring of green hills: the Naka River runs through its center past the Tenjin shopping district, high-rises line the harbor, and Hakata Station is the island's main rail hub. At night, food stalls light up the riverbanks in Nakasu, the entertainment island between two channels of the river. Behind the city the hills rise toward farmland, orchards and hot-spring towns, and fishing ports and beaches run along the coast in both directions. The climate is warm and wet, with an early spring, a long rainy season, typhoons in late summer that close the port and stop the trains for a day or two, and mild winters. Locals speak Hakata dialect, argue about ramen, celebrate their summer festival with men racing decorated floats through the streets at dawn, and feel well protected: Hawks, the Number Three hero at the start of the year, works out of Fukuoka and is known for ending cases before other heroes arrive. The economy is the port, retail, food, offices and a busy airport close to the center; ferries leave the harbor for the outlying islands, and container ships come and go around the clock. Downtown Fukuoka spreads along the bay with Tenjin, Nakasu and the harbor towers; Hakata Station lies about 4 km east of it; the Hawks Hero Agency keeps a small modern office about 4 km northeast of downtown, north of the station. A few smaller local agencies and the Fukuoka prefectural police handle what Hawks leaves, and police boxes stand at the main crossings and at the station. Ms. Joke, the Smile Hero, who also teaches the hero course at Ketsubutsu Academy, is a familiar face around Tenjin. People ride the subway, city buses and bicycles, and taxis wait at every hotel. From Hakata the shinkansen reaches Osaka in about 2.5 hours, Musutafu in about 4.5 and Tokyo in about 5, and a short flight connects Fukuoka with Tokyo. A visitor can eat at the yatai stalls, shop Tenjin, work at the port or a ramen counter, patrol with a local agency, apply to Hawks' agency, or spend an afternoon staring at the sky hoping to see red wings.
Kyushu.hiddenInfo: Fukuoka has grown used to one hero solving everything. Hawks' speed keeps street crime low and starves the smaller agencies of visible cases, so their rankings and income are slipping and some of their sidekicks sell reporters tips about where he will appear. The port is the city's soft spot: unregistered support gear comes in hidden among legal cargo, and Trigger is rumored to be arriving from Osaka by night bus. Hawks himself is busier than his public schedule shows, and few people ask where he goes.

Tartarus Waters.name: Tartarus Waters
Tartarus Waters.basicInfo: Open Pacific water about 55 kilometers south of the Izu Peninsula's tip, among the scattered Izu Islands. The maximum-security prison Tartarus stands alone on a small volcanic island behind high sea walls: black rock cliffs rise straight out of the swell, the walls follow the shoreline, and above them show a radar mast, floodlight towers and a helipad, while the prison itself is built down into the rock. The island is reached only by the armored transfer boat from the Tartarus Transfer Port, a crossing of about two hours, or by helicopter from the same port. The crossing is a long gray run over open water: the peninsula's cliffs fall away behind, other Izu Islands with their own fishing villages and ferry harbors pass as dark shapes to either side, and for the last stretch the prison island is the only thing on the horizon, growing from a smudge into a wall of rock and concrete with a single floodlit landing cut into its northern side. Only staff and guards live on the island, on long rotations, and supplies come out on scheduled boats. Around it lies a police exclusion zone: patrol boats turn back fishing boats, yachts and anything else that strays inside, and no one lands without written authorization, an escort and repeated searches. There is nothing here for tourists and no way to visit casually. The sea is deep and rough, with strong currents, long swells, fog in early summer and typhoons from late summer into autumn; on bad days the transfer boat does not sail and the island waits. Seabirds nest on the cliffs, dolphins sometimes follow the boat, and the only lights at night are the prison's floodlights and the patrol boats' searchlights. A guard force under the National Police Agency runs the island and its waters, and the Hero Public Safety Commission vets everyone who works or visits there. To the public, Tartarus Waters is a blank space on the map where the worst villains in Japan go and do not come back. A player can come here only with a purpose and papers: escorting a prisoner on the transfer boat, working a guard rotation, crewing a patrol boat, or arriving for an approved interview.
Tartarus Waters.hiddenInfo: The exclusion zone is tighter on paper than at sea. In high seas the patrol boats stay in harbor and rely on radar, and small craft can sit just outside the line for hours before anyone hails them. The guard force is stretched by a full prison and longer rotations, supply boats run late in bad weather, and the island's crews have come to treat the sea itself as the strongest wall they have.

Tartarus Coast.name: Tartarus Coast
Tartarus Coast.basicInfo: The southern tip of the Izu Peninsula, about 50 kilometers south of Musutafu and under two hours away by train or bus, where wooded hills drop to a rocky shore and fishing towns. A single coastal road winds south through tunnels and over headlands, with a local rail line and buses for the towns along it. The towns are small harbors of tiled roofs and concrete breakwaters: fishing families, inn and hot-spring keepers, retirees and a few surfers live here, and visitors come for the baths, the seafood, the cliffs and the lighthouses. Squid boats go out at dusk with strings of white lamps, morning auctions sell the night's catch on the quay, and laundry and drying fish hang side by side in the sea wind. On the point stands the Tartarus Transfer Port, a guarded harbor of concrete piers, fences, gates and watchtowers where prisoners board the armored ferry to Tartarus. Police patrol boats come and go, and only cleared staff pass the gate; the one gated road in is open only to staff, escorts and approved visitors, and anyone else is turned back at the barrier. Transfers run at set hours, usually at night: armored vans come down the coast road under police escort, traffic pulls over to let them pass, and the port's floodlights stay on until morning. Locals live beside it without much talk; the port brings jobs, guards' families rent rooms in town, and fishermen keep clear of the patrol boats. The water offshore is deep and rough, with long swells, fog in early summer and typhoons from late summer into autumn; in spring and autumn storms the boats stay tied up for days. Prefectural police keep a police box in each town and run the port's outer gate; in the towns, order is mostly a matter of neighbors who know each other. Public Quirk use is as illegal here as anywhere, and a stranger who uses one near the port draws the police in minutes. A player can soak in a hot spring, eat at a harbor diner, fish from a breakwater, hire on with a fishing crew, watch a night convoy go by, wait at the port for a transfer, or escort a prisoner to the boat with the right papers.
Tartarus Coast.hiddenInfo: The towns live beside the port without talking about it. Innkeepers rent rooms to guards' families and to lawyers waiting on transfers, and fishermen know the patrol boats' routines better than anyone; a few will take a cash fare out toward the exclusion line for a stranger who asks no questions and pays well. Spring storms have backed transfers up, and some nights two convoys come down the coast road at once. Locals mention strangers who watch the convoy road, and the police box notes them and does little more.

U.A. Campus.name: U.A. Campus
U.A. Campus.basicInfo: The forested hill country just north and northeast of Musutafu, rising from the edge of town toward the eastern foothills of Mount Fuji: cedar and oak woods, tea terraces on the lower slopes, farm hamlets, a reservoir lake and forest roads toward Hakone. Spring brings mist off the foothills every morning, June the rainy season, summer heavy heat and cicadas, autumn typhoons and red maples, winter clear cold days with Fuji white above the trees. Most of the hill belongs to U.A. Academy, Japan's national hero academy, and all of it is closed ground. Its Main Gate stands about 3 kilometers northeast of Musutafu Station, ten minutes by city bus, where a tree-lined boulevard climbs from the last town blocks to a gate plaza and bus terminal. A security wall runs through the forest around all of U.A.'s land, and the Main Gate is the only way in: sensors in the gateposts read every student ID, faculty ID and visitor pass, and anyone without one brings down the U.A. Barrier, thick steel panels that seal the opening. Visitors need an appointment, sign in at the gate's security office, wear a day pass and are met by the person they came to see. Behind the wall lie the main campus with the H-shaped glass main building, the Faculty Residence, the Heights Alliance dorms and Gym Gamma; U.A. Stadium in its own walled park beside it; and, spread up the hill, each behind its own wall and locked gate, Training Ground Gamma about 1 km west, Ground Beta about 1.5 km northwest and six more mock cities, and high in the forest about 3 km north-northeast the Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ). Campus buses leave the bay in the Courtyard and run the winding campus roads between the walled sites on class days. A training site opens only when a class or a teacher has booked it through the Faculty Office, and stands locked and empty otherwise. Quirk use on U.A. ground is allowed only in a supervised class or a booked, supervised session; anything else lands a student in front of Hound Dog, the disciplinarian. Every teacher is a working pro hero, those on call live in the Faculty Residence, and teachers walk rounds at Heights Alliance after dark. Every student lives in Heights Alliance: curfew falls each night, anyone caught out after it earns house arrest and cleaning duty, and leaving campus means signing out on the dorm's sheet, since the Main Gate passes only signed-out students and a missing sign-out reaches the homeroom teacher by morning. Signed-out students ride the city bus down to Musutafu Station or walk the boulevard in about forty minutes, and Sunday evening is the gate's busiest hour. Outside the wall the hill is ordinary country under the prefectural police: the Musutafu Police Headquarters on the city's northwestern edge, about 3.5 km northwest of the station, and the Todoroki family's walled estate on the wooded rise to the east, about 6.5 km east of the main campus, open to guests by invitation only. U.A. is the hill's great employer, and repair crews, drivers, cleaners and suppliers come up from town each morning. Mornings bring the chime carrying down to the town; weekday afternoons, campus buses run the forest roads between the training grounds.
U.A. Campus.hiddenInfo: The wall runs for kilometers through the forest, and away from the Main Gate it is watched by cameras and sensors rather than people; the Barrier stops anyone who walks up to it, not a Quirk that flies, digs or opens a way through space. The farther training sites, the USJ above all, depend on phone and alarm lines back to the main campus and are at least ten minutes from help by road. Faculty are working heroes, so on nights when several are out on patrol or on cases, fewer teachers are on the hill than the public imagines. Since All Might joined the faculty the whole country watches U.A., and every gap in its routine is worth more to an outsider than it was a year ago.

Sea off Noto.name: Sea off Noto
Sea off Noto.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan west of the Noto Peninsula, a square of deep blue water with no land in it. The peninsula's long western shore runs along the eastern horizon, its cliffs clear on fine days, with the harbors of Togi and Monzen just beyond the edge. Over the inner part the bottom is continental shelf a hundred or two hundred meters down; farther west it falls away toward the deep basins of the open sea, and the water turns from green-blue near shore to a hard ink blue. The Tsushima Warm Current runs northeast through it. Summers are mild and glassy, with squid boats stringing white lamps across the dark. From November to March the northwest monsoon drives gray swells and snow squalls onto the Noto coast, and small boats stay in port for days. Boats work these grounds for winter yellowtail, snow crab, sweet shrimp and squid, sold in Kanazawa's Omicho market within hours. Car ferries between Tsuruga and Niigata or Hokkaido pass well offshore. The coast guard patrols out of Kanazawa and Nanao, and a few heroes with water or flight Quirks are on call along the Ishikawa coast, though help out here comes slowly. A party could be on a chartered fishing boat, a ferry deck, or carried by a flying hero; Kanazawa is a little over three hours from Musutafu by shinkansen.
Sea off Noto.hiddenInfo: Out here the problems are the sea's: winter storms that swamp small boats, and unlicensed boats from elsewhere that slip into the squid grounds at night and argue with local crews over nets. Smuggling is small and sporadic, a crate passed between boats offshore. A rescue can take an hour or more; the nearest licensed heroes with sea or flight Quirks work out of Kanazawa, and the coast guard does most of the real work.

Noto Peninsula.name: Noto Peninsula
Noto Peninsula.basicInfo: The waist of the Noto Peninsula, the hooked arm of Ishikawa that reaches north into the Sea of Japan. This region runs from Hakui on the west coast and Nanao on the east up to Monzen and Anamizu; the peninsula's far tip around Wajima and Suzu continues past the northern edge. The west side faces the open Sea of Japan in wave-cut cliffs and rock arches such as Ganmon on the Noto Kongo coast; the east side wraps sheltered Nanao Bay, where the low wooded island of Notojima is tied to the mainland by two long bridges and oyster rafts line the inlets toward Anamizu. Inland is rolling satoyama country: terraced paddies, cedar groves, black-tiled farmhouses and narrow roads over hills that rarely top five hundred meters. Winters are gray, windy and wet with sea-effect snow and booming surf; summers are humid and green. Nanao is the main town, a port and rail hub with a fish market on the harbor, and just north of it Wakura Onsen lines the bay with big ryokan whose salty spring a heron is said to have found. Hakui has the ancient Keta Taisha shrine; Shika, Togi and Monzen are quiet coast towns, Monzen with the great Zen temple Sojiji Soin; Anamizu is a small fishing and oyster town. People grow rice, fish, run inns. The peninsula is known for Noto beef, winter oysters, yellowtail, squid, ishiru fish sauce and its summer kiriko festivals, when towering lantern floats are carried through the streets at night; Nanao's Seihakusai in May hauls three enormous dekayama floats through town. The Noto Kagaribi limited express runs from Kanazawa to Wakura Onsen in about an hour, the Noto Railway continues to Anamizu, local buses cover the rest, and the toll-free Noto Satoyama Kaido climbs the spine to Noto Airport near Anamizu, with flights to Haneda. Musutafu is about five hours away by shinkansen and limited express via Kanazawa; Shin-Osaka about three and a half. Small hero offices in Nanao and Hakui cover huge rural districts, every station has its police box, and at festival time sidekicks walk beside the lantern bearers while broad-shouldered locals with strength-type builds take the heaviest poles.
Noto Peninsula.hiddenInfo: Depopulation is the steady problem: shuttered shops on Nanao's side streets, empty farmhouses up the valleys, festival crews short of hands to carry the kiriko. Older residents trust the police box and the volunteer fire brigade more than flashy hero work. Real hero help is thin; the Nanao and Hakui offices can take half an hour to reach a cliff road, and serious cases call in Kanazawa, an hour south. Trouble is small: drunken festival fights, theft from empty holiday homes, oyster-raft poaching, unlicensed Quirk use in fishing, and quakes and rockfall on an aging coast road.

Toyama Bay.name: Toyama Bay
Toyama Bay.basicInfo: The northern reach of Toyama Bay, a deep, cold, U-shaped bite of the Sea of Japan between the east coast of the Noto Peninsula and the Toyama shore; nearly everything inside this region is water. The bay plunges past a thousand meters only a few kilometers from shore, and the meeting of cold deep water with the warm Tsushima Current near the surface makes it one of the richest fishing grounds in Japan, which locals call a natural fish tank. The water is dark blue and clear in summer, slate and wind-whipped in winter, when northwest gales pile up short steep seas. On clear winter and spring mornings the whole Tateyama range stands white across the bay to the southeast, three thousand meters straight up from the sea. The western edge is Noto's sheltered east coast: Tsukumo Bay with its ninety-nine little inlets, the harbor town of Ushitsu in Noto town, whose Abare festival in July hurls portable shrines into the river, the sea and roaring bonfires among towering kiriko lanterns, and Ogi, a squid port with a giant squid statue on its waterfront. Mitsuke Island, a sheer rock islet shaped like a warship, stands off the far Noto shore at the northern rim. The southeastern corner touches the Toyama coast at Nyuzen and Asahi: the green fan of the Kurobe River, fields of huge oval watermelons, and pebble beaches where people hunt jade washed down from the mountains. Set-net boats work the bay year-round for winter yellowtail, white shrimp, red snow crab and squid, and in spring the firefly squid run lights up the shore to the south. The Ainokaze Toyama Railway and the Hokuriku Expressway pass through Nyuzen and Tomari, about forty minutes from Toyama city; Ushitsu is reached by bus from Anamizu or Nanao. From Musutafu, Nyuzen is about four hours by shinkansen via Tokyo and Toyama, the Noto side closer to six. There are no regular passenger ferries; a party out here is on a fishing boat, a chartered sightseeing cruise, a coast guard patrol or a flying hero. The coast guard watches the bay from Fushiki, licensed maritime heroes based near Toyama cover the water, and deckhands with gills or webbed hands are a common sight on the boats.
Toyama Bay.hiddenInfo: The bay is quiet but frayed at the edges: aging crews and a shrinking fleet, quarrels over set-net rights, poachers after white shrimp and crab, and summer drownings off pebble beaches that drop away steeply. Foreign boats out on the open Sea of Japan worry the coast guard more than anything here. Help on the water is slow; the coast guard at Fushiki and rescue heroes around Toyama city need half an hour or more, and Noto's east coast is farther still. Petty crime is smuggling, unlicensed Quirk fishing and theft from moored boats.

Itoigawa.name: Itoigawa
Itoigawa.basicInfo: The Itoigawa coast, the far western end of Niigata, where the Northern Alps run straight down into the Sea of Japan. The northern half of the region is open sea; the land is a narrow shore strip backed by steep green ridges, running from the Toyama border in the southwest to Nadachi in Joetsu city in the northeast. Itoigawa sits on the Itoigawa-Shizuoka Tectonic Line, the western wall of the Fossa Magna rift that splits Honshu, and the whole area is a UNESCO Global Geopark, with the Fossa Magna Museum and a park where visitors can lay a hand on the fault itself. This is also Japan's jade country: jade boulders lie in the protected Kotaki River gorge, and after storms stone hunters comb the gray gravel beaches between Omi and Itoigawa for green pebbles. At the western end the Oyashirazu cliffs drop sheer into the waves, once the most feared stretch of the old coast road and now threaded by tunnels. Winters bring wild seas, sleet on the coast and deep snow a few kilometers inland; summers are hot, with foehn winds off the mountains. Itoigawa is a small city of fishing harbors, limestone quarries and cement works, sake breweries and quiet shopping streets; Nou to the east has a roadside station where stalls grill red snow crab by the dozen. Locals eat Itoigawa's black squid-ink yakisoba and anglerfish hot pot in winter. The Himekawa valley runs south toward Otari and Hakuba, with Renge Onsen high in the mountains just to the south, and the single-track Oito Line follows it through snow sheds. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Itoigawa, the Echigo Tokimeki Railway runs the coast to Naoetsu and Ichiburi, and the Hokuriku Expressway and Route 8 hug the shore. Musutafu is about three hours away via Tokyo, Tokyo a little over two, Shin-Osaka about three and a half. Visitors come for the geopark, jade hunting, crab, sea kayaking under the cliffs and hiking the old cliff road. A small hero office in Itoigawa covers the whole coast with the police, and its sidekicks spend as much time on landslide and avalanche calls as on crime.
Itoigawa.hiddenInfo: Nature is the steady threat: landslides and avalanches close the Himekawa valley road and the Oito Line most winters, and rough seas take beachcombers every year. Jade poaching from the protected Kotaki gorge and fake jade sold to tourists are the local scandal. Hero help is thin; the Itoigawa office and police handle most calls, and anything big waits on Joetsu or Toyama, forty minutes to an hour away. Villainy is small: theft at the crab stalls and harbor, drunk drivers on Route 8, and the occasional unlicensed Quirk user digging for stones.

Joetsu.name: Joetsu
Joetsu.basicInfo: Joetsu and its hinterland in southwestern Niigata, where the Kubiki Plain opens onto the Sea of Japan and climbs inland into snowy hills; a thin band of sea runs along the north, and the coast reaches from Nadachi east past the port of Naoetsu to Kakizaki under Mount Yoneyama. Joetsu city joins two old towns: Naoetsu, a port of chemical plants, fishing boats and the ferry terminal for Sado Island, and Takada, an inland castle town famous for some of the deepest snow recorded in any Japanese city. Takada's streets are lined with gangi, covered wooden arcades that keep the sidewalks open under meters of snow, and Takada Castle park holds thousands of cherry trees lit by lanterns at night in April and lotus blooming in its moats in summer. On the hill to the west stand the ruins of Kasugayama Castle, home of a famed warlord whose August festival fills the town with an armored horseback procession. Inland lie Arai in Myoko city, where chilies are bleached on the snow for kanzuri paste, the mountain villages of Yasuzuka and Ohshima, and in the southeast corner Matsudai and Matsunoyama, part of Tokamachi, with art installations scattered through rice terraces, the old Matsunoyama hot springs, and the Kiyotsu Gorge on the edge. The climate is mild in summer and brutal in winter, with snow-melt sprinklers in the roads and roof-clearing a daily chore. The Kubiki Plain grows Koshihikari rice; sake, sasa-dango rice dumplings, sweet shrimp, nodoguro and winter yellowtail fill the tables. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Joetsumyoko, about two hours from Tokyo and about three from Musutafu; the Echigo Tokimeki Railway runs the coast and up to Myoko Kogen, the Hokuhoku Line cuts east through Matsudai to Tokamachi, and the Hokuriku and Joshin-etsu expressways meet here. Sado ferries leave Naoetsu for Ogi. Visitors come for the cherry blossoms, the castle ruins, the aquarium on the shore, art walks in the hills and hot springs. A few small hero offices in Takada and Naoetsu work with the police, and in heavy winters licensed heroes with heat or strength Quirks are called out to free stranded trains and buried homes.
Joetsu.hiddenInfo: Snow is the real adversary: roof collapses, residents hurt clearing roofs, trucks stranded for hours on the expressway in whiteouts. Joetsu city has decent police and two or three small hero offices, but the hill villages of Yasuzuka, Matsudai and Matsunoyama can be an hour away in winter. Depopulation empties the uplands. Villainy is modest: theft around the port, scams on elderly residents, drunken fights in Naoetsu bars, and people paid under the table to clear snow with unlicensed Quirks.

Echigo-Yuzawa.name: Echigo-Yuzawa
Echigo-Yuzawa.basicInfo: The Uonuma country of southern Niigata, a long snowbound valley and its surrounding mountains running north from the hot spring town of Yuzawa toward Ojiya, with Tokamachi on the western edge and the wild border range of Fukushima on the east. No coast here. The Uono River flows north between low hills on the west and the Echigo Sanzan peaks, Mount Hakkai among them, on the east, and the Shinano River winds through Tokamachi and Ojiya; in the east the mountains rise to Echigo-Komagatake and the deep Okutadami dam lake on the Fukushima border. This is some of the snowiest inhabited ground on earth: two or three meters on the valley floor is normal, streets run with snow-melt sprinklers, and houses stand on high concrete bases. Summers are hot and humid in the valley, cool on the ridges. Yuzawa is the gateway, the snow country of a famous novel, a town of onsen inns, high-rise resort condos and ski slopes, one of them with a gondola that starts at a shinkansen station. Minamiuonuma holds Muikamachi, Urasa and big ski areas such as Ishiuchi Maruyama; Urasa's Bishamon temple holds a naked pushing festival every March. Uonuma's Koide is the start of the Tadami Line into Aizu. Tokamachi is a kimono-weaving town with a big snow festival in February and buckwheat noodles served on wooden trays, and Ojiya breeds koi and weaves fine ramie cloth bleached on the snow; nearby Katakai fires one of the largest fireworks shells in the world in September. Uonuma Koshihikari is the most prized rice in Japan, and the local sake is famous. The Joetsu Shinkansen stops at Echigo-Yuzawa and Urasa, about seventy-five minutes from Tokyo and about two and a half hours from Musutafu; the Joetsu Line, Iiyama Line, Hokuhoku Line and Tadami Line spread out from the valley, and the Kan-etsu Expressway runs north from the long Kan-etsu Tunnel just south of Yuzawa. Visitors ski, soak, tour breweries, buy koi, hike Hakkai and Okutadami, and eat soba. Small hero offices in Yuzawa and Muikamachi work with police and ski patrols, and in winter licensed heroes with heat or wind Quirks help clear avalanche debris from the tracks.
Echigo-Yuzawa.hiddenInfo: Weekend ski crowds bring petty theft, drunken tourists at lodges and backcountry skiers lost or buried in avalanches. Bubble-era resort condos sit half empty and cheap, drawing squatters and quiet trouble. Prized koi worth fortunes make Ojiya ponds a target for thieves. Hero help: small offices at Yuzawa and Muikamachi plus seasonal rescue staff; the Okutadami and Fukushima border wilderness is hours from anyone. Larger cases bring in Nagaoka or Niigata responders, an hour or more off.

Minamiaizu.name: Minamiaizu
Minamiaizu.basicInfo: The deep mountains of southern Aizu, a block of forested ridges and narrow valleys on the Fukushima-Tochigi border where the Kanto plain finally gives way to snow country. Most of the cell is the town of Minamiaizu and the village of Hinoemata on the Fukushima side; its southern strip belongs to Tochigi, where the hot spring hamlets of Yunishigawa, Kawamata and Okukinu sit at the head of the Kinu valley. In the southwest corner the volcanic dome of Mount Hiuchigatake, the highest peak in Tohoku, rises over the marsh lake of Ozenuma, with Aizu-Komagatake just to its northeast and the wide Oze moor just over the western edge. The Ina river runs north through Tajima, the old post town at the district's center, and the Tadami river cuts the far northwest past big hydroelectric dams. Winters are long and white, with two meters of snow on the western villages; summers are cool, skunk cabbage blooms in Oze in early summer, and October sets the beech slopes alight. People farm buckwheat, summer tomatoes and rice on the valley floors, cut timber, run inns, and keep a few ski slopes going near Takatsue. Thatched L-shaped farmhouses still stand in the Maezawa hamlet of Tateiwa, Hinoemata villagers stage their own kabuki on a thatched shrine stage in spring and late summer, and Yunishigawa keeps its legend of fugitive Heike warriors with fish grilled around sunken hearths and a June festival. The Aizu Railway runs north from Aizu-Kogen-Ozeguchi through Tajima toward Aizu-Wakamatsu; at Aizu-Kogen it joins the Yagan Railway down to Kinugawa, and through limited expresses come all the way from Asakusa. Route 121 follows the same valley, Route 352 climbs west to Hinoemata and the Oze trailheads and closes over the pass in winter, and buses are few. From Tokyo, Tajima is about three and a half hours; from Musutafu, most of five. Visitors hike Oze, soak, ski, eat hatto buckwheat dumplings and Aizu soba, and watch village kabuki. There is no hero agency here: officers at residential police posts and a licensed hero who covers the whole mountain district from a larger town answer the calls, and a farmer whose Quirk throws off heat keeps the farmhouse path clear on private land.
Minamiaizu.hiddenInfo: The villages are emptying: schools have closed, half the houses on some lanes stay shut all winter, and the few young adults who remain carry the snow clearing, the volunteer fire brigade and the festivals. Asian black bears come down to the persimmons and corn in autumn. In a blizzard or on the closed passes, real hero help is an hour or more away, so residents lean on each other and on the police posts. Trouble is small: theft from empty holiday homes, strangers stripping wild vegetables and mushrooms from private forest, and the odd thrill-seeker using an unlicensed Quirk on backcountry ski slopes.

Nasu.name: Nasu
Nasu.basicInfo: The Nasu highlands and the old Shirakawa gateway, a cell of volcano, plateau and rolling farmland across the Tochigi-Fukushima border where the road to the north once passed the Shirakawa barrier. In the west the Nasu volcanoes, with smoking Chausudake at their head, rise above the resort town of Nasu and the hot spring village of Nasu-Yumoto, where the Sesshoseki, the legendary killing stone, lies in a sulfur-yellow gully. South of them the plain of Nasushiobara spreads around Kuroiso and its shinkansen station, and the Shiobara gorge hides a string of riverside inns on the Hoki river along the western edge. The Fukushima side holds Shirakawa, a castle town with the rebuilt keep of Komine castle and its own ramen, the site of the ancient barrier just south of it, the mountain village of Nishigo where the Abukuma river rises, Yabuki, and Hatori lake in Ten'ei to the north. In the northwest corner the thatched post town of Ouchi-juku lines one wide street in Shimogo, and the eroded cliffs of Tonohetsuri stand over the Okawa river. Winter is cold and dry on the plain and snowy in the hills; summers are cool enough that wealthy families have kept villas here for a century, and the imperial family keeps one too. Dairy is the heart of the economy, along with rice, resort tourism, ski slopes, and the factories of the Tohoku corridor. The Tohoku Shinkansen stops at Nasushiobara and Shin-Shirakawa, the Tohoku main line and the Tohoku Expressway run beside it, and buses climb from Kuroiso to the highlands. Tokyo is about seventy minutes away by shinkansen, Musutafu about two and a half hours. Visitors ride the ropeway up Chausudake, soak in sulfur baths, drink fresh milk and eat soft-serve at highland farms, visit animal parks, art museums and the outlet mall, and walk Ouchi-juku eating soba with a whole leek in place of chopsticks. A small hero agency in Nasushiobara covers the resort strip with the police, and in high summer its sidekicks spend most days on traffic, lost hikers and crowd control, while a rancher whose Quirk calms skittish cattle is in demand at every livestock show.
Nasu.hiddenInfo: Two worlds share the cell: weekend resort Nasu with its villas, galleries and traffic jams, and dairy and rice villages aging fast, where farmers resent land sold off for vacation homes and solar fields. Volcanic gas closes trails near Chausudake now and then, and bears range the highland woods. The local agency is small and stretched across a wide district; backup from Utsunomiya or Koriyama is the better part of an hour away. Small villainy means villa break-ins in the off season, shoplifting at the outlets, and drunk tourists picking fights at hot spring inns.

Abukuma Highlands.name: Abukuma Highlands
Abukuma Highlands.basicInfo: The southern Abukuma Highlands and the inland half of Iwaki, a rolling upland of low granite hills, cedar plantations and small valley towns in southern Fukushima, running from the upper Abukuma river valley in the west to the edge of the Pacific coastal plain in the east. In the west lie the farm towns of Tanagura, Hanawa, Asakawa and Ishikawa along the Abukuma and its tributaries, with Fukushima Airport on its plateau near Tamakawa. The middle of the cell is quiet hill country: Samegawa, Furudono, Hirata and Ono, where the Natsui river runs through a gorge lined with a thousand cherry trees, and limestone caves open under the hills near the northern edge. In the east the land falls toward Iwaki, the biggest city on the Fukushima coast: its center, Taira, sits just inside the eastern edge, and Iwaki-Yumoto, an old coal-mining hot spring town, lies south of it beside a big indoor tropical spa resort famous for its hula dancers. Onahama's harbor sits on the southeastern corner. Winters are mild and dry by Tohoku standards, with little snow on the coast side and more in the hills; summers are humid and spring comes early. People farm rice, tobacco and vegetables, raise cattle, cut timber, quarry stone, and work in Iwaki's factories, port and offices. The Joban line and Joban Expressway reach Iwaki from Tokyo; the Ban'etsu East line and Ban'etsu Expressway cross the highlands west to Koriyama; the Suigun line runs north through Tanagura and Hanawa toward Koriyama and south toward Mito. Iwaki is about two and a half hours from Tokyo by limited express, so Musutafu is about three and a half. Visitors soak in Yumoto, eat Onahama fish and grilled mehikari, see the Natsui cherries and the caves, and watch the Jangara nembutsu dancers go house to house at Obon. Iwaki has a mid-sized hero agency and a full police headquarters; the hill towns rely on officers at residential posts and on patrols from Iwaki and Shirakawa, and a farmer whose Quirk reads the coming weather in the clouds sets the rice harvest dates for half the valley.
Abukuma Highlands.hiddenInfo: Iwaki is a working city that feels far from Tokyo's attention, and the highland towns behind it are aging and quiet, with shuttered shops along the old main streets. Long night drives on empty hill roads mean a crash or a stranded traveler may wait a long time. Iwaki's agency is the nearest real hero help for most of the cell, half an hour to an hour from the western towns. Small-time villainy: copper and cable theft from idle quarries and solar farms, illegal dumping in the hills, drunken brawls in Taira's nightlife district, and Quirk-fueled street racing on the expressway.

Iwaki Coast.name: Iwaki Coast
Iwaki Coast.basicInfo: The northern Iwaki shore and the coast of Futaba district, a thin strip of beaches, low cliffs and river-mouth towns along the Pacific in Fukushima, with almost all of the cell open sea. The land is the narrow shelf of coast between the Abukuma hills to the west and the water: from Onahama's harbor mouth on the southwest edge, the shore runs north past the white tower of Shioyasaki lighthouse on its headland, the surf beaches of Usuiso and Toyoma, the fishing town of Yotsukura with its busy roadside fish market, then Hisanohama and Suetsugi, the town of Hirono with its tall power station stacks, Naraha with the national soccer training center at J-Village, and the cherry tunnel of Yonomori in Tomioka at the northern edge. Tall seawalls line much of the shore. Everything east of the beach is the Pacific, a shelf of green-gray water darkening to deep blue offshore. The climate is the mildest in Fukushima: little snow, cool misty days in early summer when the cold Oyashio sends sea fog ashore, and clear, windy winters. People fish from small ports for flounder, monkfish, whitebait and sea urchin, farm rice on the coastal flats, work at the power stations and in Iwaki, and run a few surf shops and inns. The Joban line runs up the coast through Yotsukura, Hisanohama, Hirono and Tatsuta; Route 6 and the Joban Expressway run parallel just inland. Iwaki station is a short ride south, Tokyo about two and a half to three hours, and Musutafu about four. Visitors surf Toyoma, climb the lighthouse at Shioyasaki, eat grilled fish and sea urchin baked in the shell at Yotsukura, walk under the Yonomori cherries in April, and watch national team training at J-Village. Heroes from the Iwaki agency patrol the beaches in summer and the Obon festivals in August, police stations sit in the larger towns, and a fisher whose Quirk lets them hear shoals moving under the hull is the most sought-after crew member in Yotsukura.
Iwaki Coast.hiddenInfo: The coast towns feel forgotten between Iwaki and the cities to the north: fishing crews are aging, prices are argued over with buyers in the city, and many young adults leave for Tokyo. Sea fog and winter wind make the small harbors dangerous. Real hero help comes from Iwaki, twenty to forty minutes south by road, or from the coast guard at Onahama. Small trouble looks like night poaching of sea urchin and abalone, fuel theft from moored boats, and tourists swept off the rocks.

Sea off Oki Dozen.name: Sea off Oki Dozen
Sea off Oki Dozen.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of the Dozen islands of Oki, deep blue water that falls away from the island shelf past a hundred meters toward the deeper basin to the north. The warm Tsushima Current flows northeast through here and keeps the water clear and mild. In summer the sea is calm and glassy; in winter the northwest monsoon piles up gray swells and snow squalls that stop the island ferries for days. On clear days the cliffs of Nishinoshima's Kuniga coast and the hills of Nakanoshima stand low on the southern horizon, with Dogo's ridges farther to the southeast. These are squid grounds: on summer nights lamp boats out of Urago and Beppu hang strings of bright lights over the water, visible from the island clifftops, and longliners and small trawlers chase yellowtail, mackerel and flying fish. There are no islands inside the cell and no ferry route crosses it, only fishing boats and the occasional coastal freighter. The Japan Coast Guard patrols from its Oki station at Saigo and its Sakaiminato office, and the licensed hero who covers the Dozen islands can be raised by radio. A party could be out here aboard a chartered fishing boat from Nishinoshima, crewing a squid boat for a night, or riding with a flying or swimming hero.
Sea off Oki Dozen.hiddenInfo: The fishing grounds are quietly contested: boats from outside the area sometimes slip in to fish, and the island fleets resent it. Help is far, an hour or more by patrol boat from Saigo and longer from Sakaiminato, and in winter storms rescue may simply wait until the weather breaks. Small villainy out here is illegal fishing, dumped gear and the odd stolen boat.

Sea off Oki Dogo.name: Sea off Oki Dogo
Sea off Oki Dogo.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of Dogo, the largest of the Oki Islands, where the island's northern capes and the white islets of the Shirashima coast stand on the southern horizon. The water is deep and clear blue, dropping from the island shelf to well past a hundred meters, with the warm Tsushima Current running northeast. Summers are calm and bright, autumn brings typhoon swells, and winter brings the northwest monsoon, short steep seas and snow, with whole days when nothing small puts out from the island ports. Fishing boats from Saigo and Dogo's northern hamlets work here for squid, sea bream, yellowtail and flying fish, and on summer nights the squid boats light the water in long rows. There are no islands inside the cell. Ships bound for Saigo come in from the south, so traffic is light: a few fishing boats and the occasional cargo ship passing up the coast. The coast guard patrols from Saigo and Sakaiminato, and the small hero agency on Dogo answers calls at sea by boat. A party might be out here on a charter boat from Saigo, working a night on a squid boat, or crossing by air with a flying hero.
Sea off Oki Dogo.hiddenInfo: The island fleets are aging and catches are thinner than they were, and anger at outside boats fishing the grounds runs high in the Dogo ports. Rescue in winter seas is slow and dangerous; the nearest help is the coast guard at Saigo, an hour or more away. Petty villainy is gear theft, poached catch and a boat taken from its mooring.

Sea off Kanazawa.name: Sea off Kanazawa
Sea off Kanazawa.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the Kaga coast of Ishikawa, the water west of Kanazawa. The city itself lies just beyond the eastern edge; the only land in the cell is a thin strip of sandy shore at its southeast corner, where the Hakusan coast runs south toward Komatsu. From out here the view east is a low line of dunes and pines, Kanazawa's port cranes and, for half the year, the white mass of Mount Hakusan. The water is shelf sea, mostly under two hundred meters, green near the beaches and darkening to blue farther out, with the Tsushima Warm Current running northeast along the coast. Summers are calm and hot, good for beaches and night squid fishing. Winters bring the northwest monsoon: steep gray waves, sleet, and the December thunder locals call buri-okoshi, the yellowtail-waker. Boats out of Kanazawa Port and the small Kaga harbors work for sweet shrimp, snow crab, yellowtail and squid, and the catch reaches Kanazawa's markets the same morning. Cruise ships and freighters call at Kanazawa Port. Coast guard boats patrol from Kanazawa, and the city's hero agencies keep a few members with water or flight Quirks for sea calls. A party could be on a fishing boat from Kanazawa, a cargo ship, or flying; Kanazawa is a little over three hours from Musutafu by shinkansen.
Sea off Kanazawa.hiddenInfo: The coast is quiet; trouble is the weather and the crowds. In winter, sudden squalls catch amateur anglers and small boats, and summer beach days bring rip currents and drownings along the Kaga shore. Now and then someone with a water Quirk tries to show off offshore and needs rescuing. The nearest hero help is in Kanazawa, half an hour to an hour away by boat or air.

Kanazawa.name: Kanazawa
Kanazawa.basicInfo: The heart of the Hokuriku coast, spanning Kanazawa, the Kahoku sand coast, the Takaoka and Tonami plains of western Toyama, and Himi on the shore of Toyama Bay. The west side of the region faces the open Sea of Japan along a long straight run of beach and dunes from Kanazawa past Uchinada to the hard sands of Chirihama, where cars drive along the waterline; the east side touches Toyama Bay at Himi and the Amaharashi coast, from which the Tateyama range rises white across the water. Between them run the low Hodatsu hills and the Kurikara pass on the Ishikawa-Toyama border, and in the southeast the Iozen mountains climb toward Gokayama. Winters are gray, wet and snowy with thunder off the sea; summers are hot and humid. Kanazawa is the old castle town of the Kaga domain, an elegant city of about half a million that escaped wartime bombing: Kenrokuen garden, the castle park, the Higashi Chaya teahouse district, samurai lanes in Nagamachi, the Omicho fish market, and the huge wooden gate in front of the station. It makes nearly all of Japan's gold leaf, Kaga yuzen silk and Kutani porcelain, and eats crab, nodoguro, jibuni duck stew, oden and thick curry; the Hyakumangoku festival fills June. Takaoka is a bronze-casting city with a great Buddha and a Zen temple of national-treasure halls; Himi is famous for winter yellowtail; Tonami's plain is dotted with farmhouses in windbreak groves and blooms with tulips each spring; Inami's woodcarvers and Yuwaku's hot springs lie in the hills. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Kanazawa and Shin-Takaoka; local railways, the Takaoka tram and the Himi and Johana lines fill in, and the Hokuriku, Noetsu and Tokai-Hokuriku expressways meet here. Komatsu Airport is just south. Kanazawa is about two hours from Shin-Osaka via Tsuruga, two and a half from Tokyo and about three and a half from Musutafu. Several hero agencies work Kanazawa, smaller offices cover Takaoka and Himi, and quieter Quirk work is everywhere, from gold-leaf beaters with steady hands to a fishmonger who chills crates with a touch.
Kanazawa.hiddenInfo: Kanazawa is prosperous and proud; the tensions are crowding in the old districts, rising rents, and old families who dislike outsiders. Kanazawa has solid hero and police coverage, Takaoka and Himi smaller offices, and Tonami's scattered farms rely on police boxes twenty minutes apart. Small-time villainy: pickpockets in Omicho and Higashi Chaya, gold-leaf and antique fraud, festival scuffles, street racing on the Chirihama beach road, and unlicensed Quirk use in the Katamachi nightlife.

Toyama.name: Toyama
Toyama.basicInfo: The Toyama Plain and the Tateyama range above it, from Shinminato in Imizu east along the bay coast to Kurobe, and south and east up the steep rivers into the Northern Alps. The north edge of the region is the shore of Toyama Bay; behind it a flat green plain of rice and towns rises abruptly into mountains that top three thousand meters within forty kilometers of the sea, so the Jinzu, Joganji and Kurobe rivers rank among the steepest in Japan. Winters bring heavy snow and gray skies; summers are hot on the plain and cool above the tree line. Toyama city, a prefectural capital of about four hundred thousand, is a tidy, rebuilt city of trams, canals and the Fugan canal park, known for its centuries-old tradition of traveling medicine peddlers and a pharmaceutical industry that still employs much of the city, for glass art, and for trout sushi pressed in round boxes, white shrimp and black ramen. Shinminato has fishing canals and a tall sailing ship moored in a park; Namerikawa is famous for spring firefly squid that glow blue in the nets at night; Uozu has spring mirages and an ancient buried forest; Kurobe has spring water bubbling up across its river fan. Yatsuo, on the southern edge, hosts the Owara Kaze no Bon in early September, when dancers move silently through lantern-lit streets to the sound of a bowed fiddle. Up the mountains, the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route climbs by cable car and bus past Shomyo Falls, the highest waterfall in Japan, to Murodo, where spring snow walls tower over the road; the rock spire of Tsurugi-dake and the shrine on Tateyama's summit stand on the eastern edge, and the Kurobe Gorge Railway rattles from Unazuki Onsen up a deep canyon. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Toyama and Kurobe-Unazukionsen; Toyama city is about two hours from Tokyo, three and a half from Musutafu and two and a half from Shin-Osaka, and the Hida limited express reaches Takayama in about ninety minutes. Toyama Airport has flights to Haneda. Several hero agencies work the city, and in season mountain rescue heroes and police rescuers are stationed at Murodo.
Toyama.hiddenInfo: The mountains kill more people than villains do: climbers slipping on Tsurugi-dake's chains, spring backcountry skiers, avalanches, rockfall and sudden summer storms on the ridges. Police rescuers and rescue heroes work from Murodo and Kamiichi; a call from the high peaks can take hours when helicopters are grounded. On the plain, trouble is ordinary: supplement fraud trading on the old medicine name, theft of scrap metal, fights in the city's bar streets, and firefly squid poaching.

Hakuba.name: Hakuba
Hakuba.basicInfo: The northern Northern Alps and the Hakuba valley, deep in western Nagano: from Kurobe Dam and its lake in the west, across the Ushiro-Tateyama and Hakuba ranges, to the valley towns of Hakuba, Otari and northern Omachi and the volcanic peaks of Togakushi, Kurohime and Myoko on the eastern edge. No coast. The Hakuba Sanzan, Shirouma, Goryu and Kashimayari, form a white wall nearly three thousand meters high above the valley, with the Himekawa river running north toward the Sea of Japan and the Takase and Kurobe rivers cutting deep gorges to the west. Winters bring huge snowfalls of dry powder and bitter cold; summers are cool, green and full of hikers, with alpine flowers on the ridges and the Hakuba snow gorge holding ice into August. Hakuba village is an international ski town with big resorts such as Happo-one and Tsugaike, the ski jumps from the Nagano Olympics, chalets, bars and bakeries run by newcomers alongside old farming families; summer brings paragliding, rafting and mountain biking. Omachi is a dam and spring-water town beside the three Nishina lakes, the Nagano gateway to the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, where an electric bus runs through the mountain to Kurobe Dam, whose spillway roars from summer into autumn. Togakushi, in the east, is a highland of old shrines, a cedar avenue centuries old, ninja lore and some of the best soba in Japan. The JR Oito Line runs Matsumoto to Shinano-Omachi and Hakuba and on to Minami-Otari and Itoigawa; express buses link Hakuba to Nagano Station in about seventy minutes and to Shinjuku in about five hours. From Musutafu it is about three and a half hours via Tokyo, the shinkansen to Nagano and the bus. Visitors ski, climb, soak in onsen, eat soba and oyaki, and ride the alpine route. A small hero office in Hakuba works with the police, ski patrols and licensed rescue sidekicks, many of them multilingual for the foreign crowd, and Quirks with snow or wind sense are prized on avalanche crews.
Hakuba.hiddenInfo: Hakuba's boom brings foreign money, soaring land prices, short-staffed resorts and friction between old farming families and new lodge owners. Out-of-bounds skiers and summer hikers on the snow gorge cause most rescues. Serious hero help is in Nagano or Matsumoto, an hour or more away; Hakuba and Omachi have small offices and winter rescue leans on ski patrols and police. Villainy: theft from lodges and rental shops, drunken tourists, drug dealing in resort bars, and unlicensed Quirk stunts on the slopes.

Nagano.name: Nagano
Nagano.basicInfo: Northern Nagano and the high volcanic country on the Gunma border: the Zenkoji Plain around Nagano city, the apple towns of the Chikuma River valley, the Shiga highlands, and over the Shibu pass the hot spring town of Kusatsu in Gunma. No coast. The Chikuma River runs northeast through a wide basin of orchards, rice and towns toward Iiyama and the Niigata border; to the east the land climbs into the Shiga Kogen plateau, Mount Kusatsu-Shirane and the cabbage fields of Tsumagoi, and to the northwest lie Lake Nojiri and the ski fields of Madarao and Myoko Kogen at the corner. Winters are cold and snowy, heavy in the north; summers are warm in the basin and cool on the plateaus. Nagano city, the prefectural capital of under four hundred thousand, grew up around Zenkoji, a great temple whose stand-in for its hidden Buddha image is displayed every seven years and whose lane is lined with inns and souvenir shops; Matsushiro to the south is an old castle town. Obuse is a chestnut and art town, Suzaka and Nakano grow grapes and mushrooms, Iiyama makes Buddhist altars and gets buried in snow. Yamanouchi holds Yudanaka and Shibu Onsen with their wooden inns and the steaming valley where snow monkeys bathe, and above it Shiga Kogen's ski fields. Kusatsu, over the pass, is one of Japan's most famous onsen, its sulfurous water cooled in a steaming wooden channel in the town square and stirred with long paddles in traditional song. Food: apples, oyaki, Shinshu soba, nozawana pickles. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Nagano and Iiyama; Nagano is about eighty minutes from Tokyo and about two and a half hours from Musutafu. The Nagaden line runs to Yudanaka, the Shinano Railway north to Myoko Kogen, the Iiyama Line up the Chikuma, and the Joshin-etsu Expressway crosses the basin; Kusatsu is reached by bus from Naganohara or Karuizawa. Visitors come for Zenkoji, the monkeys, skiing, onsen and orchard fruit picking. Nagano city has several hero agencies; smaller offices and police cover the towns, and orchard families with growth or weather-sense Quirks are common at harvest.
Nagano.hiddenInfo: Nagano city is orderly and conservative; the tensions are aging orchard families, depopulating hill villages and the volcanoes, whose gas warnings close the Shiga-Kusatsu road. Nagano city has real hero coverage; Yamanouchi, Kusatsu and Iiyama rely on small offices and police thirty minutes to an hour out. Villainy: fruit theft at harvest, scams on elderly residents, pickpockets at Zenkoji, ski-lodge theft, bar fights in the city's arcades.

Deika.name: Deika
Deika.basicInfo: Deika is mountain country about 100 kilometers northwest of Tokyo, where river valleys cut between forested ridges of cedar, beech and pine. Deika City fills a wide valley in the south of the region: a clean, prosperous city whose newer districts grew around the offices and plants of Detnerat, the support-equipment maker that owns much of its land and employs most of its people, from factory hands to designers of hero gear and everyday aids for people whose Quirks make ordinary life hard. Northwest of the city rises Gunga Mountain, its upper slopes private land with few roads; a private villa sits high on it about 18 km north-northwest of the city, behind a locked gate. The region's southeastern edge runs down to the outskirts of Jaku, the neighboring city about 14 km from Deika by rail, and there, about 4 km northeast of Jaku's station, stands Jaku General Hospital, the large general hospital that serves the whole district. Between the valleys lie rice terraces, orchards, old farming hamlets with wooden storehouses, hot-spring inns along the rivers and roadside stations selling soba and pickles; farther north the ridges climb toward the snow country and the high passes. Winters are cold, with snow on the ridges into April; spring comes late, the cherry trees bloom in mid-April, and summers are cooler than on the coast, with afternoon thunderstorms in the valleys. Residents are company employees, hospital staff, shopkeepers and old farming families, polite to visitors and slow to discuss their neighbors. Deika is famous for its low crime and its neighborhood associations, which settle disputes before anyone calls the police; anything serious brings in heroes from Jaku or from Hosu, about an hour away by train. Trains link Deika with Jaku, with Hosu in about an hour, with Tokyo in about an hour and a half and with Musutafu in about two and a half hours; buses climb into the hills, and anywhere above the valleys a car is a necessity. A visitor can take temporary work at Detnerat or the hospital, join a public factory tour, shop at Deika's evening market, soak in a valley hot spring, hike the ridges, or start asking why a town this content is so careful about strangers.
Deika.hiddenInfo: Under the polite surface, Deika belongs to the Meta Liberation Army, which the rest of Japan files under history: nearly everyone in the city is a member, Detnerat pays for it, and the neighborhood associations double as its eyes. Outsiders who ask questions are noticed within a day. Gunga Mountain's upper slopes are emptier than any map admits, and something moves in its deep ravines that the valley people have learned not to ask about. Even the respected old director of Jaku's hospital keeps one door locked.

Nikko.name: Nikko
Nikko.basicInfo: Nikko and the mountains around it, a cell of volcanic peaks, lakes and gorges in western Tochigi rising from the northern edge of the Kanto plain, with a corner of eastern Gunma on its western side. At the eastern foot, the town of Nikko holds the lacquer, gold and carved gates of Toshogu shrine, Rinnoji temple and Futarasan shrine in a forest of giant cedars, reached past the red Shinkyo bridge over the Daiya river; a long avenue of Edo-era cedars leads in from Imaichi. West of town the Irohazaka hairpin roads climb to Lake Chuzenji under the cone of Mount Nantai, where the Kegon falls drop nearly a hundred meters out of the lake; beyond lie the Senjogahara moor, the Yudaki falls and the sulfur springs of Yumoto, with Nikko-Shirane, the highest peak north of Kanto, on the Gunma line. North of Imaichi the Kinu river carves a gorge through the hot spring towns of Kinugawa and Kawaji, with an Edo-period theme town and a miniature world park nearby. In the southwest the old copper town of Ashio sits in its narrow valley, and Kanuma spreads over the plain in the southeast. Summers are cool and wet with afternoon thunder, autumn color comes early and works down from the lake, and winters bring snow in the mountains and frozen waterfalls. People live on tourism, inns and crafts, on rice, strawberries and buckwheat, and in Kanuma on timber, the light soil used for bonsai, and azaleas. Tobu limited expresses run from Asakusa to Nikko and Kinugawa in about two hours; from Tokyo the shinkansen to Utsunomiya and the JR Nikko line take a little under two; from Musutafu allow about three. A steam train runs the Kinugawa line, and the Nikko-Utsunomiya road brings the cars. Visitors tour the shrines, ride the ropeway at Akechidaira, boat on Chuzenji, eat yuba and shaved ice made from natural pond ice, and catch the thousand-samurai procession in spring or Kanuma's carved festival floats in October. A small hero agency in Nikko and sidekicks loaned from Utsunomiya keep the crowds moving, and a park ranger whose Quirk follows scent trails finds lost hikers on Nantai.
Nikko.hiddenInfo: Nikko lives and dies by tourists: weekends jam the Irohazaka roads, inns compete hard, and some of the older hot spring hotels in Kinugawa stand empty and decaying. Monkeys raid snack stands, and bears and deer roam the lake district; winter storms close the high roads. Real help is close in town but slow in the mountains, and Utsunomiya is about forty minutes away. Small villainy: pickpockets and offering-box thieves at the shrines, night racing on the hairpin roads, and squatters and vandals in the abandoned hotels.

Utsunomiya.name: Utsunomiya
Utsunomiya.basicInfo: Utsunomiya and the eastern Tochigi plain, a cell of rice paddies, orchards and low wooded hills centered on Tochigi's capital in the middle of the northern Kanto plain. Utsunomiya fills the southwest of the cell, a busy city with covered shopping arcades, a castle park, a big shrine on a hill in the center, and a new light rail line running east to the factory parks and Haga. Just west of the city, in the Oya valley, soft green-gray Oya stone has been quarried for centuries, leaving cathedral-sized underground galleries and a Buddha carved into the cliff. North along the Kinu river and the Tohoku main line lie Yaita, Sakura and Otawara, with the Nasu plain opening beyond; east lie the Naka valley towns of Nasukarasuyama and Bato and the hills around Motegi, home to a motorsport circuit; the pottery town of Mashiko sits on the southern edge. The climate is continental for Kanto: hot, humid summers with afternoon thunderstorms that roll off the mountains, and cold, dry winters with a sharp north wind. Utsunomiya is known for gyoza, served in dozens of shops and argued over; for jazz bars and cocktail lounges; and for cycling, with a big road race every autumn. Around it the land grows rice, strawberries, nashi pears and kanpyo gourd strips, and the industrial parks build cars, aircraft parts and electronics. The Tohoku Shinkansen reaches Utsunomiya from Tokyo in about fifty minutes, so Musutafu is about two hours away; the Utsunomiya line, the Karasuyama line, the Tohoku Expressway and the Kita-Kanto Expressway cross the cell, and buses fill the gaps. Visitors eat gyoza, tour the Oya quarry galleries, throw pots at Mashiko, watch the July Yamaage festival in Karasuyama, where townspeople raise painted mountain scenery in the street for open-air kabuki, and fish for ayu on the Naka river. Utsunomiya has several hero agencies and the prefectural police headquarters; outlying towns have smaller offices and police boxes, and a gyoza cook whose Quirk crisps a whole pan in seconds keeps the lunch line moving.
Utsunomiya.hiddenInfo: Utsunomiya is comfortable and a little proud, with a gyoza rivalry with Hamamatsu that locals take half seriously. Beneath that, the outlying farm towns are aging and the factory parks run on long shifts and short-term contracts. Hero coverage is good in the city and thin in the eastern hills, thirty to forty minutes out. Small villainy: bicycle theft and bag snatching in the station district, Quirk brawls outside bars at closing time, strawberry and fruit theft from greenhouses, and phone scams aimed at the elderly.

Hitachi.name: Hitachi
Hitachi.basicInfo: The northern Ibaraki coast and the Kuji river hill country behind it, a cell where the southern Abukuma and Yamizo hills come down toward a rocky Pacific shore, with the eastern third open sea. On the coast, from north to south, lie Kitaibaraki with its fishing harbors of Otsu and Hirakata and the rocky coves of Izura, where a small red hexagonal hall perches on the rocks; Takahagi; and the long industrial city of Hitachi, which grew from a copper mine in the hills into a town of electrical machinery works, with a glass-walled station concourse that hangs over the sea. Tokai village lies on the southern edge. Inland, the Kuji river valley holds the old town of Hitachi-Ota with its merchant streets and the Ryujin gorge with its long suspension bridge, while Hitachi-Omiya and the town of Daigo sit near the western edge, where Fukuroda falls drops in four tiers and freezes white in a hard winter. The hills grow cedar, chestnuts and tea, the valleys rice and buckwheat. The climate is mild, with cool sea fog in early summer, little snow, and dry, bright winters. People work in Hitachi's factories, fish for monkfish, flounder and whitebait, farm and raise cattle for Hitachi beef, and run inns and seafood restaurants. The Joban line runs along the coast and the Suigun line up the Kuji valley toward Daigo and Fukushima; the Joban Expressway and Route 6 run just inland. Hitachi is about an hour and a half from Tokyo by limited express, so Musutafu is about three hours away. Visitors eat monkfish hotpot at Otsu in winter, walk Izura's cliffs, cross the Ryujin bridge in autumn color, stand under Fukuroda falls, and eat Hitachi-Ota soba and fall chestnut sweets. Hitachi has a mid-sized hero agency near the station that patrols the factory belt with the police, a small office in Kitaibaraki covers the northern harbors, and on the factory floors workers whose Quirks let them handle hot or heavy parts are prized hires.
Hitachi.hiddenInfo: Hitachi is a company town without the swagger it once had: younger workers leave, the downtown arcades are quiet, and the coast towns depend on a shrinking fleet. Industrial accidents and fires are a standing worry along the factory belt. Real hero help is minutes away in Hitachi city and half an hour from the inland valleys. Small villainy: metal and tool theft from plants, night poaching of shellfish, drug sales among bored shift workers, and unlicensed Quirk use in late-night street fights near the station.

Sea off Kitaibaraki.name: Sea off Kitaibaraki
Sea off Kitaibaraki.basicInfo: The open Pacific off northern Ibaraki and southern Fukushima, from about ten to sixty kilometers out from the rocky shore of Kitaibaraki, Takahagi and Hitachi. The water is green-gray near the coast and turns deep blue over the slope offshore, where the bottom drops from about a hundred meters to several hundred and more. Here the cold Oyashio from the north meets warm Kuroshio water, so the sea is rich, often foggy in early summer, and rough with northwest gales in winter. Boats from Otsu, Hirakata, Hitachi and Onahama work the grounds for monkfish, flounder, mackerel, sardines and whitebait. Overnight car ferries between Oarai and Hokkaido and cargo ships out of Hitachi and Onahama pass through, and on a clear day the low coast and Hitachi's factory stacks show to the west. The coast guard runs patrol boats out of Onahama and the Ibaraki ports, and maritime heroes ride out with the fishing fleet in storms. A party could be out here on a ferry, a chartered fishing boat, or carried by a flying hero.
Sea off Kitaibaraki.hiddenInfo: Fishers here argue with buyers and regulators over quotas and prices, and boats sometimes stray into each other's grounds. Fog brings near-collisions with cargo ships. Real help is the coast guard, an hour or more out from port. Petty crime is fuel and catch theft and illegal dumping from passing ships.

Sea west of Oki.name: Sea west of Oki
Sea west of Oki.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan west of the Dozen islands of Oki, where the water runs empty from Nishinoshima's western cliffs to the horizon. On clear days the sheer red walls of the Kuniga coast and the Matengai cliff stand on the eastern horizon, and from the southern part of the cell the hills of the Shimane Peninsula are faint to the southeast. The water is deep blue and clear, mostly one to two hundred meters deep over the continental shelf, with the warm Tsushima Current pushing northeast. Weather swings with the season: calm, hazy summers, autumn typhoon swells, and winter monsoon gales from the northwest that build long heavy seas. Fishing boats from Nishinoshima and the Shimane coast work here for squid, sea bream, horse mackerel and flying fish, and trawlers out of Hamada and Sakaiminato pass through. No islands lie inside the cell and no ferry route crosses it. The coast guard watches the area from Sakaiminato and Hamada, and the licensed hero covering the Dozen islands is the nearest hero help. A party might be out here on a fishing charter from Nishinoshima, on a long sea-kayak crossing in fair weather, or flying across.
Sea west of Oki.hiddenInfo: This is the empty side of the islands, so trouble out here goes unseen: boats from outside fishing where they should not, drifting wreckage and derelict hulls carried in by the current, a boater lost in fog. Help is hours away by patrol boat. Villainy is rare and petty.

Oki Dozen.name: Oki Dozen
Oki Dozen.basicInfo: The Dozen islands of the Oki archipelago, three steep volcanic islands ringing a sheltered inner bay about fifty kilometers off the Shimane coast in the Sea of Japan, with a sliver of Dogo's western shore inside the eastern edge. Nishinoshima, the largest, lies to the west, Nakanoshima lies to the east, and little Chiburijima sits to the south, its southern tip just across the line in the Oki Strait. Together they are the broken rim of an old caldera, and the inner sea between them stays calm even when the outer coast is white with surf. On Nishinoshima's western side the Kuniga coast drops in sheer red and gray cliffs, the Matengai wall rising about 250 meters straight from the sea, with the rock arch of Tsutenkyo below and cattle and horses grazing the grass on top. Winters are gray and wind-battered, with the northwest monsoon cutting the islands off for days; summers are clear, warm and blue. A few thousand people live across the three islands in small harbor villages: Ama on Nakanoshima, Beppu and Urago on Nishinoshima, Chibu on Chiburijima. They fish for squid and turban shells, farm rock oysters in the bays, raise Oki beef on the hill pastures and run family inns for summer visitors. Nakanoshima holds Oki Shrine, raised where an exiled medieval emperor spent his last years, and Nishinoshima's Takuhi Shrine is built into a cliff face on the slope of Mount Takuhi. There is no bridge to the mainland. Car ferries from Shichirui on the Shimane Peninsula and from Sakaiminato take two to three hours, the jetfoil about an hour, and a small ferry hops between the Dozen ports. From Musutafu the trip is most of a day: shinkansen to Okayama, the limited express north to Matsue or Yonago, then the boat; from Osaka it is about five hours. Each island has a resident police officer's post, and a single licensed hero covers the whole Dozen group from Nishinoshima, crossing between islands by boat. Quirks here are practical and quiet: a fisher who reads the swell by feel, a herder whose call carries across a whole pasture.
