Visitors cycle, swim in the inner bay, ride boats to the sea caves, hike the Kuniga clifftops and eat oyster rice at harbor counters.
Oki Dozen.hiddenInfo: The islands are aging and shrinking, and every family weighs whether its young adults should leave for school and work on the mainland; incomers who come for island life are welcomed but watched. The one hero covering the Dozen is stretched thin, and in bad winter weather the ferries and jetfoil stop, so real help from Matsue or the coast guard can be a day away. Villainy is small: poached abalone and turban shells, a rented boat or bicycle taken, a drunk with a strength Quirk at a harbor party, an unlicensed fixer who moves goods between islands with a Quirk and asks no questions.

Oki Dogo.name: Oki Dogo
Oki Dogo.basicInfo: Dogo, the largest and roundest island of the Oki archipelago, sitting alone in the Sea of Japan some sixty kilometers north of the Shimane Peninsula, with open water filling the rest of the cell. A sliver of Dogo's western shore lies across the line in the Dozen cell. The island is about twenty kilometers across, a dome of forested hills cut by short rivers, with rice in the valley floors and cedar on the slopes. Saigo, the port town on the southeast shore, holds most of the island's people: the ferry terminal, a shopping street, schools, the hospital and inns along the harbor. Oki Airport lies just south of town, with flights to Izumo and Osaka. Around the coast are fishing hamlets and rock shores: the eroded pale rock of the Jodogaura coast in the east, the white islets of the Shirashima coast in the north, and off the northwest shore the candle rock of Rosokujima, where sightseeing boats line up at sunset so the sun sits on its tip like a flame. Inland stand great cedars: the Yao cedar at Tamawakasu Shrine near Saigo, and the ancient Chichi cedar on a mossy hillside in the northeast. Dannu Falls drops behind a small shrine in the western hills. Dogo is known for its bull sumo, where two bulls lock horns in a ring before a cheering crowd, for Oki beef, squid dried on racks, and the black obsidian that islanders traded to the mainland in prehistory. The whole archipelago is a UNESCO Global Geopark. Winter northwest gales bring snow squalls and stop the ferries. The car ferry from Shichirui or Sakaiminato takes about two and a half hours, the jetfoil about an hour, and the flight from Izumo about half an hour; from Musutafu the trip is most of a day, by shinkansen to Okayama and the limited express to Matsue or Yonago, then sea or air. Saigo has a police station and one small local hero agency that covers the whole island by car and boat, with a sidekick posted at bull sumo days and the summer festivals. Fishers use Quirks to read currents or haul nets, and cattle farmers to calm a nervous bull. Visitors rent cars or bicycles, ride the coast boats, swim at the northern beaches and walk the geopark trails.
Oki Dogo.hiddenInfo: Dogo is the archipelago's hub, so its troubles are everyone's: a shrinking working population, a hospital short of doctors, and young adults leaving after their school years. Summer geopark crowds bring money and friction. The island's one agency is small and knows everyone; real backup comes by jetfoil or helicopter from Matsue or Yonago, an hour or more away, and in winter storms not at all. Villainy runs to fishing-gear theft, poaching in the shellfish beds, a drunken brawl after bull sumo, and now and then a mainland fugitive hoping an island is far enough.

Sea east of Oki.name: Sea east of Oki
Sea east of Oki.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan between the Oki island of Dogo to the west and the Tottori and Tajima coasts to the south and southeast. Dogo's eastern hills stand on the western horizon on clear days, and nothing else breaks the water. Here the sea falls away from the island shelf toward the deep Oki Trough, so the water is dark blue and cold beneath the warm surface current that runs northeast. Weather follows the seasons: calm summers, typhoon swells in early autumn, and winter monsoon gales with snow and heavy seas. The slopes of the trough are snow crab grounds, worked from late autumn to spring by trawlers from Tottori, Sakaiminato and Hyogo's Tajima ports, and squid boats light the water on summer nights. No ferry crosses the cell; the Oki ferries run to the west. The coast guard patrols from Sakaiminato and Saigo, and a maritime hero covering the San'in coast answers calls. A party could be out here aboard a crab trawler in season, a charter out of Tottori or Saigo, or flying across.
Sea east of Oki.hiddenInfo: Crab is valuable and the quota rules are strict, so arguments over grounds and illegal catch are the main tension between ports. In winter storms help is far and slow, hours by patrol boat. Villainy is crab poaching at sea and mislabeling at the landing.

Sea off Tajima.name: Sea off Tajima
Sea off Tajima.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the coast of Hyogo's Tajima district, with the coastal mountains above Kasumi, Shibayama and Kinosaki rising faintly on the southern horizon on clear days. The water is deep blue over the continental shelf and its outer slopes, cold below and warmed at the surface by the Tsushima Current flowing northeast. Summers are calm and hazy; winters bring northwest gales, snow and steep gray seas. These are some of the best snow crab grounds in Japan: from November to March the trawlers of Kasumi, Shibayama and Tsuiyama work the slopes for matsuba crab, and in spring the same boats haul firefly squid and flatfish. On summer nights squid boats hang lamps over the water. No islands lie inside the cell, and only fishing boats and a few coastal freighters cross it. The coast guard patrols from its offices along the Tajima and Tango shore, and a maritime hero covering that coast answers calls. A party might be out here on a crab trawler in season, a charter from Kasumi, or flying over.
Sea off Tajima.hiddenInfo: The crab is worth a great deal, so the tension is over quotas, poaching and mislabeled catch at market, and the ports compete fiercely for buyers. In winter storms rescue is slow and dangerous; the nearest help is the coast guard and a hero on the coast, an hour or more away. Villainy is poaching and small-scale smuggling.

Sea off Tango.name: Sea off Tango
Sea off Tango.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of the Tango Peninsula, off Kyoto Prefecture's only coastline. There is no land inside it; to the south the peninsula's cliffs and the white lighthouse on Cape Kyoga stand out on clear days, and the Tajima coast of Hyogo runs off to the southwest. The water is shelf sea, one to a few hundred meters deep, a clean deep blue in summer and slate gray in winter, carried northeast by the Tsushima Warm Current. Summer is mostly calm, with squid boats lighting the horizon at night. From November the northwest monsoon takes over, with heavy swells, snow showers and gales that close the small harbors for days. These are snow crab grounds: boats from Taiza and Kasumi go out for the November-to-March season, and Taiza crab carries a tag of its own in Kyoto markets. Flatfish, squid and yellowtail are caught year-round. The overnight car ferry from Maizuru to Otaru in Hokkaido heads north through these waters. The Japan Coast Guard's regional headquarters for this coast is at Maizuru, and ships from the Maritime Self-Defense Force base there pass through on exercises. A party could be aboard the Hokkaido ferry, on a crab boat out of Taiza, or carried by a flying hero; the Tango coast is about two and a half hours from Shin-Osaka, and close to five from Musutafu.
Sea off Tango.hiddenInfo: Crab season brings the only real friction: poaching boats working closed grounds at night, and crews squabbling over tags and quotas. The naval and coast guard presence at Maizuru keeps serious smuggling rare. A rescue out here is an hour or more for a patrol boat; the nearest hero agencies are in Maizuru and Toyooka, with few sea-capable members.

Sea off Echizen.name: Sea off Echizen
Sea off Echizen.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the Echizen coast of Fukui Prefecture, west of Fukui city and north of the mouth of Wakasa Bay. No land falls inside it; the Echizen coast's dark cliffs lie just past the eastern edge, with Cape Echizen near the southeast corner and the columnar andesite cliffs of Tojinbo farther north. The water is shelf sea, a hundred to a few hundred meters deep, blue-green inshore and deep blue offshore, carried northeast by the Tsushima Warm Current. Summer is calm and clear; in some late summers and autumns, giant drifting jellyfish come in on the current and foul nets for weeks. Winter belongs to the northwest monsoon, with gray swells breaking white against the cliffs and wild narcissus blooming on the slopes above. This is the home water of Echizen crab, the prized male snow crab landed with a yellow tag at Echizen and Mikuni harbors from November to March, and of sweet shrimp, flatfish and squid. Long-distance car ferries from Tsuruga to Niigata and Hokkaido pass through. The coast guard works out of Tsuruga and Fukui, and Fukui's hero agencies cover the coast with a handful of members who can fly or swim long distances. A party could be on a ferry deck, a crab boat out of Echizen harbor, or in the air; Fukui is about two and a half hours from Musutafu.
Sea off Echizen.hiddenInfo: Crab season is serious money, and catches sometimes change hands quietly at sea to dodge quotas. Jellyfish years ruin nets and tempers, and crews blame each other. Beyond that the sea is quiet: weather and accidents are the real danger, and hero help from Fukui or Tsuruga takes an hour or so.

Fukui.name: Fukui
Fukui.basicInfo: The northern Fukui plain and the Kaga hot-spring country across the Ishikawa line, a broad rice basin between the Sea of Japan to the west and the snowy foothills of Mount Hakusan to the east. The western half of the cell is open sea; the shore runs north past Tojinbo's columnar andesite cliffs and the old port of Mikuni at the mouth of the Kuzuryu River, then along the sandy Kaga coast toward Komatsu. Inland, the Kuzuryu, Asuwa and Hino rivers water a flat patchwork of paddies, with Fukui city, the prefectural capital, in the middle: a tidy town around an old castle moat, with department stores, a small tram line and dinosaur statues outside the station. North of it lie Maruoka, with one of Japan's oldest surviving castle keeps; Awara's hot-spring inns; and, over the border, the Kaga spa towns of Yamashiro and Yamanaka, with Komatsu and its airport on the plain beyond. In the eastern hills the Zen head temple of Eiheiji sits among towering cedars, monks sweeping its corridors at dawn, and farther up the valley at Katsuyama a great dinosaur museum stands near real fossil beds. Summers are humid and hot, winters gray, wet and heavy with snow. People farm rice, weave synthetic textiles, make Kutani porcelain around Komatsu and Nomi, and run inns. Food is Echizen crab in winter, grated-radish soba, sauce katsudon and sweet shrimp. The Hokuriku Shinkansen runs north-south through Komatsu, Kaga-Onsen, Awara-Onsen and Fukui, with the Hokuriku Expressway beside it and the Echizen Railway fanning into the valleys. Musutafu is about two and a half hours away by way of Maibara and Tsuruga, Shin-Osaka under two. Fukui and Komatsu have small hero agencies and police boxes on the main streets; licensed heroes cover the mountain valleys by car in winter, and snow-clearing crews often include someone with a heat or strength Quirk working under permit.
Fukui.hiddenInfo: Fukui is quiet and comfortable, and its worries are depopulation and snow. In heavy winters roads close, elderly residents get cut off in the hills, and rooftop-shoveling accidents keep local heroes busy. Small-time crime is copper and crop theft, onsen-town pickpockets and drunken fights in the Katamachi bar district. Serious incidents pull hero help in by shinkansen from Kanazawa or Osaka, an hour or more away.

Shirakawa-go.name: Shirakawa-go
Shirakawa-go.basicInfo: Deep mountain country where Ishikawa, Gifu and Toyama meet, around the sacred peak of Mount Haku and the Shokawa River valley. No coast and almost no flat land: the Ryohaku mountains rise in steep forested ranks, Hakusan's summit cones reaching about twenty-seven hundred meters in the southwest, while the Shokawa winds north through gorges and dam lakes past Shirakawa village and the Gokayama hamlets toward the Toyama plain. To the west the upper Tedori River runs down past Shiramine and Torigoe toward Tsurugi, home of the head shrine of the Hakusan faith. Snowfall is enormous, two meters or more in the valleys, and the villages are cut off by drifts in bad winters; summers are short and green with cool mornings, and autumn color fills the gorges. Shirakawa-go's Ogimachi and Gokayama's Ainokura and Suganuma are UNESCO World Heritage villages of gassho-zukuri farmhouses, steep thatched roofs built like praying hands, where families once raised silkworms and made saltpeter in the attics; some houses are still homes, others are inns, museums and noodle shops. On winter evenings the villages are lit up beneath the snow, and in autumn residents test the water cannons that protect the roofs from fire. Shirakawa's October Doburoku festival pours cloudy home-brewed sake, and Gokayama dances the Kokiriko with clapper sticks in September. Food is mountain food: hoba miso grilled on magnolia leaves, Hida beef, grilled char, firm Gokayama tofu, mountain vegetables and soba. The Tokai-Hokuriku Expressway tunnels through the range with exits at Shokawa, Shirakawa-go and Gokayama; the Hakusan White Road toll road crosses the mountains to Ishikawa from June to November. There is no railway: buses run to Takayama in about fifty minutes, Kanazawa in about seventy-five and Nagoya in about three hours. From Musutafu it is about four and a half hours via Nagoya, from Shin-Osaka about three and a half via Kanazawa. Visitors walk the villages, climb Hakusan as pilgrims have for centuries and sleep in thatched inns. There is no hero office; police boxes, the fire brigade and licensed heroes from Takayama or Kanazawa on call are all the protection here.
Shirakawa-go.hiddenInfo: Overtourism weighs on small resident communities: tour buses, trespassers in private homes, drones and litter. Fire is the nightmare for thatch, and visitors with fire Quirks are watched closely. No hero lives here; help from Takayama or Kanazawa is an hour or more by expressway, longer in snow. Trouble is small: theft from inns, illegal mountain-vegetable picking, bears on Hakusan trails and lost hikers.

Takayama.name: Takayama
Takayama.basicInfo: The Hida highlands of northern Gifu: the old merchant town of Takayama, Hida-Furukawa and Kamioka to the north, the Okuhida hot springs under the Northern Alps to the east, and the upper Jinzu valley climbing out of Toyama. No coast. This is a high basin ringed by mountains, with the Miya River running north through Takayama and Furukawa toward the Sea of Japan, and in the east the Okuhida valleys rising to the Hotaka and Kasagatake ridges and the volcanic dome of Norikura on the eastern edge. Winters are cold and snowy, summers mild, and autumn turns the hills red and gold. Takayama is a castle town of dark-timbered merchant houses in the Sanmachi lanes, sake breweries with cedar balls over their doors, and two morning markets by the river; it hosts the Takayama Festival in April and October, when gilded yatai floats with mechanical puppets parade through town. Hida carpenters, yew carvers and lacquerers still work here, and the town is known for Hida beef, soy-glazed dango, hoba miso and its soy-broth ramen. Furukawa is a quieter canal town of white-walled storehouses and carp-filled waterways with a drum festival in April; Kamioka is an old mining town above which a giant neutrino detector sits deep inside a mountain. Okuhida's onsen villages, Hirayu, Fukuji and Shin-Hotaka, have riverside open-air baths, and a two-decker ropeway climbs to over two thousand meters facing the Hotaka peaks; buses climb to Norikura's highland. The JR Takayama Line runs from Toyama through Furukawa to Takayama and on south to Gero and Nagoya; the Hida limited express takes about two and a half hours from Nagoya and ninety minutes from Toyama. The Chubu-Jukan Expressway leads east toward Matsumoto, and buses run to Shirakawa-go, Kamikochi, Kanazawa and Tokyo. From Musutafu it is about four hours via Nagoya; from Shin-Osaka about three and a half. Visitors stroll the old town, ride the ropeway, soak in Okuhida and hike the Alps. A small hero agency in Takayama works with the police, and sidekicks patrol the festival crowds while float teams use careful strength Quirks on the steepest turns.
Takayama.hiddenInfo: Takayama's wooden old town lives in fear of fire, and tourist crowds strain the narrow lanes. Bears come down into orchards in lean years, and the Okuhida mountains produce steady rescues of hikers and skiers. Hero help: a small Takayama agency and Hida police; bigger responses come from Gifu or Toyama, an hour and a half off. Villainy: pickpockets at the morning markets and festivals, fake Hida beef and craft fraud, theft from onsen lodges, and drunk drivers on mountain roads.

Matsumoto.name: Matsumoto
Matsumoto.basicInfo: Central Nagano from the Matsumoto basin and Azumino up to Kamikochi and the Hotaka peaks, and south to Shiojiri and the north shore of Lake Suwa. No coast. The west of the region is the Hida Mountains, the Japanese Alps proper: Yarigatake's spear point, the Hotaka ridge and Norikura's eastern slopes, with Kamikochi in a high valley below them on the Azusa River; the east is the broad flat Matsumoto basin, with rice, apple orchards and clear springs, rising to the Utsukushigahara plateau. Lake Suwa lies in the southeast corner. Winters are cold and dry with sharp blue skies and modest snow on the basin; summers are warm by day and cool at night; the Alps hold snow into early summer. Matsumoto, a city of about two hundred and forty thousand, is built around a black-walled castle that is a national treasure, with the old Nakamachi storehouse street, the frog-themed Nawate market lane, craft shops, and hot spring towns at Asama and Utsukushigahara. Azumino to the northwest is spring-fed farmland with huge wasabi fields, art museums and roadside shrines carved with paired deities; Shiojiri makes wine and lacquerware; Okaya and Suwa have a silk-mill and precision-manufacturing past, and Lake Suwa's August fireworks are among Japan's largest. The great Suwa shrine holds the Onbashira festival every six years, when crowds ride huge logs down steep slopes. Local food includes soba, horse sashimi, sanzokuyaki fried chicken, oyaki, wasabi and Shinshu miso. The Chuo Line's Azusa limited express runs from Shinjuku to Matsumoto in about two and three quarter hours, the Shinano limited express links Nagoya, Matsumoto and Nagano, and the Oito Line runs north to Hakuba. The Nagano and Chuo expressways cross the region, a small local airport sits south of the city, and Kamikochi is closed to private cars, reached by train and bus. From Musutafu it is about three and a half hours via Nagoya. Visitors tour the castle, hike Kamikochi and climb the Alps. A few hero agencies work Matsumoto and Suwa, mountain rescuers base at Kamikochi in season, and a farmer with a water-sense Quirk is a common figure in the wasabi beds.
Matsumoto.hiddenInfo: The Alps bring the most emergencies: fallen climbers on Yarigatake and the Hotaka ridge, lost hikers, bears and sudden storms; police and rescue heroes work from Kamikochi and helicopters. Matsumoto and Suwa have small agencies, and the nearest larger forces are in Nagano or Nagoya. Tensions: tourism pressure in Kamikochi, aging farmers, a manufacturing slowdown in Suwa. Villainy is petty: thefts from mountain huts and onsen inns, scams, fights in Matsumoto bars, and unlicensed Quirk use at festivals.

Karuizawa.name: Karuizawa
Karuizawa.basicInfo: Eastern Nagano and the Gunma border around Mount Asama: the resort highland of Karuizawa, the Saku and Ueda basins along the Chikuma River, and in the south the Kirigamine and Tateshina plateaus. No coast. Mount Asama, an active volcano of about two and a half thousand meters, dominates the north, usually trailing a thin plume, with the black lava fields of Onioshidashi on its Gunma flank. Southwest of it the Chikuma River runs northwest through the basins of Saku, Komoro and Ueda; the Usui pass on the eastern edge drops steeply toward Gunma past a red-brick railway viaduct; the south rises to the Yatsugatake's northern peaks and the meadows of Kirigamine around Lake Shirakaba. Winters are cold and clear with little snow; summers are cool, foggy and green, which is why Tokyo's wealthy have kept villas here for more than a century. Karuizawa is a forest town of villas, churches, an old shopping street, a big outlet mall south of the station, golf, waterfalls and luxury hotels; in winter it skates and curls. Saku is a carp-eating city with a star-shaped fort and a deep-space antenna in its southern hills; Komoro has castle ruins and wineries; Ueda is a castle town of the Sanada clan with garlic-soy yakitori; Unno-juku is a preserved post town on the old Hokkoku Kaido road. Local food includes soba, carp, dairy, highland vegetables and jam. The Hokuriku Shinkansen stops at Karuizawa, Sakudaira and Ueda; Karuizawa is about an hour from Tokyo and about two hours from Musutafu. The Shinano Railway runs Karuizawa to Komoro and Ueda, the Koumi Line goes south from Komoro, and the Joshin-etsu and Chubu-Odan expressways cross the basin; buses run to Kusatsu. Visitors cycle forest lanes, shop, hike Asama's outer slopes and the Kirigamine meadows, and soak in onsen. In summer extra hero patrols cover Karuizawa for the villa crowd; Saku and Ueda keep small offices, and wealthy families quietly hire licensed sidekicks for estate security.
Karuizawa.hiddenInfo: Karuizawa's divide between rich villa owners and year-round workers shows in rents and tempers. Winter empties the villas, and burglary follows. Asama's eruption warnings close the summit zone, and tourists keep ignoring them. Hero help is good in Karuizawa summer, thin in winter; Nagano city or Tokyo is under an hour by shinkansen. Villainy: villa break-ins, outlet-mall shoplifting rings, reckless driving on the Usui pass, and bar fights in Ueda and Saku.

Jaku.name: Jaku
Jaku.basicInfo: Jaku is the hill and basin country northwest of Tokyo where the Kanto Plain meets the mountains, about 100 kilometers from the capital. Jaku City sits at the north of the region, a quieter regional city in a mountain basin with residential hills around a busy downtown, an old covered shopping arcade, a castle-park of moats and cherry trees, and a station where the local lines meet; its large general hospital, Jaku General Hospital, stands about 4 km northeast of the station, just over the line into the Deika valleys, and Deika itself lies about 14 km away by rail. South and east the land opens onto the northern edge of the plain: river towns along wide gravel riverbeds, silk-era warehouses turned into cafes, cabbage and konnyaku fields, wind-swept orchards and long straight roads lined with farm shops and chain stores, while to the west the ridges climb toward the high passes and the volcanoes. Winters bring the dry, cold karakaze wind off the mountains and bright clear days; summers are among the hottest in Japan, with fierce afternoon thunderstorms; spring comes in mid-April with the cherries on the castle moat. Residents are office and factory workers, farmers, shopkeepers and commuters into Tokyo, practical people who grumble about the wind and the trains. Jaku has two small hero agencies and the city police, and anything serious brings in heroes from Hosu, about an hour away by train. Trains link Jaku with Deika, with Hosu in about an hour, with Tokyo in about an hour and a half and with Musutafu in about two and a half hours; expressway buses run to the capital, and outside the towns a car or a bicycle is how people get around. A visitor can shop in the old arcade, recover at the hospital, work a farm or a factory shift, ride the local lines out to the hot springs in the hills, or follow the road northwest to Deika.
Jaku.hiddenInfo: Jaku is not the Meta Liberation Army's city yet, and their reach into it shows as money from Deika, purchase offers for shops and land, and polite visits to the city council and the hospital board. Its two small agencies are stretched thin and grateful for any sponsor, which makes them easy to court. Small-time villainy here is theft from farms and warehouses, and drunken Quirk fights after festival nights.

Ashikaga.name: Ashikaga
Ashikaga.basicInfo: The northern edge of the Kanto plain where Tochigi, Gunma, Saitama and Ibaraki meet, a flat, crowded cell of rivers, rice fields and old textile cities just north of the Tokyo sprawl. The Tone river crosses the southern half from west to east, and the Watarase river comes down from the Ashio hills past Kiryu and Ashikaga to the huge reed marsh of the Watarase retarding basin near the four-prefecture border. North of the Tone lie Kiryu, a silk weaving city in the hills on the western edge; Ashikaga, site of Japan's oldest school and a flower park famous for its giant wisteria; Sano with its ramen and outlet malls; Tochigi city, with white-walled warehouses along a canal; Tatebayashi with its azalea hill and the temple of the shape-shifting tea kettle; Ota with its car plants; and Oyama in the east, a shinkansen town on the Omoi river. South of the Tone sit Gyoda, with its ancient burial mounds and rice paddy art, Kazo, Hanyu, Kuki, and Kumagaya near the Arakawa in the southwest. Summers are brutally hot, and Kumagaya has held the national heat record; winters are dry and windy, with the cold karakaze blowing off the mountains. People work in factories and warehouses, weave and dye, grow rice, wheat, lettuce and strawberries, and commute toward Tokyo. Kumagaya has Joetsu and Hokuriku Shinkansen stops and Oyama a Tohoku one, each well under an hour from Tokyo; the Ryomo line links Oyama to Kiryu, Tobu lines fan out from Asakusa, and the Tohoku, Kita-Kanto and Ken-O expressways cross the plain. From Musutafu, most towns here are about two hours away. Visitors see the wisteria in late April, eat Sano ramen, Kiryu's broad himokawa noodles and Gyoda's zeri fry croquettes, tour the burial mounds, and join the crowds at Kumagaya's July fan festival. Each city has a small hero agency, police boxes stand at every station, and on summer afternoons sidekicks with cooling Quirks are posted at outdoor festivals to treat heatstroke.
Ashikaga.hiddenInfo: The textile cities are past their best years: weaving sheds stand empty, downtown arcades are shuttered, and the plain is filling with logistics warehouses that bring trucks and night shifts. Heatstroke kills people here every summer. Hero help is never more than fifteen or twenty minutes away, but the agencies are small and busy. Small villainy looks like car and catalytic converter theft rings, illegal dumping on river banks, vandalism in empty mills, and Quirk-fueled fights in parking lots after dark.

Tsukuba.name: Tsukuba
Tsukuba.basicInfo: Southwestern Ibaraki and the mountain of Tsukuba, a cell of flat farmland, lotus ponds and research campuses on the eastern Kanto plain, with a corner of southern Tochigi in the north. Mount Tsukuba stands alone in the middle, its twin summits Nantai and Nyotai reached by cable car and ropeway, with a great shrine at its foot and old stone lanterns along the trails. South of it the planned Tsukuba Science City spreads its wide boulevards, national laboratories, a space agency center, a large student population and the terminus of the Tsukuba Express. Tsuchiura, on the western inlet of Lake Kasumigaura in the southeast, is an old castle and canal town ringed by lotus fields and famous for its October fireworks competition. Ishioka lies north of it under the Yasato fruit hills, Kasama with its potteries and great Inari shrine sits in the northeast, and along the Kinu and Kokai rivers in the west lie Shimotsuma, Chikusei's Shimodate, the silk weaving town of Yuki, the old Makabe merchant streets of Sakuragawa, and Moka in Tochigi. The northern edge touches the pottery town of Mashiko. The land is low and fertile: rice, lotus root, chestnuts, pears, grapes, strawberries and sweet potatoes, plus factories and logistics centers along the expressways. Summers are hot and humid, winters dry and windy with the occasional heavy snow. The Tsukuba Express reaches Tsukuba from Akihabara in about forty-five minutes; the Joban line runs through Tsuchiura and Ishioka; the Mito line crosses the north through Yuki and Kasama; the Kanto Railway, the Moka Railway with its weekend steam train, and the Joban, Ken-O and Kita-Kanto expressways fill in. From Musutafu, Tsukuba is about two hours. Visitors climb Mount Tsukuba and buy toad-oil salve from the street performers, tour science exhibitions, eat lotus root dishes in Tsuchiura and chestnut sweets in Kasama, and see the chrysanthemum festival at Kasama's Inari shrine in autumn. Tsukuba hosts a small hero agency that works closely with laboratory security, police boxes stand at every station, and sidekicks earn overtime at the fireworks, where a hero with a wind Quirk keeps the smoke off the crowd.
Tsukuba.hiddenInfo: Tsukuba's newcomers, researchers and students from across Japan and abroad, live a separate life from the old farm villages around them, and new housing estates on old paddies are a quiet sore point. The laboratories worry more about stolen data and prototypes than street crime. Hero help is quick in Tsukuba and Tsuchiura and twenty to thirty minutes out in the paddies. Small villainy: bicycle theft, burglary of empty farmhouses, unlicensed Quirk practice in empty lots, and phone scams that target elderly farmers.

Mito.name: Mito
Mito.basicInfo: Mito and the central Ibaraki coast, a cell of flat farmland, lakes and long sand beaches facing the Pacific, with the eastern half open sea. Mito, the prefectural capital, sits on a ridge between the Naka river and Lake Senba, around the Kairakuen garden with its three thousand plum trees and the old domain school of Kodokan. East of it, Hitachinaka holds the fish market and harbor of Nakaminato, a seaside park whose hills turn blue with nemophila in spring and red with kochia in autumn, and the sweet potato fields that make dried hoshi-imo. Oarai, just south, is a beach and port town with an aquarium, a torii gate standing on surf-washed rocks, and an overnight ferry to Hokkaido. Behind the coast lie Lake Hinuma, known for its shijimi clams, Ibaraki Airport near Omitama, the eastern reaches of Lake Kasumigaura and Lake Kitaura with their lotus fields and fishing villages, and Hokota, the melon capital, above a straight, empty beach running south. Tokai village marks the northern edge. Summers are warm and humid, winters dry and bright with little snow, and spring winds raise dust over the fields. People grow melons, sweet potatoes, lotus root and rice, raise pigs and Hitachi beef, fish in the lakes and off the coast, and work in Mito's offices and the Hitachinaka factories. The Joban line and Joban Expressway put Mito about an hour and a quarter from Tokyo; the Suigun line runs north, the Mito line west, the Oarai Kashima line down the coast, and a little seaside railway runs from Katsuta out to the beach at Ajigaura. From Musutafu allow about two and a half hours. Visitors eat natto in every form, monkfish hotpot in Oarai in winter and melons in Hokota in summer, see the plum blossoms in February and March, ride the ferry north, and swim at Oarai. Mito has several hero agencies and the prefectural police headquarters; summer beach patrols use sidekicks with water Quirks, and a melon grower whose Quirk senses ripeness by touch picks the best fruit for the auction.
Mito.hiddenInfo: Ibaraki runs a long joke about being Japan's least attractive prefecture, and Mito people are prickly about it; downtown is losing shops to the malls and to Tokyo. Rip currents on the beaches drown swimmers every summer. Real hero help is quick in Mito and Hitachinaka and fifteen to thirty minutes out in the lake country. Small villainy: loud motorcycle gangs and drag racing on the coast roads, crop theft from melon and sweet potato farms, and scams on the elderly.

Kashima-nada.name: Kashima-nada
Kashima-nada.basicInfo: The Kashima-nada, the open Pacific off the long straight beaches of central Ibaraki, here between about twenty-five and seventy-five kilometers from shore, east of Oarai, Hokota and Kashima. The coast is a low line of sand and pine with a few tall stacks at Kashima, often lost in haze. The water is green near shore and deep blue offshore, where the bottom falls off the shelf past two hundred meters into the slope. Nada means rough water, and the name is earned: warm Kuroshio and cold Oyashio water meet here, swells roll in unbroken from the open ocean, early summer brings fog, and winter brings hard northwest winds. Purse seiners from Hasaki, Oarai and Nakaminato chase sardines and mackerel, and smaller boats work flounder and whitebait nearer the beach. The overnight ferries between Oarai and Hokkaido run north through these waters, and cargo ships make for Kashima's industrial port. The coast guard patrols from the Ibaraki ports, and maritime heroes answer the rare distress calls. A party could be out here on the Hokkaido ferry, a fishing charter, or carried by a flying hero.
Kashima-nada.hiddenInfo: Fishing crews here are aging and hard-pressed, and quarrel among themselves over the sardine grounds. Fog and swell sink small boats every few years. Real help is the coast guard, an hour or more from port. Petty villainy is catch and fuel theft, illegal dumping from ships, and the odd stowaway on the Hokkaido ferry.

Sea off Izumo.name: Sea off Izumo
Sea off Izumo.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the western tip of the Shimane Peninsula, north and west of the cape of Hinomisaki. The cape and its tall stone lighthouse stand just beyond the cell's southeastern corner, with the green ridges of the peninsula running east behind them, and on clear days the hills of the Oki Dozen islands show low to the northeast. The water is clear blue over the shelf, around one to two hundred meters deep, with the Tsushima Current running northeast along the coast. Summers are calm, autumn brings typhoons, and winter brings strong northwest monsoon winds and heavy seas that pound the cape. Fishing boats from the small ports of the Izumo coast and from Hamada work here for squid, horse mackerel, sea bream and flying fish, which are caught in early summer and grilled and dried for the region's ago broth. Few ships cross; the Oki ferries run farther east. The coast guard watches from Hamada and Sakaiminato, and a maritime hero working the Shimane coast is the nearest hero help. A party could be out here on a fishing boat from one of Izumo's little harbors, a charter out of the Hinomisaki port, or crossing by air.
Sea off Izumo.hiddenInfo: The waters off the cape are rough and rescues are more common than crimes. The fishing towns are aging, and outside boats working close to shore stir anger. The nearest help is the coast guard and heroes on the Izumo coast, about an hour away. Villainy is petty: gear theft and poaching.

Oki Strait.name: Oki Strait
Oki Strait.basicInfo: The Oki Strait, the stretch of the Sea of Japan between the north coast of the Shimane Peninsula and the Dozen islands of Oki. The peninsula's green ridges and fishing coves line the southern horizon, a few of its headlands just reaching the cell's southern edge; small Chiburijima, southernmost of the Dozen, pokes just inside the northern edge, with Nishinoshima and Nakanoshima rising beyond it. The water is clear blue and mostly fifty to a hundred meters deep, with the Tsushima Current flowing northeast. Summers are calm; winters bring northwest gales and steep seas that cancel sailings. This is the islands' lifeline: car ferries and the jetfoil run from Shichirui on the peninsula and from Sakaiminato to the Oki ports, the ferry taking two to three hours and the jetfoil about an hour. Fishing boats from both sides work here for squid, sea bream, yellowtail and flying fish, and set nets lie off the peninsula's coves. The coast guard patrols from Sakaiminato, and heroes from the Shimane coast and the islands cross by boat or air when called. A party is most likely here aboard the ferry or the jetfoil, or on a fishing boat.
Oki Strait.hiddenInfo: Everything the islands need comes across this strait, so a canceled ferry is everyone's problem and the ferry line's finances are a constant worry. The boats see small trouble: theft, drunks, the odd fugitive heading for the islands. The coast guard and island heroes can respond within an hour in fair weather; in storms, help waits.

Sea off Mihonoseki.name: Sea off Mihonoseki
Sea off Mihonoseki.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of Mihonoseki, the eastern tip of the Shimane Peninsula, and the mouth of Miho Bay. Jizozaki cape and its white lighthouse stand on the southwestern horizon, the long sweep of the Yumigahama spit and the bulk of Mount Daisen rise to the south, and on clear days Dogo is a low gray shape to the north. The water is clear blue, mostly fifty to a hundred and fifty meters deep, with the Tsushima Current flowing northeast. Summers are calm; in winter the northwest monsoon brings heavy seas and snow squalls. The Oki ferries and jetfoil from Sakaiminato and Shichirui cross the western part, and boats from Sakaiminato, one of Japan's busiest fishing ports, are everywhere: purse seiners after mackerel and sardines, boats landing bluefin tuna in early summer, and crab trawlers in winter. Cargo ships come and go from Sakaiminato harbor. The coast guard office at Sakaiminato is close by, and the hero agencies of Sakaiminato and Yonago answer calls at sea. A party could be out here on the Oki ferry, a fishing or charter boat from Sakaiminato or Mihonoseki, or crossing by air.
Sea off Mihonoseki.hiddenInfo: Busy port waters mean busy small crime: unlicensed fishing, catch fraud, worries about goods slipped off cargo ships, and labor tension on the boats. Help is close, with the coast guard and Sakaiminato heroes under an hour away, though winter storms still make rescue dangerous.

Sea off Tottori.name: Sea off Tottori
Sea off Tottori.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the central Tottori coast, from the Tottori Dunes and Aoya in the east to the Yurihama and Kotoura shore in the west. The coast lies just beyond the cell's southern edge, so the dunes show as a pale strip on the southeastern horizon, with the green Chugoku Mountains behind and, on clear days, Mount Daisen far to the southwest. The water is clear blue near shore and deepens northward past a hundred meters, with the Tsushima Current flowing northeast. Summers are calm and hot, good for swimming and diving off the rocky stretches; winters bring northwest gales, high surf onto the dunes and snow squalls. Tottori port and the small harbors along the shore send out boats for squid, flying fish, sea bream and, in winter, snow crab, and divers take wild rock oysters in summer. Ships are few. The coast guard watches from its offices along the coast, and the hero agencies of Tottori city can reach the water within half an hour. A party could be out here on a fishing or charter boat from Tottori, a sea kayak along the coast, or a flight over the dunes.
Sea off Tottori.hiddenInfo: The shore here is quiet and the trouble is ordinary: poaching of oysters and abalone, unlicensed boats, and swimmers caught by rip currents off the dunes. Help is close by Sea of Japan standards, the coast guard and Tottori heroes within half an hour or so. Winter seas make rescue slow.

Kinosaki Coast.name: Kinosaki Coast
Kinosaki Coast.basicInfo: The northern coast of Hyogo's Tajima district on the Sea of Japan, a strip of rugged shore running east to west along the cell's southern edge, with open sea filling everything to the north. The coast is part of the San'in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark: headlands of volcanic rock, sea caves, pine-topped islets and small coves with fishing villages under steep hills. From east to west: Kinosaki Onsen near the mouth of the Maruyama River, with Genbudo's basalt columns just upstream; Takeno, with its long sandy beach and narrow streets of dark-boarded fishing houses; Shibayama and Kasumi, the two great crab ports of the coast; the tall Amarube Viaduct carrying the railway high above Amarube village; and Hamasaka toward the western edge, where the islets of the Uradome coast begin across the line in Tottori. Kinosaki is the heart of it: a willow-lined canal with stone bridges, old wooden inns, and seven public bathhouses that guests walk between in yukata and wooden geta, the clatter echoing down the street at night. Winters are snowy and gray with wild seas, and that is crab season, when matsuba crab comes in to Kasumi and Shibayama and the inns fill with crab dinners. Summer brings swimmers to the beaches at Takeno and Kasumi. Inland the hills climb quickly toward the Tajima highlands, home of the black cattle that Kobe and Matsusaka beef come from, and wild storks reintroduced in the Toyooka basin to the south are sometimes seen wading near the river mouth. The San'in Main Line links the coast; limited expresses reach Kinosaki from Kyoto in about two and a half hours and from Shin-Osaka in under three. From Musutafu, Kinosaki is about five hours by shinkansen and limited express. Local buses and the coast road reach the villages. Kinosaki has a police box by the canal and a small hero agency covering the onsen town and nearby coast, with extra sidekicks walking the bathhouse street on busy winter weekends. Quirks help in the crab sheds and on the boats, and an inn worker with a heat Quirk keeps the outdoor bath just right. Visitors bathe, eat crab, tour the sea caves by boat, walk the geopark trails and photograph the viaduct.
Kinosaki Coast.hiddenInfo: The coast lives on two seasons, crab and summer, and the rest of the year is quiet and aging; inns compete hard and some are failing. Kinosaki's crowds draw pickpockets, bath-locker thieves and peepers with sight Quirks, and the crab trade has its share of mislabeled crab and poached catch. The small Kinosaki agency handles most of it; heavier help comes from Toyooka, and real numbers from Kobe or Osaka are about three hours away. Winter storms and snow on the line can cut the coast off for a day.

Tango Peninsula.name: Tango Peninsula
Tango Peninsula.basicInfo: The northern half of the Tango Peninsula, the thumb of Kyoto Prefecture that juts into the Sea of Japan, and the open water around it. Only about a fifth of the cell is land: the peninsula's rounded, forested hills, its rocky northern tip at Cape Kyoga with a white lighthouse on the cliff, and the coves and sandy bays along its west and east sides; everything north of the shore is sea. On the western shore lie the town of Amino and Kotohiki-hama, a beach whose sand squeaks underfoot, and farther west the calm lagoon of Kumihama Bay. Inland, the old weaving town of Mineyama sits in a valley where looms still clatter making Tango chirimen silk crepe. On the north coast the fishing port of Taiza lands snow crab each winter. On the eastern shore, Ine wraps around a sheltered bay lined with funaya, two-story boathouses built right on the water with boats parked beneath the family rooms, and its Urashima shrine keeps the old fisherman's legend. The climate is Sea of Japan: warm, clear summers good for beaches and diving, and winters of strong wind, snow and rough gray sea. People fish, weave, grow rice in narrow valleys and run small inns serving crab, yellowtail, barazushi and local sake. The Kyoto Tango Railway runs along the peninsula's base through Mineyama and Amino; elsewhere local buses wind along the coast road, and the Kyoto Jukan Expressway ends just to the south. Amanohashidate is a short bus ride south, Shin-Osaka about two and a half hours, Musutafu about five. A small hero agency in Kyotango covers the whole peninsula with a few members, and police boxes in each town handle most matters; one old fisher's weather-reading Quirk is trusted more than any forecast.
Tango Peninsula.hiddenInfo: The peninsula is aging and emptying, and the young move to Kyoto or Osaka. The friction is between old crab families and newcomers opening inns and guesthouses. Crime is small: theft from unlocked homes, crab poaching, a tourist who strays too close to the cliffs. A serious incident would draw help from Maizuru or Fukuchiyama, an hour or more away, and Kyoto's agencies after that.

Wakasa Bay.name: Wakasa Bay
Wakasa Bay.basicInfo: The outer and middle reaches of Wakasa Bay, the wide bight of the Sea of Japan between the Tango Peninsula and Cape Echizen. The water is sheltered and fairly shallow, mostly under a hundred meters, clear blue-green in summer and calm enough for kayaks along the shore. A sliver of land shows at the edges: the forested tip of the Tsunegami Peninsula in the southeast and the western shore of the Tsuruga Peninsula on the eastern rim, while the bird island of Kanmurijima rises near the western edge off Maizuru. The inner bay's ria coast, with its drowned inlets and the towns of Obama and Takahama, lies just to the south. Winter winds bring snow and short, steep waves. The bay is known for Wakasa tilefish, mackerel, oysters and, in winter, snow crab; set-nets and small trawlers work out of Obama, Takahama and Mihama. Overnight car ferries from Tsuruga and Maizuru to Hokkaido cross the bay mouth. The coast guard's regional headquarters and a Maritime Self-Defense Force base sit at Maizuru, so gray ships and patrol boats are a common sight. A party could be on a sightseeing boat from Obama, a ferry, a fishing boat or a sea kayak, or flying with a hero; Obama is about three and a half hours from Musutafu.
Wakasa Bay.hiddenInfo: Everywhere else is sleepy. Trouble is poaching from shellfish beds, quarrels over set-net rights, and summer boating accidents. Help comes from Maizuru, Tsuruga or Obama within the hour.

Tsuruga.name: Tsuruga
Tsuruga.basicInfo: The southern Echizen country of Fukui Prefecture, from the deep harbor of Tsuruga Bay north across the Takefu basin and east into the Ono basin and the mountains toward Gifu. The western edge is coast: Tsuruga Bay, sheltered and deep, with the Tsuruga Peninsula on its west side, and farther north the steep Echizen coast, where Echizen harbor lands the famous yellow-tagged crab and terraced slopes bloom with wild narcissus in winter. Tsuruga is a working port city: car ferries leave for Niigata and Hokkaido, freighters load at the quays, and the long Kehi pine grove lines the beach east of the harbor. Kehi Shrine's great vermilion torii stands near the station, and the Hokuriku Shinkansen now begins here. North over the Kinome pass and the old Hokkoku road lie the craft towns of Echizen-Takefu and Sabae: knife forges, lacquerware, handmade washi paper in Imadate, and the workshops that make most of Japan's eyeglass frames. East across the mountains, the Ono basin holds a small castle town on a grid of spring-fed streets, its castle on a hilltop that floats above the morning fog in autumn. Beyond that the land climbs into the Kuzuryu valley and the steep, empty ranges of the Gifu border. Winters are snowy and gray, summers hot and green. Food is grated-radish soba, Echizen crab, grilled mackerel and, in Ono, taro and clear spring water. The shinkansen stops at Tsuruga and Echizen-Takefu; the Hapi-Line runs local trains up the corridor, the Obama line west, and the Hokuriku and Maizuru-Wakasa expressways meet near Tsuruga. Musutafu is about two hours away by way of Maibara, Shin-Osaka about an hour and a half on the Thunderbird limited express. Tsuruga and Takefu each have a small hero agency and police boxes; heroes cover the eastern mountains by car, and in the knife workshops more than one smith's Quirk helps at the forge.
Tsuruga.hiddenInfo: Ordinary trouble is port-side: undeclared cargo, fights between ferry crews, theft from parked trucks along the expressway. The eastern mountains empty out more every year. Fukui's agencies are half an hour north; bigger help comes from Osaka or Kanazawa by rail.

Gujo.name: Gujo
Gujo.basicInfo: Gujo is the mountain heart of Gifu's Okumino country, a cell of steep cedar ridges and clear rivers running from the upper Nagara valley in the east, across the Neo and Ibi headwaters, to the Kuzuryu gorge on the Fukui side in the west. No coast reaches it; the Ryohaku mountains wall the north and the Nobi plain opens just beyond the southern edge. The Nagara River rises near Hirugano and runs south through Shiratori, Yamato and the old castle town of Gujo Hachiman, its water so clean that people rinse vegetables in stone tanks along the lanes. Winters bring deep snow to the northern highlands, where the Takasu, Washigatake and Hirugano ski slopes fill with buses from Nagoya; summers are green and cool at night, with mist in the valleys and ayu fishers standing waist-deep in the rapids. Gujo Hachiman's white castle sits on a hill above a grid of wooden houses, canals and narrow bridges that local swimmers leap from in August. The town is famous for Gujo Odori, a summer dance held on some thirty nights from July into September, with four all-night dances at Obon when the streets stay full until dawn, and for workshops that make the lifelike plastic food seen in restaurant windows across Japan. West over the passes, the Neo valley keeps a vast old cherry tree and the raw scarp of the fault that tore open in the great Nobi earthquake; farther west, Kuzuryu Lake fills a dam in the Fukui mountains. People farm small terraced fields, work timber and tourism, run inns and soba shops, or commute down the valley to Mino and Seki. The Tokai-Hokuriku Expressway threads the Nagara valley north toward Toyama, the little Nagara River Railway runs up from Mino-Ota to Hokuno, and the Kuzuryu Line climbs from Fukui. Musutafu is about three hours away by shinkansen to Nagoya and an expressway bus up the valley; Osaka is about two and a half hours by road. Visitors canoe, fish, ski and dance in yukata through summer nights. Each town keeps a police box or two, and a small hero office in Gujo Hachiman covers a huge district of valleys, sending sidekicks to steer the Obon dance crowds; snowplow crews with strength or heat Quirks clear the passes under municipal permits.
Gujo.hiddenInfo: Gujo's quiet trouble is emptiness: the valleys lose young families to Nagoya, schools merge, and hamlets on the Ibi and Neo headwaters keep only a handful of households, so a fall on ice or a missing hiker can go unnoticed for a day. Summer dance crowds bring pickpockets, drunken scuffles and the odd unlicensed Quirk show-off on the canal bridges; winter brings stranded drivers on the Hirugano grades and thefts from ski-lot cars. Bears raid orchards in autumn. Real hero help is the small Gujo Hachiman office and the prefectural police; anything serious waits for teams driving up from Gifu or Nagoya, about an hour and a half away.

Mount Ontake.name: Mount Ontake
Mount Ontake.basicInfo: Mount Ontake is a cell of high volcano and deep valleys straddling the Gifu-Nagano border, from the Hida River gorges and the hot-spring town of Gero in the west to the sacred peak itself and the Kaida highlands on the Kiso side in the east. Ontake rises to 3,067 meters, a broad, scree-covered active volcano whose summit still breathes steam; shelters and volcanic warnings line the trails, and pilgrims of the Ontake faith climb in white robes through the summer, ringing bells and chanting past stone monuments to their founders. Its Gifu flank holds Nigorigo, one of Japan's highest hot-spring hamlets, and the many waterfalls of Hida-Osaka; its Nagano flank holds Otaki village, a ropeway, ski slopes and the Kaida plateau, cold rolling grassland where small, sturdy Kiso horses are bred and buckwheat grows for soba. Winters are long and heavily snowed above the valleys; autumn turns the larch gold and the maples red. South of the mountain lie the Tsukechi gorge, cypress forests and the Kashimo hamlet with its farm-village kabuki stage. Gero, on the Hida River, is the region's town and one of Japan's three famous hot springs: a strip of ryokan along the river with free foot baths, a folk village of thatched gassho farmhouses on the hill, and fireworks over the water on winter weekends. Kanayama and Hagiwara are quiet railway towns, and Higashi-Shirakawa grows tea and fells cypress. Locals eat Hida beef, keichan chicken fried with miso and cabbage, salt-grilled river fish on skewers and valley tomatoes. The JR Takayama Main Line follows the Hida River north, with the limited express Hida reaching Gero from Nagoya in about an hour and forty minutes; Route 41 runs beside it, and buses cross the passes to Kiso-Fukushima on the Chuo Line. From Musutafu the trip is about three hours by shinkansen to Nagoya and the Hida north. Visitors soak, raft the Hida, climb Ontake from the Nagano trailheads, ski and stargaze from the highlands. Gero has a police station, a few police boxes along the valley and a modest hero office that also patrols the onsen strip; mountain rescue on Ontake falls to prefectural teams, local guides and licensed heroes with flight or sensing Quirks.
Mount Ontake.hiddenInfo: The mountain is the quiet worry here: Ontake is active, and every tremor fills the guesthouses with talk and empties them of bookings, while trailhead shops depend on climbers who may stay away. Gero's onsen strip sees peeping, luggage theft from ryokan lobbies and the occasional drunken guest misusing a Quirk in the baths. Lost hikers, bear encounters and winter crashes on Route 41 are routine. Real hero help is thin: the small Gero office and the prefectural police, with heavier response an hour or more away in Takayama, Gifu or Nagoya.

Kofu.name: Kofu
Kofu.basicInfo: Kofu is the cell of the Kofu basin in Yamanashi, a flat bowl of orchards and towns ringed by some of Japan's highest mountains: the Southern Alps rise on the west with Mount Kita, the country's second-highest peak, the Yatsugatake range closes the northwest, and the granite crags of Mount Kinpu and Mount Mizugaki stand to the north. The Fuefuki and Kamanashi rivers drain the basin south into the Fuji River; there is no coast, and Mount Fuji shows over the Misaka hills to the south. The basin is one of the sunniest places in Japan, broiling in summer and sharp and dry in winter, with wide swings between day and night that sweeten the fruit. Kofu, the prefectural capital, spreads around its castle ruins and station, with arcades, a gem-polishing and jewelry trade as old as the crystal diggings in the northern hills, and a shrine to the old Takeda lords; a spring festival parades armored samurai through the streets. Around it lie Kai, Fuefuki with its Isawa hot springs and peach orchards that turn the slopes pink in April, the vineyard terraces of the basin rim, Nirasaki and Minami-Alps at the foot of the western wall, and Hokuto, Kobuchizawa and Kiyosato on the cool Yatsugatake skirts, with dairy farms and summer cottages. People grow grapes, peaches, cherries and highland lettuce, make wine, polish stones, keep onsen inns and commute into Kofu. They eat hoto, thick flat noodles stewed with pumpkin in miso, sweet-glazed chicken giblets and fruit in every form. The Chuo Main Line carries the limited expresses Azusa and Kaiji from Shinjuku to Kofu in about an hour and a half, the Chuo Expressway runs beside it, the Minobu Line and Chubu-Odan Expressway descend the Fuji River valley to the Pacific coast, and the little Koumi Line climbs to Nobeyama, the highest station on JR. Musutafu is about two and a half hours away by train via Fuji, or about two hours by expressway bus around the mountain. Visitors pick fruit, taste wine, soak and climb. Kofu has the prefectural police headquarters and several hero agencies; licensed heroes cover the mountain districts by car and by air, and fruit growers with plant or weather-sensing Quirks work under agricultural permits.
Kofu.hiddenInfo: Kofu's undercurrent is a basin aging and thinning out: shuttered shops in the old center, abandoned orchards, and seasonal farmhands from abroad who are easy to cheat. Fruit theft just before harvest is a real crime here, along with burglaries of wineries and jewelry workshops and loan sharks circling the gem trade. Climbers get lost or hurt in the Southern Alps and Yatsugatake every season. Kofu's agencies answer quickly inside the basin; the mountain districts wait much longer, and anything large brings help from Tokyo, about an hour and a half away.

Chichibu.name: Chichibu
Chichibu.basicInfo: Chichibu is a cell of forested mountains on the western edge of the Kanto plain, where Saitama, Tokyo and Yamanashi meet in the Okuchichibu range: the Chichibu basin at the north, the green gorges of Okutama in the middle, the Chuo corridor of eastern Yamanashi along the south, and Mount Takao at the southeast corner looking out over the Tokyo suburbs. Mount Kumotori, the highest point in Tokyo, and the long ridge of Mount Daibosatsu rise near the center, and on clear days Mount Fuji stands over the southern ridges. The Arakawa flows north out of the Chichibu basin, the Tama River rises in the Okutama hills and fills Lake Okutama behind the Ogochi Dam, and the Sagami River runs east past Otsuki and Uenohara into Lake Sagami. There is no coast. Summers are humid, autumn color is spectacular and winters bring frost. Chichibu city is an old silk and pilgrimage town of wooden shopfronts, a great shrine and a circuit of thirty-four Kannon temples, lying under the quarried limestone face of Mount Buko; its Night Festival in early December hauls lantern-lit floats up a slope under winter fireworks, and in spring the Hitsujiyama hillside blooms pink with moss phlox. Okutama is a hiking and river town of canyoning, kayaks on the Tama, the Nippara limestone cave, wasabi terraces and trout fishing, and Mount Mitake has a cable car and pilgrim lodges. In Yamanashi, Otsuki keeps the old Saruhashi cantilever bridge over a gorge, and the slopes of Enzan and Katsunuma are covered with grape trellises and wineries. Locals eat waraji katsudon, buckwheat soba, grilled miso potatoes and grapes. Seibu limited expresses reach Chichibu from Ikebukuro in about eighty minutes, the Chichibu Railway runs a steam train in season, the JR Ome Line ends at Okutama, and the Chuo Line and Chuo Expressway run through Otsuki and Takao toward Tokyo. Musutafu is about two and a half hours away by way of Tokyo, or by road around Fuji; Tokyo is one to two hours depending on the valley. The towns keep police boxes and small hero offices, agencies from the western Tokyo suburbs cover the weekend crowds on Takao, and rescue heroes and mountain police pull lost hikers off the Okutama trails.
Chichibu.hiddenInfo: Chichibu's mountains sit close to the capital yet empty out behind the trailheads, which makes them a place where things get left: illegal dumping in the gorges, abandoned cars on forest roads, the odd small-time crook lying low in a rented cabin. Weekend crowds on Takao and Okutama bring theft, reckless driving on the mountain roads and river drownings in summer. Deer and bears are a farm nuisance. Hero help is close at the eastern edge, within half an hour from the Tokyo suburbs, but slow in the western valleys, where police and volunteer fire brigades often arrive first.

Chiba.name: Chiba
Chiba.basicInfo: Northwestern Chiba and the Tokyo Bay shore, the eastern wing of the capital's sprawl: dense suburbs, the Keiyo industrial coast, and beyond them rice paddies, peanut fields and the low plateau around Narita. The western edge runs along the Edogawa river through the last of Tokyo's eastern wards, and across the river lie Ichikawa, Matsudo, Funabashi and Urayasu, where a huge theme resort sits on reclaimed land. The bay shore curves southeast past the Makuhari district's convention halls, stadium and office towers to Chiba city, the prefectural capital, with its port tower, a castle-style museum and a suspended monorail swinging between its districts; steelworks and refineries line the shore south of it. To the north lie Kashiwa, Nagareyama, Noda with its soy sauce breweries, and the Tone river, beyond which Toride, Moriya, Ryugasaki and Ushiku belong to Ibaraki, with the giant bronze Buddha of Ushiku standing over the fields near the northern edge. Inland, Lake Inba, Sakura with its samurai houses, windmill and national history museum, Yachimata's peanut fields, and Narita, where the great Shinshoji temple anchors an old street of eel restaurants, lead to the international airport on the eastern edge. The climate is mild and humid, with hot summers, typhoon rain in early autumn and dry, clear winters. People commute into Tokyo, work at the port, the airport, the steel and chemical plants and the logistics parks, or farm peanuts, nashi pears, carrots and rice. The Sobu, Keiyo and Joban lines, the Keisei railways, the Tozai subway, the Tsukuba Express and the Narita Express run in from Tokyo; Chiba station is about forty minutes from Tokyo Station, so Musutafu is about an hour and a half away. Visitors shop at Makuhari, walk Narita's temple street and watch its July Gion festival floats, see the tulips around Sakura's windmill in April, and dig clams on the bay beaches. Chiba has many hero agencies and busy police; heroes cover the big stations and the airport alongside police and customs officers, and Quirk-assisted cargo handlers work the port on private ground.
Chiba.hiddenInfo: Chiba is Tokyo's overflow: bed towns where neighbors barely meet, an industrial bay coast of shift workers, and a constant flow of strangers through the airport. Agencies here compete with the capital's for talent and attention and often lose. Hero response is fast in the cities and at the airport, fifteen to twenty minutes in the rice country. Small villainy: luggage theft and petty smuggling around the airport, pickpockets on packed trains, fraud rings running call centers from quiet suburbs, and unlicensed Quirk brawls in Funabashi's and Chiba's nightlife streets.

Choshi.name: Choshi
Choshi.basicInfo: The eastern tip of the Kanto plain where the Tone river meets the Pacific, a cell split by the river into Chiba's Choshi and Katori on the south bank and Ibaraki's Kashima shore on the north, with the eastern third open sea. Choshi sits at the very end, a fishing city on a blunt headland: the white lighthouse of Inubosaki stands on the cape, the Byobugaura cliffs run southwest from it, and the long Kujukuri beach begins past Iioka and runs out of the cell to the south. North of the river mouth, the sand coast of Hasaki and Kamisu is lined with wind turbines, then Kashima's deep-water industrial port, steelworks and petrochemical plants face the sea, and Kashima city, between the port and Lake Kitaura, holds one of Japan's oldest shrines in a deep forest along with a well-known soccer stadium. Upriver, Katori shrine faces Kashima's across the water, the canal town of Sawara keeps willows, old merchant houses and great festival floats, and Itako spreads its iris gardens and boat canals between the lakes. In the west, Narita Airport's runways and an aviation museum at Shibayama sit on the plateau, with Asahi, Yokoshiba and Tako farming the plain below. The climate is mild: cool summers for Kanto thanks to the sea, warm winters, sea fog in early summer, and strong winds on the cape. People fish, brew soy sauce in Choshi's big breweries, grow cabbage, vegetables and rice, make steel and chemicals at Kashima, and work at the airport. The Sobu main line and Narita line bring limited expresses from Tokyo to Choshi in about two hours; the Kashima line serves Kashima, the little Choshi Electric Railway runs out to Inubosaki and keeps itself going by selling wet rice crackers, and highway buses run often from Tokyo to Kashima and Choshi. Musutafu is about three hours away. Visitors watch the New Year's first sunrise at Inubosaki, eat sardines, mackerel and saury at the fishing port, see Sawara's summer and autumn float festivals, ride Itako's iris boats in June, surf Hasaki, and visit both great shrines. Choshi and Kashima each have a small hero agency, the coast guard handles the sea, and a fish market worker whose Quirk chills whatever it touches keeps the catch fresh.
Choshi.hiddenInfo: Choshi's boom days are over: the port still lands huge catches, but the town center is aging and quiet, and the little railway survives on goodwill. Across the river, Kashima's industrial port draws contract workers who come and go. Real hero help is local and thin, and larger backup from Chiba or Narita is about an hour away. Small villainy looks like catch fraud and theft at the fish market, fights among crews ashore, petty smuggling through the ports, and thieves working the airport parking lots.

Sea off Choshi.name: Sea off Choshi
Sea off Choshi.basicInfo: The open Pacific east of Cape Inubo, from just off Choshi's headland out about fifty kilometers, where the Kuroshio current leaves the coast of Japan and turns east into the ocean. Warm, deep-blue Kuroshio water meets the colder, greener Oyashio here, and the mixing makes one of the richest fishing grounds in Japan, with frequent fog in early summer and sharp chop where the currents collide. The shelf is narrow and the bottom falls quickly past several hundred meters. Boats from Choshi, Hasaki and Kashima fish sardines, mackerel, saury and squid in great numbers, and Choshi's port often leads the country in landings. Ships bound for Tokyo Bay and Kashima's industrial port round the cape in a steady line, and the lighthouse at Inubosaki and the cliffs of Byobugaura show to the west. The coast guard patrols these waters out of Choshi, and maritime heroes ride out with it in storms. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a coast guard cutter, or carried by a flying hero.
Sea off Choshi.hiddenInfo: Competition for fish is fierce, with talk of boats under-reporting their catches. Heavy shipping means near-misses with fishing boats in fog. Help is the Choshi coast guard, under an hour from port. Small villainy: catch fraud, fuel theft, and the occasional night transfer of smuggled goods between ships.

Sea off Iwami.name: Sea off Iwami
Sea off Iwami.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan off the Iwami coast of western Shimane, with the shore of Gotsu and Hamada just beyond the cell's southeastern corner. The green coastal hills and the town lights of Gotsu are visible on the southeastern horizon, and the long shape of Mount Sanbe rises inland to the east. The water is a deep, clear blue over the shelf, one to two hundred meters deep, with the Tsushima Current flowing northeast. Summers are calm and clear; autumn brings typhoon swells; winter brings northwest gales, high seas and snow squalls. Boats from Hamada, one of the biggest fishing ports on the San'in coast, work here for blackthroat seaperch, horse mackerel, squid and flatfish, and smaller boats from Gotsu and the Iwami hamlets fish closer in. No islands lie inside the cell, and only fishing boats and a few coastal freighters cross it. The coast guard patrols from Hamada, and a maritime hero covering the Shimane coast is the nearest hero help. A party could be out here on a fishing boat from Hamada, a charter, or flying over.
Sea off Iwami.hiddenInfo: The fishing towns on this coast are aging and catches are falling, so tempers flare over grounds and outside boats. Help is an hour or more away by boat from Hamada, and winter seas stop rescues outright. Villainy is petty: poaching and stolen gear.

Izumo Taisha.name: Izumo Taisha
Izumo Taisha.basicInfo: The western end of the Izumo plain and the Shimane Peninsula where they meet the Sea of Japan, a cell that is mostly open water, its coast running southwest from the cape of Hinomisaki to the Oda shore. The land is a narrow wedge along the eastern and southeastern edges. Its center is Izumo Taisha, one of the oldest and most revered shrines in Japan, at the foot of green hills on the eastern edge. Its main sanctuary is the tallest in Japan, and the twisted straw rope over the Kagura hall is as long as a bus. Worshippers come to pray for good marriages and lasting bonds, bowing twice and clapping four times. In the tenth month of the old calendar the gods of all Japan are said to gather here, so Izumo calls it the month with gods, and a bonfire rite on Inasa Beach, just west of the shrine, welcomes them ashore. Shinmon-dori, the approach street, is lined with shops selling Izumo soba in stacked lacquer boxes, red-bean zenzai and charms. North along the coast road stand vermilion Hinomisaki Shrine and Hinomisaki Lighthouse, Japan's tallest stone lighthouse, above cliffs where black-tailed gulls nest on Fumishima islet. South runs a line of fishing hamlets and coves, Taki, Kute and the Oda shore, with the singing sand of Kotogahama near the southern edge and Mount Sanbe's northern slopes at the border. Oda is a quiet small city of fishers, farmers and commuters; the old silver mine of Iwami Ginzan lies just beyond the cell to the south. Winters are gray and windy, with some snow. The Ichibata line runs from Matsue along Lake Shinji to Izumo Taisha-mae, JR's San'in Main Line runs down the coast through Oda, and buses run from Izumo-shi station and the airport. From Musutafu it is about six hours by shinkansen to Okayama and limited express to Izumo-shi, or a flight from Tokyo. From Osaka it is about four hours by train or highway bus. A police box stands at the shrine approach, and a small hero agency in Izumo sends sidekicks to the shrine when New Year and festival crowds swell. Quirks turn up in daily life: a soba maker who never tires, a fisher with a feel for the weather. Visitors pray, eat soba, watch the sunset from Inasa Beach and swim in summer.
Izumo Taisha.hiddenInfo: Izumo lives on pilgrims, and the prosperity is uneven: the approach street booms while the fishing hamlets and Oda empty out. Crowds at New Year and in the month with gods bring pickpockets, fake fortune-tellers, matchmaking hustlers and Quirk users selling blessings. The local agency is small; help from Izumo city is within half an hour, but a major incident means heroes from Hiroshima or Okayama, hours away. On the cliffs and coves, rescue work is a bigger part of the job than villainy.

Matsue.name: Matsue
Matsue.basicInfo: The heart of Shimane: the city of Matsue, Lake Shinji, the Izumo plain and the eastern Shimane Peninsula, with the Okuizumo hills rising to the south. The Shimane Peninsula forms the north, a low wall of green ridges whose coast is cut by fishing coves such as Kaga, where boats enter the sea cave of Kaga no Kukedo. Below it lie two linked lakes: brackish Lake Shinji in the west, famous for its sunsets and tiny shijimi clams, and the larger Nakaumi lagoon in the east, with Daikonshima island and its peony gardens. Matsue, the prefectural capital, sits on the channel between them, a city of canals around one of Japan's few original castle keeps, black-walled, with pleasure boats circling the moat under low bridges. Samurai houses line the northern moat. Tamatsukuri Onsen, south of the lake, is an old hot spring town. West of the lake spreads the Izumo plain, farm villages with tall pine windbreaks around each house, and the city of Izumo on the Hii River, with the airport, malls and factories. The Hii River country to the south is the land of the eight-headed serpent legend, with Yaegaki and Kamosu shrines near Matsue, Kisuki's riverbank cherries, and in Okuizumo the old tatara iron smelting that still makes steel for swordsmiths. The Adachi Museum of Art near Yasugi is known for its garden. On the eastern edge the Eshima Ohashi bridge arches steeply across Nakaumi toward Sakaiminato, a busy fishing port of red snow crab and tuna, with a street of bronze yokai statues and the ferry to the Oki Islands. Winters are damp and gray with some snow. Foods: shijimi soup, Izumo soba, the lake's seven delicacies, sweets with matcha. JR's San'in Main Line runs along the lake's south shore, the Ichibata line along the north shore, and two expressways carry the cars. The limited express from Okayama takes about two and a half hours; from Musutafu it is about six hours by train, or a flight to Izumo. From Osaka, about three and a half hours. Matsue and Izumo each have small hero agencies and police boxes; sidekicks patrol the castle area and the autumn water lantern festival. Quirks here run to lake and farm work, like a clam digger who feels shells through the mud.
Matsue.hiddenInfo: Matsue and Izumo are comfortable but aging, losing jobs and young adults to the cities beyond the mountains. The castle town draws tourists and with them minor theft and Quirk scams; Izumo's malls see shoplifting and the odd brawl. The local agencies are small but steady; a serious villain means calling heroes from Okayama or Hiroshima, two or three hours away. In the Okuizumo hills the danger is landslides and floods on the Hii River more than crime.

Mount Daisen.name: Mount Daisen
Mount Daisen.basicInfo: Western Tottori and the mountain that rules it: Mount Daisen, the highest peak in the Chugoku region at about 1,730 meters, with the Yonago plain, the Yumigahama spit and Miho Bay at its feet and the Hiruzen highlands to the south. Seen from the west, Daisen is a near-perfect cone, so people call it Hoki Fuji; from the north and south it is a jagged wall of crumbling ridges. Its slopes carry a vast beech forest, the ski runs above Daisen town, and the long stone-paved approach to Daisenji temple and Ogamiyama Shrine, an old center of mountain worship. Snow lies deep in winter; summer brings hikers up the summit trail before dawn. Yonago, western Tottori's commercial hub, is a working city near the Hino River's mouth, with Kaike Onsen's seaside hotels just north. The Yumigahama spit runs northwest from Yonago, a long bow of white sand and black pines between Miho Bay and the Nakaumi lagoon, with the airport and the fishing port of Sakaiminato near its tip. Across a narrow channel to the north, the eastern tip of the Shimane Peninsula holds Mihonoseki, an old port of stone-paved lanes and Miho Shrine, head shrine of the god of fishers and trade, whose boat rites draw crowds. Yasugi, on the western edge, is known for its loach-scooping folk dance. South, the Hino valley climbs through rice villages to the Okayama border and the Hiruzen highlands, a broad plateau of Jersey dairy farms and campgrounds under three gentle peaks. East, Kotoura's coastal farmland runs toward Kurayoshi. Food: Sakaiminato tuna and crab, Daisen dairy, Hiruzen's sweet-sauce yakisoba. The limited express from Okayama reaches Yonago in about two hours, the Yonago Expressway runs south past Hiruzen, the San'in Line follows the coast, and flights from Tokyo take about an hour and a half. From Musutafu the trip is about five hours by train; from Osaka, about three and a half by highway bus. Yonago has police stations and a few small hero agencies; a licensed mountain rescue hero works Daisen's trails, and sidekicks watch the beaches in summer. Farmers and fishers put practical Quirks to work. Visitors climb, ski, soak at Kaike, cycle Hiruzen and walk Mihonoseki's lanes.
Mount Daisen.hiddenInfo: Daisen's beauty hides real danger: the summit ridges crumble, winter whiteouts catch climbers, and rescue is a big part of local hero duty. Yonago is a modest city with a modest underside: small-time drug dealing, bar fights and Quirk scams aimed at the elderly. Sakaiminato's docks see catch fraud and labor disputes. Local agencies handle most of it; serious backup comes from Okayama, about two hours south, or from Matsue across the lagoon. In the Hiruzen highlands the worst crime is usually cattle or produce theft.

Tottori.name: Tottori
Tottori.basicInfo: The heart of Tottori Prefecture: the city of Tottori and its famous sand dunes in the east, Kurayoshi in the west, and the forested Chugoku Mountains rising to the south. The coast runs east to west along the cell's northern edge, a line of beaches, dunes and small ports. The Tottori Dunes, just north of the city, stretch about sixteen kilometers along the shore, rising into tall ridges where visitors climb, sandboard and ride camels; a sand sculpture museum nearby changes its theme yearly. Tottori city, a quiet prefectural capital, sits on the Sendai River below the old castle hill of Mount Kyusho. West along the coast lie Hakuto Shrine and beach, home of the legend of the white hare of Inaba, and Lake Togo with the hot spring town of Hawai on its shore. Kurayoshi, inland, keeps an old merchant quarter of white-walled storehouses along a canal. South of it, Misasa Onsen has radon hot springs and riverside baths, and on Mount Mitoku a temple hall clings to a sheer cliff at the top of a steep, rooted climb. Farther south the mountains rise to the Okayama border, cedar valleys and quiet villages such as Chizu with its preserved thatched farmhouses. Winters bring deep snow and heavy seas, and August days are hot and clear. The region grows twentieth-century pears and rakkyo scallions on the sandy fields, and its ports bring in snow crab, squid and rock oysters. Tottori's Shan-shan Festival in August fills the streets with umbrella dancers. The limited express from Osaka to Tottori through Chizu takes about two and a half hours. The San'in Main Line links the coast towns, an expressway runs south over the mountains, and flights from Tokyo land at the airport just west of the city. From Musutafu the trip is about four and a half hours by shinkansen and limited express. Tottori city and Kurayoshi each have police stations and a few small hero agencies; sidekicks patrol the dunes and the August festival, and one licensed hero covers the mountain towns. Quirks show up in farm and fishing work, like a pear grower who senses ripeness. Visitors walk the dunes, soak at Misasa and Hawai, climb Mount Mitoku and eat crab in winter.
Tottori.hiddenInfo: Tottori is Japan's least populous prefecture and feels it: shuttered shops in the town centers, aging villages in the mountains, young adults leaving for Osaka. Tourists at the dunes and hot springs bring car break-ins and the odd scam. The local agencies are small; real numbers come from Osaka or Okayama, two to three hours away. In winter, heavy snow and closed roads isolate mountain villages, and the coast's sand and sea draw more rescues than crimes. Villainy is mostly petty: produce theft, poaching, a Quirk-fueled drunk at the festival.

Toyooka.name: Toyooka
Toyooka.basicInfo: The Tajima highlands of northern Hyogo, inland from the Sea of Japan: the lower Maruyama River valley around Toyooka, the Yabu and Asago valleys to the south, and the high, snowy Hyonosen range in the west. The cell is almost all land. Toyooka sits on a flat, flood-prone basin where the Maruyama runs slowly north toward the sea; rice paddies there are farmed without pesticide so that reintroduced Oriental white storks, once extinct in the wild, can feed in them, and the great white birds are a common sight on rooftops and poles. Kinosaki's hot springs lie just over the northern edge.
