South of Toyooka, Izushi is a small castle town of stone walls, a wooden clock tower and dozens of shops serving buckwheat noodles on small plates. Farther south, Yabu and Yoka line the river's upper valley, and at Asago the ruins of Takeda Castle crown a ridge that rises above an autumn sea of clouds, earning it the name castle in the sky. The old Ikuno silver mine lies at the southern edge, its tunnels open for tours. The western mountains are cattle country, home of the Tajima black cattle from which Kobe beef descends, with ski slopes at Hachi-Kita and Hyonosen and the hot-spring village of Yumura, where people boil eggs in the scalding springs. Summers are hot in the basins, winters gray and deeply snowy. Toyooka also makes a large share of Japan's bags and cases. The JR Sanin line runs up the Maruyama valley and the Bantan line south to Himeji, the Kitakinki Toyooka Expressway links to the Bantan road, and a small airport at Toyooka has flights to Osaka. Shin-Osaka is about two and a half hours by the Konotori limited express, Musutafu about four and a half. Toyooka has a small hero agency, and licensed heroes cover the valleys from there and from Yoka; a cattle farmer whose Quirk calms livestock is the kind of thing everyone in a village knows about.
Toyooka.hiddenInfo: The worries are aging villages, winter isolation and the cattle trade: Tajima breeding stock is valuable, and theft of calves or bloodlines is a known rural crime. Hikers and skiers go missing on Hyonosen. Small villainy is copper theft, shoplifting at roadside stations and onsen-town drunkenness. Major hero help is two hours away in Kobe or Osaka; local heroes handle almost everything alone.

Maizuru.name: Maizuru
Maizuru.basicInfo: The Tango and Tamba country of northern Kyoto Prefecture, from the sea at Maizuru and Miyazu south through the Yura River valley to Fukuchiyama and Ayabe and the low Tamba hills along the Hyogo line. In the north, Maizuru lies on a deep, many-armed harbor: East Maizuru is a naval town of red-brick warehouses, gray Maritime Self-Defense Force ships and a coast guard headquarters, with the overnight ferry to Otaru in Hokkaido leaving from its port, while West Maizuru is an older castle and fishing town. Westward along the coast, Miyazu Bay holds Amanohashidate, a pine-covered sandbar more than three kilometers long that visitors view upside-down between their legs from the Kasamatsu lookout, with Chion-ji temple at its south end and Kono Shrine at the north. Behind Miyazu rise the Oe mountains, home in legend of the demon Shuten-doji. The Yura River winds south through steep valleys to Fukuchiyama, a busy rail junction and castle town that floods when the river rises and logs some of Kyoto Prefecture's hottest summer days, and to Ayabe, a quiet textile and paper town. Southern Tamba is gentle hills, chestnut groves, black-soybean fields and thatched farmhouses, often under thick autumn morning fog. Winters bring snow in the north and wet cold in the basins. People fish, farm, work at the port and the base, and commute by rail. Food is Maizuru's sea bream and squid, Miyazu's oysters and torigai cockles, Tamba chestnuts and wild boar. The JR Sanin line runs through Ayabe and Fukuchiyama, the Maizuru line to East Maizuru, the Fukuchiyama line south to Osaka, and the Kyoto Tango Railway along the coast; the Maizuru-Wakasa and Kyoto Jukan expressways cross the cell. Shin-Osaka is under two hours, Kyoto about an hour and a half, Musutafu three and a half to four. Each of the main towns has a small hero agency and police boxes, and the naval presence keeps the port orderly; at harvest, a chestnut grower with a gentle telekinetic Quirk shakes whole trees clean in minutes.
Maizuru.hiddenInfo: The region is stable but slowly shrinking, and the base and the ferry bring outsiders through constantly. Small-time trouble is car break-ins at Amanohashidate, fights in East Maizuru's bars and shellfish poaching. Floods on the Yura draw every local hero out at once. Bigger help is in Kyoto and Osaka, an hour and a half or more away.

Wakasa.name: Wakasa
Wakasa.basicInfo: The inner Wakasa Bay coast of Fukui and the wild mountains behind it, stretching south over the watershed into the forested uplands of northern Kyoto and the western flank of the Hira range above Lake Biwa. The north edge is a drowned ria coast: Obama sits on its own small bay, Takahama to the west has the bay's best swimming beaches under Mount Aoba, the Wakasa Fuji, with steep wooded headlands between them. Obama is an old port town of temples, quiet wooden streets and lacquer workshops that make most of Japan's lacquered chopsticks. Each March, at Jingu-ji and on the Onyu River, a night fire ceremony sends sacred water toward Nara's Todai-ji. From Obama the old Mackerel Road runs southeast through the post town of Kumagawa-juku and the Kutsuki valley toward Kyoto, once carrying salted mackerel to the capital overnight. South of the watershed lies a deep, quiet country: the Ashiu forest, one of the largest natural forests left in western Japan; the hamlet of Miyama with its dozens of tall thatched farmhouses; and the Keihoku and Hanase valleys, where cedar plantations and narrow roads wind toward Kyoto's northern suburbs. The Hira peaks on the east rise past a thousand meters, with Lake Biwa just beyond. Winters are snowy, summers mild on the coast and cool in the mountains. Food is grilled mackerel, heshiko mackerel fermented in rice bran, Wakasa tilefish and wild mountain vegetables. The JR Obama line and the Maizuru-Wakasa Expressway follow the coast; buses run the Mackerel Road and up the valleys. Shin-Osaka is about two and a half hours, Musutafu about three and a half by way of Tsuruga. Obama has a small hero agency and police boxes; the mountain villages rely on a few licensed heroes who drive long loops, and a forestry crew may include someone whose Quirk lets them feel rot inside a trunk.
Wakasa.hiddenInfo: Inland, depopulation leaves empty houses that squatters and petty thieves use, and deer and bears get into fields; a bear in a village is the most common emergency. Small crime is theft from roadside stores and illegal dumping in the hills. Kyoto's agencies are an hour or two away; most days the local heroes are alone.

Lake Biwa.name: Lake Biwa
Lake Biwa.basicInfo: The northern half of Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, with the Shiga shores around it and the Ibuki and Sekigahara country to the east. About a third of the cell is water: the lake's broad northern basin, blue and wind-ruffled, with the steep forested islet of Chikubushima and its temple and shrine reached by tour boat, and inhabited Okishima nearer the east shore. On the east side, Nagahama is an old market town with a black-walled glass quarter and an April festival of kabuki staged on float tops; Maibara is a rail junction and the region's shinkansen stop; and Hikone keeps an original castle keep on a hill above its moat, with the Genkyu-en garden below. Behind them the hills rise to Taga Taisha shrine, and Mount Ibuki lifts its bald, snowy dome to the northeast, famous for medicinal herbs and alpine flowers. Just over the Gifu line sits Sekigahara, the old battlefield in a narrow pass. The west shore is quieter: Takashima's lakeside villages, Shirahige Shrine's vermilion torii standing in the water, the cherry tunnel at Kaizu Osaki and the Makino plateau. The far north, around Lake Yogo and Shizugatake, is snowy farm country. Winters are cold, with heavy snow in the north and around Ibuki; summers are hot and humid, and each July Hikone's lakeshore hosts a crowd-drawing contest of homemade human-powered aircraft launched off a platform. Food is Omi beef, funazushi fermented carp, Biwa trout, ayu and duck hot pot. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Maibara, about an hour and a half from Musutafu and forty-five minutes from Shin-Osaka; the Biwako, Hokuriku and Kosei lines circle the lake, and the Meishin and Hokuriku expressways meet at Maibara. Boats link Nagahama, Hikone and Imazu to Chikubushima. Each town has a small hero agency and police boxes, a lake patrol watches the water, and at the July flight contest sidekicks with flight Quirks stand by to fish out pilots.
Lake Biwa.hiddenInfo: Lake country is comfortable and busy with commuters, and Hikone and Nagahama see tourist crowds on weekends. Trouble is drowning and boating accidents, poaching of protected lake fish, and theft at festivals. Sekigahara's pass is a choke point where snowy expressway pileups are the worst emergencies of the year. Big-city hero help is under an hour away in Kyoto, Nagoya or Osaka.

Nagoya.name: Nagoya
Nagoya.basicInfo: Nagoya is the cell of the Nobi plain and the core of Japan's third great metropolitan area: Nagoya city at the southeast, Gifu and Ogaki to the northwest, the old towns of Inuyama, Seki and Mino along the northern hills, and between them a flat, crowded patchwork of suburbs, rice fields and factories cut by the Kiso, Nagara and Ibi rivers. The Yoro hills close the southwest, the Mino highlands rise to the north and east, and Ise Bay lies just beyond the southern edge. Summers are among the hottest and most humid in the country; winters are dry and bright, with a cold wind off Mount Ibuki that can push snow through the Sekigahara gap to the west. Nagoya is a big, broad-avenued industrial capital of more than two million people: the castle topped with golden dolphin-tigers, the department stores and underground malls of Sakae and the towers over the station, the bargain arcades and temple of Osu, and the TV tower in the Hisaya Odori park. Its economy runs on cars, aerospace and machine tools. Gifu sits under Mount Kinka, whose summit castle looks down on the Nagara River, where cormorant fishers work by torchlight from May to October. Inuyama keeps one of Japan's oldest original castles above the Kiso River, Seki makes knives and blades from a long smithing tradition, Mino makes handmade washi paper behind fire-wall rooftops, and Ogaki is a city of springs and moats. Nagoya food is its own cuisine: miso katsu, peppery tebasaki wings, hitsumabushi eel over rice, kishimen noodles and generous morning sets at coffee shops. The Nagoya Festival parades in October and Inuyama's floats in spring. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Nagoya and Gifu-Hashima; JR, Meitetsu and Kintetsu lines fan across the plain, the subway rings the city, and expressways and the Komaki airfield tie it together. Musutafu is about an hour and a quarter away by shinkansen; Shin-Osaka is under an hour. Nagoya hosts dozens of hero agencies, from large downtown offices to neighborhood ones, with sidekicks on every major street and a heavy police presence; the outer towns keep smaller agencies, and factory workers with strength or materials Quirks hold workplace licenses.
Nagoya.hiddenInfo: Nagoya's undercurrents are industrial: subcontractor plants squeezed by the big makers, foreign laborers in cramped dormitories, parts theft and quarrels on the shop floor, and the Nishiki nightlife district where small gangs collect protection money. Purse snatching, car theft and Quirk-fueled street fights are ordinary city crime, and smuggling moves along the expressways between Tokyo and Osaka. Hero response inside Nagoya is fast, often minutes; in the river towns and the western rice country a call can take half an hour.

Nakatsugawa.name: Nakatsugawa
Nakatsugawa.basicInfo: Nakatsugawa is the cell of the Tono hills in southeastern Gifu and the northeastern edge of Aichi: rolling granite uplands and pottery towns between the Nobi plain and the Kiso valley, with Mount Ena standing at the northeast corner. In the west lie Tajimi, Toki and Mizunami, the heart of Mino ware, where kilns and ceramics works have fired bowls and tiles for centuries; Seto, the pottery city that gave Japan its everyday word for ceramics, sits at the southwest corner. The middle holds Ena and its dammed Kiso River gorge, Iwamura with its merchant street under the ruins of a high mountain castle, and Akechi, a village that keeps a Taisho-era townscape. In the northeast, Nakatsugawa spreads along the Kiso River below Mount Ena, and on the ridge above it the post towns of Magome and Tsumago keep the stone paths, wooden inns and water wheels of the old Nakasendo highway; walkers do the trail between them in a few hours. The southern hills of Toyota hold Obara, where cherry trees bloom in autumn among the maples, and Mount Sanage rises above the Aichi plain. Summers in the low basins are notoriously hot, with Tajimi often among the hottest towns in Japan; the uplands are cooler, autumn is long and bright, and winter brings frost and a little snow. People make ceramics, run small factories and quarries, grow chestnuts, rice and tea, and commute to Nagoya. Local foods are kuri kinton chestnut sweets, gohei-mochi grilled rice cakes in sesame-walnut miso and hebo wasp-larvae rice. The JR Chuo Main Line runs from Nagoya through Tajimi to Nakatsugawa with the limited express Shinano, the Chuo Expressway follows it, the Akechi Railway runs a single car to Akechi, and the Taita Line links Tajimi to Mino-Ota. A new maglev line is being dug through the hills near Nakatsugawa, with construction yards and tunnel portals in the valleys. Musutafu is about two and a half hours away by shinkansen to Nagoya and the Chuo Line. Visitors walk the Nakasendo and browse pottery fairs. Each town keeps police boxes and a small hero office; most hero work here is traffic and industrial accidents along the Chuo corridor, and potters with heat Quirks fire their kilns under licenses.
Nakatsugawa.hiddenInfo: Nakatsugawa's undercurrent is a slow drain of people toward Nagoya and a quarrel over the maglev works: tunnel spoil, failing wells and construction money split neighbors. The pottery trade is full of small shops struggling, and counterfeit wares and kiln-equipment theft turn up. Walkers on the Nakasendo get lost or hurt, and bears visit the chestnut orchards. Hero help is within half an hour along the Chuo corridor, much slower in the back hills.

Iida.name: Iida
Iida.basicInfo: Iida is the cell of the southern Ina valley in southern Nagano, where the Tenryu River runs south between two walls of mountains: the tail of the Central Alps and the Kiso hills on the west, and the high Southern Alps on the east, where Mount Akaishi, Mount Hijiri and Mount Arakawa top 3,000 meters along the Shizuoka border. Iida city sits on river terraces in the northwest; south of it the Tenryu enters long gorges past Tenryukyo and the hamlets of Tenryu village before the valley narrows toward the dam country of the Aichi-Shizuoka border. The east is roadless high forest: the Toyama valley at the foot of the Alps, the Shimoguri hamlet perched on steep slopes, the Shirabiso highland with its views of the range, and the upper Oi River country on the Shizuoka side. The air is clear and dry, summers warm, winters cold with little snow in the valley floor; Achi village to the southwest is known for some of the darkest night skies in Japan. Iida is a small city of apple-tree avenues, a castle-town grid rebuilt after a great fire, and crafts: it makes most of Japan's mizuhiki paper cord for gift wrapping, holds a summer puppet theater festival, and keeps more barbecue restaurants per head than almost anywhere. The countryside grows apples, pears and ichida persimmons that hang drying from farmhouse eaves in autumn. In December the Toyama valley's Shimotsuki festival boils water in iron cauldrons all night while masked gods dance through the steam. The JR Iida Line winds through the valley from Toyohashi to Okaya, slow and full of remote stations; the Chuo Expressway reaches Iida from Nagoya, expressway buses run to Nagoya in about two hours and Tokyo in about four, and a new maglev station is being built near the city. Musutafu is about four hours away by shinkansen to Toyohashi and the Iida Line, or by road via Nagoya. Visitors ride boats down the Tenryu gorge, stargaze at Achi, soak at the Hirugami hot springs and climb the Southern Alps. Iida has a police station and a couple of small hero offices that cover enormous districts; heroes with flight or speed Quirks are prized here, and orchard growers with plant Quirks work under permits.
Iida.hiddenInfo: Iida's undercurrent is distance: the eastern and southern valleys are among the emptiest in Honshu, landslides close roads, and elders live alone far from clinics. Crime is quiet, mostly theft from vacant houses, phone frauds and the occasional fugitive who thinks the valley a good place to vanish. Climbers in the Southern Alps need rescue every season. Hero help from Iida takes an hour or more to reach the far hamlets; larger response comes from Nagoya or Matsumoto.

Fujinomiya.name: Fujinomiya
Fujinomiya.basicInfo: Fujinomiya is the cell west of Mount Fuji: the paper-mill city of Fuji on the coast at the southeast corner, Fujinomiya town on the mountain's southwest skirt, the Asagiri plateau and three of the Fuji Five Lakes in the northeast, the Fuji River valley through Yamanashi's Minobu country in the middle, and the empty foothills of the Southern Alps around the upper Oi and Abe rivers in the west. Mount Fuji's summit stands just beyond the eastern edge, filling the sky. Fuji city's shore at Tagonoura is the region's only coast, a strip of dark sand and a small fishing harbor with Suruga Bay to the south. The Fuji River, fast and gray with gravel, comes down from the Kofu basin through gorges and reaches the sea just south of the city. The climate runs from mild on the coast to cold on the plateau. Fuji is an industrial city of paper and pulp mills whose white smokestacks frame the volcano, and Tagonoura lands tiny shirasu whitebait. Fujinomiya is a gateway town of the mountain, built around the head Sengen shrine; it is known for chewy Fujinomiya yakisoba, trout farms fed by spring water, and dairy and tea on the lower slopes. North of town the Shiraito Falls spill in hundreds of silken threads from a curved lava cliff, and the Asagiri plateau grows grass for dairy cows and launches paragliders. Lakes Motosu, Shoji and Sai lie in a dark sea of lava forest, Aokigahara, where wind and ice caves open in old lava tubes. Up the Fuji valley, Minobu is a temple town on a cedar mountain, home of the head temple of the Nichiren school and its famous weeping cherries. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Shin-Fuji, the JR Tokaido and Minobu lines meet at Fuji, the Tomei, Shin-Tomei and Chubu-Odan expressways cross the region, and Route 139 climbs north around the mountain's western side to the lakes. Musutafu, the neighbor to the southeast, is about fifteen minutes away by kodama, and Tokyo about an hour and ten minutes. Visitors camp by the lakes, paddle and tour the caves and falls. Fuji and Fujinomiya keep police stations and several hero agencies; mountain and forest rescue is a constant job for licensed heroes with flight or sensing Quirks.
Fujinomiya.hiddenInfo: Fujinomiya's undercurrents are the mills and the mountain. Fuji's paper industry is shrinking, leaving older workers anxious and some mill land idle, while tourist traffic on Route 139 brings crashes, illegal camping and litter around the lakes. Hikers and campers get lost in the lava forest, and search parties are a familiar sight. The Minobu valley is emptying. Hero help is quick in Fuji and Fujinomiya and close at hand from the busy cities to the east; the western Alps valleys wait an hour or more.

Kamino and Yokohama.name: Kamino and Yokohama
Kamino and Yokohama.basicInfo: Kamino and Yokohama is the western shore of Tokyo Bay and the hills behind it, about 30 kilometers southwest of central Tokyo and about an hour east of Musutafu by the Tokaido line, where the capital's sprawl runs down to the sea. Yokohama is a working port city of piers, container docks, cranes and harbor parks, with Chinatown's painted gates a short walk inland, a waterfront of red-brick warehouses turned into shops and restaurants, and ferries and cruise ships along the quays; its harbor district is busy day and night with dock crews, truckers, tourists and late-shift bars. About 11 kilometers northwest of the harbor lies Kamino Ward, a tired old ward of shuttered shops, aging apartment blocks, idle warehouses and winding backstreets, where small bars hide down alleys and half the storefronts have not opened in years. Takoba Municipal Stadium stands among sports fields about 12 kilometers southwest of the harbor and hosts school meets, local tournaments and the Commission's licensing exams. Beyond them the land breaks into wooded hills and commuter towns; south along the coast lie the old temple town of Kamakura with its giant bronze Buddha and beaches, the naval port of Yokosuka, and the Miura Peninsula, its tip of fishing harbors and radish fields facing the mouth of the bay. Summers are hot and humid with sea breezes, typhoons in late summer close the port for a day or two, and winters are mild and bright. The economy is the port, shipping, logistics and factories along the bay, the restaurants of Chinatown, tourism and the commuters who ride north into Tokyo every morning. The prefectural police keep order, with police boxes at the stations and harbor patrols on the water; heroes and police patrol the harbor often and Kamino rarely, and the ward's residents have stopped expecting them. People get around by commuter rail into Tokyo in half an hour, local lines and buses, harbor water buses and taxis. A visitor can eat through Chinatown, walk the harbor parks, take dock or warehouse work, sit a licensing exam at Takoba, ride down to the Kamakura beaches, or vanish into the backstreets of a ward nobody watches.
Kamino and Yokohama.hiddenInfo: On the coast the underworld's trade runs quietly: brokers working out of Yokohama's port and Chinatown move unlicensed gear and hired muscle through the container yards, and Kamino's backstreet bars are where small-time villains go looking for cash work. Lately one new buyer with money and no reputation has been hiring through those brokers, and almost nobody has asked who it is. Kamino's empty warehouses are rented through shell companies and visited at night, and the ward's few police boxes log nothing they cannot explain.

Boso Peninsula.name: Boso Peninsula
Boso Peninsula.basicInfo: The middle of the Boso Peninsula, a cell running from the Tokyo Bay shore across low, deeply cut hills to the Pacific at Katsuura, with its western strip in the bay. On the bay side, the Aqua-Line bridge and tunnel come ashore at Kisarazu after crossing from Kawasaki by way of the Umihotaru rest island; around it lie the tidal flats of Banzu, where families dig clams, and south along the shore Kimitsu's steelworks, Futtsu's sandspit cape and nori beds, and the ferry port of Kanaya under the quarried cliffs and great carved Buddha of Mount Nokogiri. Sodegaura and Ichihara to the north are refinery and petrochemical towns at the end of the Keiyo industrial belt. Inland the Boso hills are no higher than a few hundred meters but steep and tangled, with cedar, bamboo and river gorges like Yoro, the castle town of Otaki, the spring water and sake breweries of Kururi, and Lake Kameyama. On the Pacific side Mobara is a market and natural gas town, and Katsuura on its rocky southeastern coast holds one of Japan's great morning markets and a famous fiery tantanmen. The climate is mild and moist, warm in winter, with heavy typhoon rain in early autumn; flowers bloom early and the hills turn color late. People work the bay plants, commute to Tokyo by bus over the Aqua-Line, farm rice, vegetables and flowers, fish, and keep inns and golf courses. The Uchibo, Kururi and Sotobo lines, the Kominato Railway and the little Isumi Railway serve the cell; the Tateyama and Ken-O expressways and the Aqua-Line carry most travelers, and a car ferry crosses from Kurihama to Kanaya in about forty minutes. Highway buses reach Kisarazu from Tokyo Station in about an hour, so Musutafu is about two hours away. Visitors dig clams at Kisarazu, ride the ropeway up Nokogiri, hike the Yoro gorge in late autumn, visit Otaki castle, and eat Katsuura tantanmen and namero, minced raw fish with miso. Small hero agencies in Kisarazu and Ichihara cover the bay; Katsuura and the hill towns rely on the police and roving licensed heroes, and a nori farmer whose Quirk lets them breathe underwater tends the seaweed lines.
Boso Peninsula.hiddenInfo: Boso feels close to Tokyo yet left behind: the hill villages are aging fast, storm damage to roofs and cedar forests lingers, and wild boar and invasive muntjac deer strip the fields. The bay towns live on heavy industry and fear the day the plants close. Hero help is twenty minutes away on the bay and much longer in the hills. Small villainy: illegal dumping in hill valleys, theft of copper wire and solar panels, drunk fights in the industrial towns, and smugglers using small harbors.

Kujukuri Coast.name: Kujukuri Coast
Kujukuri Coast.basicInfo: The southern half of Kujukuri beach and the Isumi coast, a slim strip of dune, pine and fishing town along Chiba's Pacific shore, with nearly all of the cell open sea. The land is the edge of the Boso plain and its beach: from Katakai fishing harbor in Kujukuri town south past Shirako's tennis courts and hot springs, Chosei, and Ichinomiya's surfing beach at Tsurigasaki to the low cliffs of Cape Taito, then the rocky coves and harbor of Ohara in Isumi, where the beach finally gives way to the Boso hills. Behind the dunes lie rice paddies, onion fields and greenhouse rows, with the Sotobo line and its stations a few kilometers inland. Everything east is open Pacific, steel blue on a calm day, with long, even swells that make this one of the best surf coasts near Tokyo. Winters are mild and sunny, summers breezy, and typhoons hit hard in early autumn. People fish for sardines and clams, catch spiny lobster at Ohara, farm, run surf shops, beach houses and tennis camps, and commute to Chiba and Mobara. The Sotobo line brings limited expresses from Tokyo to Kazusa-Ichinomiya in about an hour, the Isumi Railway runs inland from Ohara through spring rape-blossom fields, and the Kujukuri toll road runs along the dunes. From Musutafu allow about two and a half hours. Visitors surf Ichinomiya, eat grilled clams and sardine dishes at Katakai, watch the September festivals where portable shrines are carried into the surf at Tsurigasaki and Ohara, and walk the long beach at dawn. A small hero agency in Mobara covers the coast; in summer, sidekicks and lifeguards with water and wind Quirks watch the beaches, and police boxes stand in each town.
Kujukuri Coast.hiddenInfo: Surfers and weekend homeowners from Tokyo have pushed up rents in Ichinomiya, and older fishing families feel squeezed out. Rip currents and typhoon surf drown visitors most years. Hero help is fifteen to thirty minutes away in Mobara, and the sea belongs to the coast guard. Small villainy looks like thefts from beach cars and surf shops, night poaching of spiny lobster and clams, and drunken Quirk scuffles at summer beach bars.

Pacific off Kujukuri.name: Pacific off Kujukuri
Pacific off Kujukuri.basicInfo: The open Pacific forty to ninety kilometers off Kujukuri beach, a wide, empty reach of deep-blue ocean east of the Boso Peninsula. The coast is below the horizon, and only cloud over the land marks where it lies. The bottom is far down, beyond the shelf and slope, more than a kilometer deep across most of the cell. The warm Kuroshio swings northeast through here, bringing bonito and flying fish in spring and summer, and long swells roll in steadily from the southeast. Typhoons cross in late summer and autumn, and winter brings strong northwest winds and short, steep seas. Purse seiners from Katakai and Choshi chase sardines, and bonito boats from Katsuura and Ohara work the edges of the current. Cargo ships bound for Tokyo Bay and the northern ports pass in steady lines. The coast guard watches from the air and from patrol boats out of Choshi and Tateyama, with maritime heroes on call. A party could be out here on a passing ship, a deep-sea fishing boat, or carried by a flying hero.
Pacific off Kujukuri.hiddenInfo: Little happens out here: the danger is weather, fatigue and collisions in poor visibility. Help is the coast guard, an hour or more away by sea and quicker by helicopter. Small-time villainy at sea means illegal dumping from ships and boats fishing out of season.

Waters off Tsushima.name: Waters off Tsushima
Waters off Tsushima.basicInfo: The open water just north of Tsushima, where the Korea Strait widens into the Sea of Japan. Only the very tip of Tsushima's northern shore brushes the southern edge; everything else is sea, a deep blue over a shelf that drops past a hundred meters, with the Korean coast just below the northwestern horizon and nothing but water to the north and east. The warm Tsushima Current runs steadily northeast through it and keeps the winters mild, but from December to February the northwest monsoon raises short, steep seas that cancel small-boat trips, and typhoons sweep through in late summer. High-speed ferries between Busan and Hitakatsu, the port at Tsushima's north end, cut across the southwest corner in a little over an hour, and cargo ships bound for the strait pass in steady lines. On summer nights the horizon glows with the lamps of squid boats out of Tsushima's northern harbors; squid, yellowtail and sea bream are the catch. Coast guard patrol boats from Tsushima watch these border waters closely, and a licensed hero who can fly or swim long distances is called out for ferry emergencies, since the nearest large agencies are in Fukuoka, more than two hours away by fast boat. A party is out here on a ferry, a chartered fishing boat, or carried by a flying hero.
Waters off Tsushima.hiddenInfo: These are border waters, and most trouble here is quiet: foreign fishing boats straying over the line at night, small-time smugglers hiding contraband in fish holds, drift nets cut loose. The coast guard handles nearly all of it. Real hero help is far off; even a flying hero out of Fukuoka needs well over an hour, so crews in trouble rely on each other first.

Sea off Nagato.name: Sea off Nagato
Sea off Nagato.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of the Nagato coast of Yamaguchi Prefecture, a square of water with no land in it at all. The shore lies over the southern horizon, where the sea cliffs of Omijima and the headlands around Senzaki show as a low line on clear days; to the east, beyond this water, the small island of Mishima rides alone. The sea is a deep navy over a continental shelf a hundred meters and more down, carried northeast by the warm Tsushima Current. Summers are calm and hazy; from November the northwest monsoon piles up whitecaps and gray swells that keep small boats in port for days at a time. It is a working fishing ground: boats out of Senzaki, Tsunoshima and Hagi set nets and long-lines for yellowtail, sea bream and kensaki squid, and squid boats hang rows of bright lamps here on summer nights. Cargo traffic between the Kanmon Strait and the ports of the Sea of Japan coast passes well offshore. The coast guard office at Senzaki patrols these grounds, and maritime heroes from the Shimonoseki and Kitakyushu side are an hour or more away. A party is out here aboard a fishing boat, a coast guard cutter, or carried by a hero who can fly.
Sea off Nagato.hiddenInfo: Mostly empty water, and that is the danger: an engine failure here means drifting a long way before anyone notices. Unlicensed boats work the squid grounds at night with their lights off, and local fishermen complain of foreign boats on their grounds. Hero help means a call to the coast guard first and a long wait.

Sea off Mishima.name: Sea off Mishima
Sea off Mishima.basicInfo: Open Sea of Japan north of Hagi, holding one real island: Mishima, a small, steep-sided green island about forty-five kilometers offshore near the western edge. A few hundred people live there around one harbor village, fishing and raising Mishima cattle, a rare native breed protected as a natural monument, and a field of ancient stone burial mounds lies along its shore. A ferry from Hagi port reaches the island in a little over an hour and is canceled often in winter. The rest is open water, deep blue over the shelf and carried northeast by the warm Tsushima Current. Hagi's smaller islands and the long ridges of the Abu coast show to the south on clear days, and the Shimane shore lies beyond the eastern horizon. Summers are calm; winter northwesterlies raise gray seas for weeks. Boats from Hagi, Susa and Mishima fish for squid, sea bream and yellowtail, and squid boats light the dark on summer nights. The coast guard watches from Hagi and Senzaki; Mishima itself has a resident police post and depends on the mainland for anything more. A party is out here on the ferry, a fishing boat, or with a flying hero.
Sea off Mishima.hiddenInfo: Mishima's worry is the ordinary island one: fewer people each year, the ferry as the only lifeline, and a long wait for help in a storm. Petty trouble is rare and personal. Out on the water, night poachers and foreign boats on the squid grounds are the coast guard's business; a serious emergency means a helicopter or a flying hero from the mainland, an hour or more away.

Hamada.name: Hamada
Hamada.basicInfo: Hamada is a stretch of the San'in coast in western Shimane where the Chugoku Mountains come almost straight down to the Sea of Japan. Most of this cell is open water: the sea fills the north and west, and the land is only the southeastern corner, a strip of shore and steep hills running northeast from the mouth of the Takatsu River near Masuda, through the small town of Misumi, to the port city of Hamada on the eastern edge. Behind narrow beaches and rocky capes, cedar ridges climb within a few kilometers, cut by short rivers, terraced paddies and hamlets roofed in the glossy red-brown Sekishu tiles of Iwami. Winters are gray and raw, with northwest monsoon winds, sleet and heavy surf; summers are humid and bright, and the water at beaches such as Kokubu turns clear blue. Hamada, a fishing city of a few tens of thousands, is one of the busiest ports on this coast, known for nodoguro blackthroat seaperch, squid, flatfish and horse mackerel split and dried on racks along the harbor. Above the harbor stand the stone walls of Hamada Castle, the Hamada Marine Bridge arches out to Setogashima island, and the AQUAS aquarium north of town has belugas that blow bubble rings. Misumi makes Sekishu washi, a UNESCO-listed mulberry paper. This is the home ground of Iwami kagura, the fast, drum-driven shrine dance whose climax is the eight-headed serpent Orochi, its coils pouring smoke; troupes perform at autumn shrine festivals and on weekend stages all year. The single-track San'in Main Line hugs the coast, its Super Oki limited express running to Shin-Yamaguchi and Izumo. The Hamada Expressway climbs south over the mountains, express buses reach Hiroshima in about two hours, and Iwami Airport near Masuda has flights to Haneda. From Musutafu it is most of a day, about six hours by shinkansen to Hiroshima and bus; from Fukuoka it is about three and a half hours by shinkansen and the Super Oki. One small hero agency in Hamada covers the coast from Masuda to Gotsu, police boxes sit by the stations, divers with cold-proof or gill-breathing Quirks work the cooperative's turban-shell grounds under license, and sidekicks walk the shrine grounds on kagura nights.
Hamada.hiddenInfo: The coast is aging and emptying: young people leave for Hiroshima, Osaka and Fukuoka, boats sit idle, and the fishing cooperative watches closely for poachers. Small-time trouble here is a Quirk-user stripping abalone and sea urchin from cooperative grounds at night, fuel and gear stolen from moored boats, fights in harbor bars, and the odd kagura performer who tries a real fire Quirk on stage and gets cited for it. The coast guard office in Hamada handles the sea; serious hero backup comes from Hiroshima, two hours over the mountains, so the local agency improvises and leans on the police.

Iwami.name: Iwami
Iwami.basicInfo: Iwami is the mountain heart of old Iwami Province in central Shimane, a cell of steep forested ridges and narrow valleys that touches the Sea of Japan only along its northwest edge. There the port town of Gotsu sits at the mouth of the Gonokawa, the longest river in the Chugoku region, and the coast runs northeast past the old hot-spring port of Yunotsu to the singing-sand beach of Kotogahama at Nima; the sea lies northwest of that line and everything else is land. Inland, the Gonokawa loops through gorges and quiet river towns such as Kawamoto and Misato, beside the rusting bed of the closed Sanko Line. In a wooded valley in the northeast lies Iwami Ginzan, the silver mine that once fed a large share of the world's silver and is now a World Heritage site: the Omori street of wooden merchant houses, the Ryugenji shaft open to visitors, and forest trails past shrines and hundreds of old tunnel mouths. The grassy volcanic domes of Mount Sanbe rise on the northeast edge, with Sanbe Onsen and pastures at their foot. The south is cold high plateau along the Hiroshima border, the farm towns of Onan and northern Kitahiroshima, with ski slopes at Mizuho Highland and Geihoku. Winters bring gray skies and deep snow inland; autumn fills the valleys with morning fog. Gotsu fires Iwami-yaki pottery, famous for huge glazed water jars, and the red Sekishu roof tiles seen across the region; elsewhere people grow rice, cut timber, hunt wild boar, brew sake and run inns for heritage visitors. Yunotsu is a small World Heritage hot-spring town of tiled bathhouses, and Iwami kagura is danced at shrines in every valley. The San'in Main Line and the Super Oki follow the coast through Gotsu; the Hamada Expressway crosses the southern plateau, and express buses run to Hiroshima, the nearest big city, in about two and a half hours. From Musutafu it is most of a day, six hours or more by shinkansen to Hiroshima and bus. Police boxes sit in each town, one or two licensed heroes cover dozens of valleys by car and on foot, heritage wardens ask visitors not to use Quirks inside the old shafts, and farmers with strength Quirks haul timber and snow under their work permits.
Iwami.hiddenInfo: Depopulation is the slow crisis: empty houses, shuttered schools, boar and deer stripping the fields, and roads cut by landslides in the rainy season. Small-time trouble is treasure hunters crawling into unmapped Ginzan shafts after silver ore, thieves lifting old tiles and pottery from abandoned houses, night speeders on the mountain roads, and an unregistered Quirk-user poaching ayu. Real hero help is far: Hiroshima is over two hours south and Matsue more than that, so rescues depend on police, volunteer fire brigades and whichever hero is on duty in the district.

Miyoshi.name: Miyoshi
Miyoshi.basicInfo: Miyoshi is the high basin country of northern Hiroshima Prefecture, where the Chugoku Mountains spread into rolling plateaus, river valleys and the forested peaks of the Hiba Mountains along the Shimane border. It is all land, far from any coast. In the southwest, the river town of Miyoshi sits where three rivers meet to form the Gonokawa, and in summer cormorant fishers work the river at night by firelight; in the center, Shobara spreads across a farming basin, and to the north the wooded ridges of Hiba-Dogo-Taishaku Quasi-National Park climb toward Mount Hiba, said in old myth to hold the grave of the goddess Izanami, and Mount Dogo. Across the northern edge lie the Shimane uplands of Iinan and Okuizumo, old tatara iron-smelting country of terraced paddies and cedar. The climate is inland and sharp: snowy winters with ski slopes at Hiba and Dogo, warm summers, and in autumn the famous sea of fog that fills the Miyoshi basin before dawn, seen from hilltop lookouts. People farm rice, grapes and pears, raise Hiba beef cattle, cut timber and work in small factories along the expressways. Miyoshi is a town of a few tens of thousands with an old merchant street, a winery, kagura stages and a museum of yokai and spirit stories; Shobara has hot springs, a big prefectural park and the scattered villages of Saijo, Tojo and Takano. The Chugoku Expressway runs east-west through both towns and crosses the Onomichi-Matsue Expressway at Miyoshi, a crossroads for trucks and buses: about an hour and a half to Hiroshima, an hour to Onomichi on the Inland Sea. The Geibi Line runs from Hiroshima through Miyoshi and Bingo-Ochiai toward Niimi, the Fukuen Line comes up from Fukuyama, and the Kisuki Line climbs north through switchbacks into Okuizumo. From Musutafu it is about five hours by shinkansen to Hiroshima or Fukuyama and a bus or local train inland. Visitors watch cormorant fishing, hike Hiba, ski and soak in valley onsen. Each town has police boxes and one small hero office covering a huge rural district, farmers with weather-sense or strength Quirks are valued at harvest, and sidekicks patrol the summer river festival and the expressway rest stops.
Miyoshi.hiddenInfo: This is hollowing-out country: aging farmers, closed schools, rail lines with three trains a day and talk of cutting more. Hikers still report the Hibagon, the shaggy ape-man of old Mount Hiba sightings; today people blame mutant-type hermits or nobody at all, and it draws curious visitors. Small-time trouble is theft from expressway rest stops and truck lots, illegal dumping in the forests, cattle and fruit theft at night, and Quirk-assisted poaching. Serious hero backup comes from Hiroshima, an hour and a half south.

Takahashi.name: Takahashi
Takahashi.basicInfo: Takahashi is the hill country of western Okayama Prefecture, the Kibi Highlands, where the Takahashi River and the Asahi River cut long valleys south from the Chugoku Mountains toward the Inland Sea. It is entirely land, a plateau of low rounded hills, terraced paddies, vineyards and cedar forest that rises toward the northern ranges. In the south, the old castle town of Takahashi lines the river under Bitchu Matsuyama Castle, the highest mountaintop castle in Japan with an original keep, which on autumn mornings floats above a sea of clouds; the town keeps samurai houses, the dry garden of Raikyuji temple and a quiet river walk. Up on the plateau to the west, the hamlet of Fukiya is a street of red-ochre bengara houses from its copper and pigment days, and to the north the river town of Niimi sits among limestone hills riddled with caves such as Ikura and Makido. In the northeast lie the Maniwa towns of Katsuyama, with its street of hanging noren curtains and sake breweries, and Kuse and Ochiai along the Asahi River, a lumber and wood-processing district. Winters are cold with snow in the north, summers hot in the valleys, and autumn brings fog and red maples. People grow Pione and other grapes, peaches and rice, raise the Chiya black cattle of Niimi, work in sawmills and small factories, and dance Bitchu kagura at shrine festivals. The JR Hakubi Line runs up the Takahashi valley from Kurashiki through Takahashi and Niimi toward Yonago, and the Yakumo limited express reaches Takahashi from Okayama in about forty minutes and Niimi in about an hour; the Kishin Line heads east from Niimi toward Tsuyama, and the Geibi Line west into Hiroshima. The Chugoku Expressway crosses the north, meeting the Okayama and Yonago expressways at Hokubo and Ochiai. From Musutafu it is about three and a half hours by shinkansen to Okayama and the Yakumo; Osaka is about two hours. Visitors climb to the castle at dawn, tour caves, ride the valley lines and stay in small inns. Police boxes sit in each town, a licensed hero covers several valleys from Takahashi, and limestone quarry crews and vineyard workers use permitted Quirks on the job.
Takahashi.hiddenInfo: Takahashi and Niimi are shrinking and aging, and the valley roads and rail lines were badly damaged by floods within living memory, so heavy rain makes people nervous. Small-time trouble is fruit theft from vineyards before harvest, burglary of empty houses, cave explorers getting lost or stuck, and Quirk-users doing unpermitted work for cash. Hero response from Okayama or Kurashiki takes the better part of an hour, longer in snow, so police and the local hero handle most things themselves.

Tsuyama.name: Tsuyama
Tsuyama.basicInfo: Tsuyama is eastern Okayama Prefecture from the Mimasaka basin in the north to the Bizen hills by the Inland Sea, a cell that is almost all land except a sliver of coast at Hinase in the far southeast corner. The Yoshii River runs south through the middle from the mountains to the plain, the Asahi River skirts the west, and between them lie rolling hills, rice basins, orchards and pine-covered ridges. In the north, the castle town of Tsuyama, a city of about a hundred thousand, sits beneath the massive stone walls of Kakuzan Park, one of the finest cherry blossom sites in western Japan; the old Joto merchant street, a fan-shaped engine shed full of preserved locomotives and bowls of hormone udon make it a regional hub. East of it lie the hot springs of Yunogo at Mimasaka and a motor-racing circuit in the hills; south, the Misaki and Kumenan farm towns and Tanjoji temple. In the south the land turns to Bizen: Inbe, where Bizen ware is fired unglazed in wood-burning kilns, its brick chimneys and pottery shops lining the streets; Shizutani School, an old lecture hall roofed in Bizen-ware tiles among the hills; Wake and Akaiwa, famous for white peaches and Muscat grapes; and Hinase, a small port on the Inland Sea known for oysters and oyster okonomiyaki. Okayama's northern suburbs reach in along the south edge. Winters are cold and sometimes snowy in the north, mild in the south; summers are hot and dry, typical of the sunny Setouchi climate. The Tsuyama Line runs up from Okayama in about an hour and ten minutes, the Kishin Line crosses east to Himeji and west to Niimi, the Inbi Line climbs north to Tottori, and the Ako Line serves Inbe and Hinase near the coast; the Chugoku Expressway crosses the north and the Sanyo Expressway the south. From Musutafu it is about four hours by shinkansen to Okayama and the Tsuyama Line, and express buses reach Tsuyama from Osaka in about two and a half hours. Visitors see the castle hill in spring, shop for pottery, soak at Yunogo and eat oysters at Hinase in winter. Tsuyama has its own small hero agency and police station, potters with heat-resistant hands are common at the kilns, and sidekicks patrol the cherry blossom crowds.
Tsuyama.hiddenInfo: The north is depopulating while the south feeds commuters into Okayama. Small-time trouble is theft of valuable pottery from kilns and galleries, fruit theft before harvest, bike gangs on the Chugoku Expressway, and Quirk-users doing unlicensed heavy work in the quarries and lumber yards. Okayama's hero agencies are thirty minutes to an hour away by car, so the Tsuyama agency and the prefectural police cover most incidents across the north.

Himeji.name: Himeji
Himeji.basicInfo: The Harima plain of western Hyogo, from the Seto Inland Sea shore at Himeji, Aioi and Ako north into the folded hills and river valleys at the southern edge of the Chugoku Mountains. The southern fringe is coast and industry: the Harima industrial belt of steelworks, shipyards, power plants and tank farms lines the shore from Takasago west past Himeji's Shikama port, and ferries leave from there for Shodoshima and the small Ieshima islands just offshore. Himeji itself is a large, busy city laid out around Himeji Castle, the brilliant white keep on its hill, with a broad, straight avenue running north from the shinkansen station to the gate; the mountaintop temple of Engyo-ji sits in cedar woods on Mount Shosha to the northwest, reached by ropeway. Each October the Nada Fighting Festival sends portable shrines crashing into one another before a huge crowd. West along the coast, Aioi has a deep inlet with a shipyard and an oyster festival, and Ako is a quiet castle town of salt-making and the memory of its forty-seven retainers. Inland, Tatsuno is a small castle town of breweries making light Harima soy sauce and of hand-pulled somen noodles; Fukusaki, on the Ichikawa River, is a gentle farm town with statues of water imps along its stream; Shiso and Sayo are wooded mountain country of rivers, ayu fishing and small hot springs, and a giant ring-shaped research facility sits on a hilltop near Kamigori. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild. Food is Himeji oden with ginger soy, almond toast, conger eel and Ako salt. The Sanyo Shinkansen stops at Himeji and Aioi; the JR Kobe and Sanyo lines, the Sanyo Electric Railway and the Bantan and Kishin lines run out from Himeji, and the Sanyo and Chugoku expressways cross the cell. Shin-Osaka is half an hour away, Musutafu about two and a half hours. Himeji has several hero agencies and busy police; the hill towns each keep a police box and are covered by licensed heroes on patrol, and at the Nada festival sidekicks with strength Quirks stand ready to catch a toppling shrine.
Himeji.hiddenInfo: Himeji is a big working city with big-city problems on a modest scale: gang remnants in the nightlife streets near the station, theft and fencing around the industrial port, and festival brawls that get out of hand when Quirks come out. The castle draws pickpockets as well as tourists. The coastal industrial zone has strict security and occasional accidents that need heroes with fire or rescue Quirks. Kobe's larger agencies are thirty minutes away.

Kobe.name: Kobe
Kobe.basicInfo: The upper half of the Kobe and Hanshin city belt and the hill country behind it: central Kobe's Sannomiya and Kitano districts, the Rokko mountains, Arima's hot springs and, inland, the Sanda and Tamba-Sasayama country to the north and the Miki and Nishiwaki farmlands to the west. The south edge runs along Kobe's downtown, so Sannomiya, Motomachi and Chinatown sit just inside the line while the harbor, Harborland and Port Island lie just beyond it. Kobe is a big, cosmopolitan port city squeezed between sea and mountains: department stores and arcades in Sannomiya, old Western merchant houses climbing the Kitano slope, sake breweries lining the Nada shore to the east, and, just over the ridge, Arima, an ancient hot-spring town of narrow lanes and iron-red springs. The Rokko range rises steeply behind it all, with cable cars, hiking trails and the famous night view over the bay. Eastward, the city runs without a break through wealthy Ashiya and Nishinomiya, past Koshien Stadium, to Takarazuka and its revue theater. North and west the land opens into gentle rice valleys: Sanda's commuter towns, Tamba-Sasayama's castle town of black soybeans, chestnuts and wild-boar hot pot, Tachikui's kilns of rustic Tamba pottery, Miki's carpentry tools and sake-rice fields, and Nishiwaki's weaving mills and the spot it marks as the navel of Japan. Summers are humid and hot, winters mild in the city and colder inland. Food is Kobe beef, Chinatown dumplings, Nada sake and Kobe's bakeries and sweet shops. The Sanyo Shinkansen stops at Shin-Kobe, about two and a quarter hours from Musutafu and fifteen minutes from Shin-Osaka; JR, Hankyu and Hanshin lines run side by side toward Osaka, the Kobe Electric Railway serves Arima and Sanda, and the Chugoku, Sanyo, Hanshin and Shin-Meishin expressways cross the cell. Kobe has many hero agencies and a heavy police presence; downtown, a sidekick with a sticky-handed Quirk directing crowds at a crossing is nothing unusual.
Kobe.hiddenInfo: Kobe is a port city with a long history of organized crime, much reduced since the rise of heroes; the old groups survive in loan-sharking, smuggling through the harbor and protection rackets in the nightlife streets. Sannomiya's crowds draw pickpockets and unlicensed Quirk scuffles, and Arima's wealthy guests draw thieves. Out-of-town villains pass through, but help from Osaka's agencies is twenty minutes away.

Osaka North.name: Osaka North
Osaka North.basicInfo: Osaka North is the northern half of the Osaka metropolis and the corridor of cities around it, west of Musutafu: Shin-Osaka Station, the shinkansen terminal, the office towers and underground malls of the Umeda district, river-delta neighborhoods of canals and elevated highways, and inland the old capital of Kyoto and the shore of Lake Biwa at Otsu. Rivers and canals cut the flat city into islands of offices and markets, expressways ride on concrete pillars above them, and past the last apartment blocks the land climbs into wooded hills dotted with temples, commuter towns and rice fields, tied to Osaka by private railways that seem never to stop. Kyoto, about 40 km northeast, is a city of temples, shrines, wooden townhouses and tourists, with its own police and a few old, dignified agencies. Summers are hot and humid, with a rainy season at the start and typhoons near the end; winters are short and mild; spring fills every riverbank with cherry-blossom parties. Kansai people talk fast, joke hard, haggle by habit and speak their own dialect, and they expect a hero to be approachable: a pro who will not banter with a shopkeeper or stop for a photo gets heckled, and a slow one gets heckled louder. The economy runs on trade, food, offices and small business, and Osaka eats out more than anywhere in the country. Shin-Osaka Station lies about 8 km north of downtown Osaka, which sits just over the line in Osaka South. Fat Gum's cheerful agency sits in a low building about 5 km north-northeast of downtown, a short ride from Shin-Osaka, and Sir Nighteye's analysis-driven agency fills two floors of an office building about 7 km northwest of downtown, west of the station. Established local agencies, Fat Gum's among them, work the streets with the Osaka police: agencies split the patrol districts, police boxes stand at the big crossings, and the arcade shopkeepers' associations keep a close eye on who protects them. People get around by subway, by the local and private lines that fan out from the big terminals, by bicycle on every sidewalk and by taxi after the last train. The shinkansen from Shin-Osaka runs east to Musutafu in about 2 hours and Tokyo in about 2.5, and west to Fukuoka in about 2.5. Students of Shiketsu Academy, U.A.'s closest rival, are a common sight in their peaked caps. A visitor can shop Umeda's underground malls, visit Kyoto's temples, work an office or a kitchen, patrol with a local agency, or intern with Fat Gum or Sir Nighteye.
Osaka North.hiddenInfo: Fat Gum's agency and the prefectural police drug squad both work the trickle of Trigger, the Quirk-boosting street drug, through the nightlife districts and share little; Sir Nighteye's agency is quietly watching an old yakuza house on the southeastern outskirts for its own reasons. Agencies compete for the shopkeepers' associations' consulting fees, and some cut corners to win them. Underworld brokers meet clients in back-street bars near the big terminals and pay well for quiet work.

Iga.name: Iga
Iga.basicInfo: The hill country between Lake Biwa, Kyoto and Ise Bay: the southern shore of Lake Biwa around Moriyama and Yasu, the Koka and Shigaraki uplands, the Iga basin, the Suzuka range, and the Tsu plain running down to Ise Bay. A corner of the lake reaches into the northwest, and the southeast edge touches the Ise Bay shore at Tsu. The lakeside end is commuter country of new housing, factories and rice fields around Moriyama, Ritto, Yasu and Ryuo, with Mount Mikami's neat cone rising over the plain. To the southeast the land climbs into wooded hills: Koka, old home of the Koga ninja and of traveling medicine peddlers; Shigaraki, a pottery town where ceramic tanuki stand outside every kiln and shop; and, hidden in the forest nearby, a mountaintop art museum. Over the pass lies the Iga basin, where Iga Ueno's castle on its high stone wall looks over a ninja museum and the birthplace of the poet Basho, and where braided silk cord, Iga pottery and Iga beef are made. East, the Suzuka range runs north-south along the Shiga-Mie line, with Gozaisho's ropeway and trails, and at its foot the old Tokaido post towns of Seki and Kameyama keep rows of latticed wooden houses. The plain ends at the prefectural capital, Tsu, a modest city of offices, a great temple of the Takada Shin Buddhist sect and some of Japan's best-loved eel restaurants. Summers are hot, winters cold and dry inland and snowy on the high Suzuka. The JR Kusatsu and Kansai lines, the Iga Railway's ninja-painted trains, the Shigaraki Kohgen line and Kintetsu's Nagoya line serve the cell, and the Meishin, Shin-Meishin and Ise expressways cross it. Tsu is about two hours from Musutafu by way of Nagoya, Iga Ueno about three, and Shin-Osaka is an hour or so from most of the cell. Tsu and the lakeside towns have hero agencies and police; licensed heroes cover the hills, and in Iga a few ninja-themed hero costumes draw tourists.
Iga.hiddenInfo: Prosperous and calm, with factories and commuter towns in the north and quiet farm villages in the hills. Trouble is ordinary: theft from logistics yards along the expressways, speeding and wrecks on the Shin-Meishin, burglaries of empty farmhouses, and tourists in Iga who think a ninja costume entitles them to climb walls. Hero help from Kyoto, Nagoya or Osaka is within an hour.

Ise Bay.name: Ise Bay
Ise Bay.basicInfo: Ise Bay is the cell where the Nobi plain meets the sea: the head of Ise Bay and the port of Nagoya at the north, the Mie shore of Kuwana, Yokkaichi and Suzuka along the west, the long Chita Peninsula reaching south down the middle, and the western arm of Mikawa Bay with Hekinan and Nishio on the east. Ise Bay is the open water west of Chita; Mikawa Bay is the sheltered water east of it. Both are shallow, greenish and crowded with ships, the islands of Himaka and Shinojima sit near the southern edge, and the Suzuka mountains rise behind the Mie coast. Summers are hot, with late typhoons; winters dry and windy. The northern shore belongs to Nagoya's southern wards: Atsuta Shrine, one of Japan's most important, in its grove of giant camphors; the container and car terminals of the country's busiest cargo port; the aquarium at the Garden Pier; and steel and chemical works on reclaimed land. Across the water, Kuwana is known for grilled clams and the outlet and amusement complex at Nagashima, Yokkaichi for its petrochemical complex whose lit towers draw night-view cruises and for thick tonteki pork steaks, and Suzuka for its motor-racing circuit and its old Tsubaki shrine. On Chita, Tokoname has a pottery path of brick kiln chimneys and walls of old jars and pipes, Handa has black-walled vinegar and sake breweries along a canal, and Chubu Centrair airport stands on an artificial island offshore; farther south are beaches, fishing harbors, and octopus and fugu on the islands. On the Mikawa side, Hekinan and Takahama fire roof tiles, Nishio grows much of Japan's matcha tea, and Isshiki raises eels. The Isewangan Expressway crosses the port on three cable-stayed bridges, Meitetsu lines run down Chita to the airport and the southern tip, Kintetsu and JR follow the Mie coast, and small ferries cross to the islands. Musutafu is about an hour and a half away by shinkansen to Nagoya and a train south; Osaka is about an hour and a half by Kintetsu. Hero coverage is dense on the Nagoya waterfront and in the Mie cities, maritime heroes and the coast guard watch the shipping lanes, and dock workers with lifting Quirks hold harbor licenses.
Ise Bay.hiddenInfo: Ise Bay's undercurrent is the port: theft from container yards, smuggled goods moving through car terminals and fishing harbors, and day laborers drawn into small rackets. The petrochemical belt worries residents with leaks and fires that can grow into major emergencies quickly. Southern Chita's quiet harbors and the islands see poaching and boat theft. Police and hero response is fast around Nagoya port and Yokkaichi, slower on southern Chita and the islands, where the coast guard or a maritime hero may be the nearest help.

Mikawa.name: Mikawa
Mikawa.basicInfo: Mikawa is the cell of eastern Aichi: the Okazaki plain and the car city of Toyota in the northwest, the Mikawa highlands rising behind them, the head of Mikawa Bay with Gamagori and the root of the Atsumi Peninsula in the south, Toyohashi on the plain of the Toyo River, and most of Lake Hamana in the southeast corner on the Shizuoka border. Mikawa Bay is the calm, shallow inner water to the southwest, ringed by clam flats and seaweed farms; the Pacific surf breaks beyond the Atsumi hills, just outside the southern edge. Lake Hamana is a broad brackish lagoon opening to the sea at its southern mouth, with Kosai on its western shore and the Kanzanji hot springs on its eastern shore. Summers are hot and sticky, winters mild and dry with a sharp wind. Toyota is an industrial city built around car plants, with supplier factories filling the surrounding towns and workers from across Japan and abroad; the Korankei gorge on its northeast edge is famous for autumn maples. Okazaki is an old castle town, birthplace of the first Tokugawa shogun, known for dense, dark Hatcho miso aged in great cedar vats and for summer fireworks over the Yahagi River. Toyohashi is a port and farming city with a streetcar line, a castle park, and huge greenhouses of cabbage, flowers and quail; its harbor brings in more imported cars than any other in Japan. Gamagori has hot springs, a shrine on the little bay island of Takeshima and seaside resorts. In the hills, Shinshiro holds the old Nagashino battlefield and the cedar-lined stairs of Mount Horaiji, and the Toyokawa Inari temple draws huge crowds at New Year. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Toyohashi, JR and Meitetsu lines link the cities to Nagoya, the Iida Line climbs north up the Toyo valley, the Aichi Loop Line connects Okazaki and Toyota, and the Tomei and Shin-Tomei expressways cross the region. Musutafu is about an hour and a quarter away by shinkansen, and Nagoya about half an hour beyond. Visitors tour castles and plants, eat Lake Hamana eel and soak at the hot springs. The cities keep many hero agencies and busy police, and plant security, rescue and factory-safety work employ heroes and Quirk-licensed workers alike.
Mikawa.hiddenInfo: Mikawa's undercurrent is dependence on one big industry: when car orders dip, temporary workers lose dormitory beds and jobs together, and resentment pools in the factory suburbs. Parts and catalytic-converter theft, glass-eel poaching on Lake Hamana and frauds aimed at elderly farm households are common. The cities answer calls quickly; the hill villages around Shinshiro and Shitara wait far longer, with Toyohashi or Okazaki teams half an hour to an hour away.

Hamamatsu.name: Hamamatsu
Hamamatsu.basicInfo: Hamamatsu is the cell of western Shizuoka's Enshu country: the city of Hamamatsu in the southwest corner, Iwata, Fukuroi, Kakegawa and Kikugawa strung east across the Tokaido plain, and behind them the folded green hills of the Tenryu and Oi river valleys climbing north toward the Akaishi mountains. The Pacific shore of the Enshu-nada, with its long dunes and kite beach, runs just beyond the southern edge, and the eastern shore of Lake Hamana touches the west. The Tenryu River, wide and gravel-bedded, cuts down the middle from Sakuma and Futamata to the sea; the Oi River runs down the east through Kawane, where tea terraces cling to the slopes. The climate is mild and sunny, with the famously strong, dry Enshu winds of winter and humid summers with typhoons. Hamamatsu is a big manufacturing city famous for musical instruments and motorcycles and for a large Japanese-Brazilian community with its own shops, churches and samba nights; it is proud of its gyoza, served in rings around a heap of bean sprouts, and of the eel from the lake. In early May the Hamamatsu Festival flies giant kites over the dunes by day and parades lantern-lit palace floats through town by night. Iwata and Fukuroi have farms, factories and greenhouses of crown melons; Kakegawa has a rebuilt wooden castle and deep-steamed green tea, and Akiha shrine on its mountain draws pilgrims seeking protection from fire. The Oigawa Railway runs vintage steam trains up the Oi valley to Senzu, and the Tenryu Hamanako Railway loops through the northern hills. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Hamamatsu and Kakegawa, the JR Tokaido Line and the Enshu Railway serve the plain, the Tomei and Shin-Tomei expressways cross it, and the Iida Line passes through Sakuma in the far north. Musutafu is under an hour away by shinkansen, and Nagoya about half an hour. Visitors eat gyoza, ride the steam trains and raft the Tenryu. Hamamatsu has many hero agencies, a city police headquarters and constant traffic patrols; heroes with wind or flight Quirks are welcome at kite season, and small offices cover the hill valleys with long drives.
Hamamatsu.hiddenInfo: Hamamatsu's undercurrent is a working city under strain: factory layoffs hit migrant families hardest, language barriers leave people easy to exploit, and tensions surface around bars and crowded housing blocks. Motorcycle gangs race the coastal roads and the Tenryu riverbed at night. The Tenryu hill country loses people every year, leaving empty houses to squatters and thieves. In the city, police and hero response is quick; in the northern valleys it can take most of an hour.

Shizuoka.name: Shizuoka
Shizuoka.basicInfo: Shizuoka is the cell of central Shizuoka on the western shore of Suruga Bay: the prefectural capital at the center, the port of Shimizu and the Miho pine spit to its east, the fishing city of Yaizu and the tea towns of Fujieda and Shimada to the southwest, and the Makinohara tea plateau and Mount Fuji Shizuoka Airport in the far southwest. The eastern part of the cell is open water: Suruga Bay, the deepest bay in Japan, dark blue and dropping past 2,000 meters close offshore, with the hills of the Izu Peninsula's western coast in view across it and the mouth of the Fuji River at the northeast corner. Land lies west of the bay, water east. The climate is mild, sunny and seldom frosty, Mount Fuji standing to the northeast in clear winter air; summers are humid and typhoons strike in autumn. Shizuoka city keeps the moats and rebuilt turrets of Sunpu Castle, the Sengen shrines on Shizuhata hill, and the Kunozan shrine, reached by more than a thousand stone steps from the strawberry greenhouses on the coast; the Nihondaira plateau above it has a ropeway and one of the classic views of Fuji. The city is Japan's tea capital, a center of plastic-model making, and home of Shizuoka oden, simmered in black broth and dusted with fish powder. Shimizu is a tuna port with a waterfront market, Miho no Matsubara's pine beach looks across the water to Fuji, and Yui and Kambara on the northeast shore net and sun-dry pink sakura shrimp. Yaizu lands more skipjack and tuna than almost any port and smells of katsuobushi smoke. In early November, the Daidogei World Cup fills the city's streets and parks with street performers. The Tokaido Shinkansen stops at Shizuoka, the JR Tokaido Line and the Shizuoka Railway run along the coast, the Tomei and Shin-Tomei cross the region, and a car ferry crosses the bay from Shimizu to the Izu coast in about an hour. Musutafu, the neighbor to the east across the head of the bay, is about twenty minutes away by kodama and under an hour by local train. The city has a large hero presence and a prefectural police headquarters; the coast guard and maritime heroes patrol the bay, and fishing crews with water Quirks work under licenses.
Shizuoka.hiddenInfo: Shizuoka's undercurrents are quiet and coastal: a fishing fleet with fewer crews each year and foreign trainees worked hard on the tuna boats, smuggling worries at Shimizu's container berths, and steep tea farms left unharvested as their owners age. Typhoons and the long-feared Tokai earthquake shape daily life, from tsunami towers on the beaches to school evacuation drills. City hero response is fast; the tea hills and the upper Abe valley wait longer, and agencies from the cities to the east are close enough to help in a large incident.

Izu Oshima.name: Izu Oshima
Izu Oshima.basicInfo: Izu Oshima, the largest and nearest of the Izu Islands, a round volcanic island about 15 km long sitting in open water where Sagami Bay meets the Pacific, with the Izu Peninsula's east coast on the western horizon and the Boso Peninsula's southern tip off to the northeast. Most of the region is sea: a deep blue channel crossed day and night by ships bound into and out of Tokyo Bay. At the island's center rises Mt. Mihara, an active volcano of 758 m whose caldera holds the Ura-sabaku, a wide black desert of cinder and old lava; trails circle the crater rim, and steam still seeps from the rock. The lower slopes are thick with camellia, wild cherry and pine, and the island is known for its camellias: groves line the roads, camellia oil is pressed for hair and cooking, and the Camellia Festival runs from late January into March, when island women in the old indigo anko dress greet visitors at the pier. Motomachi on the west coast is the main town and ferry port, with inns, shops and a seaside open-air bath that looks across the water to Mt. Fuji. Okata on the north coast takes the ferries when the west side is rough, and Habu in the south is an old fishing port in a round crater bay, its lanes of wooden houses climbing the slope. On the southwest road, a cliff of layered ash bands is known as the giant baumkuchen. Islanders fish for alfonsino, bonito and spiny lobster, dry flying fish into pungent kusaya, grow ashitaba greens, and run inns and dive shops. The climate is mild and wet, warmed by the Kuroshio, with windy winters and hard typhoons in late summer and autumn. Jetfoils from Tokyo's Takeshiba pier take under two hours and a night ferry docks at dawn; from Musutafu, a short train to Atami and a jetfoil of about 45 minutes take under two hours. Small planes fly from Chofu in about 25 minutes. A ring road circles the island, served by buses, rental cars and scooters. Visitors hike the crater, soak in the hot springs, dive off black-rock coves and eat ashitaba tempura and fresh sashimi. A police box in Motomachi and a small local hero office cover the island, and a lobster diver who can hold her breath for an hour works the grounds under a co-op permit.
Izu Oshima.hiddenInfo: The island watches Mt. Mihara the way other towns watch the weather: older islanders remember being shipped off the island when the volcano last erupted, and every tremor fills the town office with calls. The local hero office is one licensed hero and a sidekick for the whole island; real backup comes from the mainland by jetfoil or helicopter, an hour or more away, and none of it moves in a storm. Trouble is small: out-of-season abalone and lobster poaching by visiting divers, drunk weekenders on scooters, unlicensed Quirk stunts on the crater trails, and stranded tourists when the boats stop running.

Southern Boso.name: Southern Boso
Southern Boso.basicInfo: The southern tip of the Boso Peninsula, a ring of flower-growing hills and rocky coves where Chiba ends in the Pacific, with most of the cell open sea to the south. Tateyama sits on the calm bay of the same name on the western shore, with a reconstructed castle on its hill and the little island of Okinoshima tied to the shore by a sandbar; south of it, past the loquat orchards of Tomiura, the flower fields and diving coves of Minamiboso run to Nojimazaki lighthouse at Shirahama, the southernmost point of the Kanto mainland. The coast then turns northeast through Chikura and Wada, a small whaling port that still lands a few beaked whales each summer, to Kamogawa, a resort town with a marine park, the bay of Tainoura where wild sea bream gather, and the terraced rice paddies of Oyama Senmaida in the hills behind. Mount Atago, the highest point in Chiba at just over four hundred meters, rises in the middle. The Kuroshio runs close offshore and keeps the winters nearly frost-free; rape blossoms, stock and poppies bloom in the fields from January, summers are breezy, and typhoons strike hard. People grow flowers and loquats, dive for abalone and turban shells, fish, raise dairy cattle in the hills where Japanese dairying began, and run inns, beach houses and campsites. The Uchibo line reaches Tateyama and the Sotobo line Kamogawa, meeting at Awa-Kamogawa; highway buses from Tokyo come over the Aqua-Line to Tateyama in about two hours, and the Boso Flower Line road follows the southern shore. Musutafu is about three hours away, or less by car and the Kurihama ferry. Visitors pick flowers in winter, swim and dive at Tateyama and Shirahama, watch the women divers' festival in July, eat sanga-yaki fish patties, whale jerky and fresh sea bream, see the marine park, and look out across the sea to the volcano of Izu Oshima on the southwest horizon. A small hero agency in Tateyama and the police cover the peninsula's tip, and in summer sidekicks with water Quirks patrol the beaches alongside lifeguards.
Southern Boso.hiddenInfo: The tip of Boso is beautiful and emptying: its towns are among the oldest in Kanto, a few storm-damaged roofs still wear blue tarps, and summer crowds strain the roads and the patience of locals. Rescues often come by sea. Real hero help is twenty to forty minutes away by road and longer from Chiba. Small villainy: poaching of abalone and spiny lobster from protected beds, thefts from campsites and beach cars, and reckless tourists using unlicensed Quirks on the cliffs.

Pacific off Boso.name: Pacific off Boso
Pacific off Boso.basicInfo: The open Pacific off the southeastern Boso coast, from just off Onjuku, Katsuura and Kamogawa out about fifty kilometers to sea. The shelf here is narrow and cut by deep submarine canyons, so the water drops quickly to a kilometer and more, dark blue and clear. The Kuroshio sweeps past close to the peninsula, warm and fast, carrying bonito, flying fish and sea turtles; the sea is mild in winter and rough under typhoons in late summer and autumn. Fishing boats from Katsuura, Ohara and Kamogawa work the current for bonito and the deep slopes for kinmedai, the red splendid alfonsino this coast is famous for, while divers and pots take spiny lobster near shore. Ships bound in and out of Tokyo Bay pass offshore, and the low green hills of the peninsula show to the north and west. The coast guard patrols from Tateyama and Choshi, and maritime heroes back it up in storms. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a passing ship, or carried by a flying hero.
Pacific off Boso.hiddenInfo: The current is the danger here: swimmers and small boats get carried off, and fog rolls in fast. Fishers complain about outsiders working their kinmedai grounds. Help is the coast guard, half an hour to an hour from Tateyama or Choshi. Small villainy at sea: lobster poaching, catch fraud, and illegal dumping from passing ships.

Tsushima.name: Tsushima
Tsushima.basicInfo: The northeastern corner of Tsushima, the long mountainous island in the middle of the Korea Strait, and a wide stretch of the strait's eastern channel beside it. Only the island's north end falls inside: Kamitsushima, with the port of Hitakatsu, the white-sand cove of Miuda Beach and fishing villages tucked into drowned inlets along the east shore. The island's spine of forested ridges runs on south and west, out of this square, toward Izuhara, the main town, and the airport. East of the shore everything is open water, deep blue and fast-moving, with the warm Tsushima Current setting northeast and Okinoshima and the Kyushu coast far beyond the eastern horizon. On a clear day the hills and apartment towers of Busan, about fifty kilometers away, can be seen from the observatory at the island's northern tip, and Korean is heard in Hitakatsu's shops as often as Japanese. The land is steep, almost all cedar, cypress and broadleaf forest, with rice and buckwheat in narrow valley floors. Winters are mild but windy, summers humid, and typhoons and winter gales cut the island off from the mainland for days. People fish for squid, conger eel and yellowtail, keep native honeybees in hollow-log hives, and run guesthouses for visitors from both countries. The rare Tsushima leopard cat lives in these forests, and road signs ask drivers to slow down for it. Local food is iriyaki fish hot pot, rokubee noodles made from sweet potato starch, and grilled conger eel. Route 382 runs the length of the island; Hitakatsu to Izuhara is about two hours by car or island bus. Fast ferries from Busan reach Hitakatsu in a little over an hour; from Hakata, jetfoils reach Izuhara by way of Iki in a little over two hours, and a slower car ferry calls at Hitakatsu directly. From Musutafu the trip takes most of a day: shinkansen to Hakata, then a boat or a short flight from Fukuoka. Hitakatsu has a police box, a coast guard office and one small hero office whose licensed hero covers the whole north of the island, mostly sea rescues, lost hikers and festival crowds. Visitors swim at Miuda, kayak the inlets, hike forest trails and eat fresh squid by the harbor.
Tsushima.hiddenInfo: Tsushima is a border island and feels it: the coast guard and police watch the strait closely, and smuggling in fish holds is the classic local crime. Beaches on the exposed coasts collect drift trash from across the sea. The population keeps shrinking as young people leave for Fukuoka. Other trouble is small and local: theft from unattended shrines, cut fishing nets, the odd drunken quarrel at the port. Serious hero help is far; Fukuoka is two hours away by jetfoil, longer in bad weather.

Okinoshima.name: Okinoshima
Okinoshima.basicInfo: The open Genkai-nada between Tsushima and the Kyushu coast, holding the sacred island of Okinoshima near its southwestern edge. Okinoshima is a small, steep, forested island about sixty kilometers off Munakata, the innermost sanctuary of Munakata Taisha; for more than a thousand years offerings for safe passage were left among its rocks, and it is a World Heritage site. No ordinary visitor may land: a single priest keeps the shrine in rotation, bathing in the sea before setting foot on shore, and nothing on the island may be carried away. Around it the water is deep blue and clear, a hundred meters or more over the shelf, with the warm Tsushima Current setting northeast. Winter northwesterlies make this one of the roughest stretches of water off Kyushu; summers are calmer, with sea fog in early summer. The overnight ferry between Shimonoseki and Busan crosses here, and cargo ships work the lanes toward the Kanmon Strait. Boats from Munakata's Oshima and Kanezaki fish the grounds around the island for sea bream, yellowtail and squid. The coast guard patrols out of Fukuoka and Kitakyushu, and maritime heroes from Fukuoka, more than an hour away by fast boat, answer emergencies. A party is out here aboard a ferry, a fishing boat, or with a flying hero.
Okinoshima.hiddenInfo: The island's taboos are taken seriously, and anyone landing without leave, a curious diver or a flier hunting for photos, is met by the coast guard and a very unhappy shrine. Otherwise the troubles are those of open water: night poaching, a fishing boat's engine dying far from shore, and help that is an hour or more away even for a flying hero.

Tsunoshima.name: Tsunoshima
