Tsunoshima.basicInfo: The northwestern corner of Yamaguchi Prefecture, where Honshu ends on the Sea of Japan: the rocky Hibiki-nada coast of northern Shimonoseki and western Nagato, the island of Tsunoshima, and a broad stretch of open sea to the west and north. Most of the square is water; the land is a strip along its southeast side. Tsunoshima is a low, grassy island ringed by white sand and water so clear it shows emerald and cobalt over the shallows, joined to the mainland at Hohoku by the Tsunoshima Bridge, nearly one point eight kilometers long and one of the most photographed drives in Japan. A stone lighthouse from the early Meiji years stands on the island's western tip and can be climbed. Along the mainland shore, small fishing villages and rice terraces sit between headlands, and JR San'in Main Line trains run in sight of the sea through Takibe and Kogushi toward Nagato. The climate is mild and sunny in summer, gray and windy in winter, when northwesterlies throw spray over the roads. Locals fish, dive for sea urchin and abalone, grow rice and run cafes and inns for the summer crowds; the food is fresh squid, sea urchin bowls and kawara soba, green tea noodles served sizzling on a hot roof tile, a Shimonoseki dish. There is no expressway here; people drive the coast road, Route 191, or ride the slow local trains. Shin-Shimonoseki on the Sanyo shinkansen is about an hour south by car; from Musutafu the trip takes around five hours, from Hakata about two. Licensed heroes from the Shimonoseki area cover the district on wide patrols, police boxes stand in the larger villages, and summer lifeguards with water or wind Quirks work the beaches under license. Visitors drive the bridge, swim and snorkel, rent bicycles on the island and watch the sun go down over open sea.
Tsunoshima.hiddenInfo: Weekend and holiday traffic jams the bridge and the narrow coast road, and visitors who ignore weather warnings get stranded or swept off rocks. Sea urchin and abalone poaching is a quiet, steady problem that the fishing cooperatives take personally. Other small crime is car break-ins at scenic lots and unlicensed fliers buzzing the bridge for photos. Real hero help comes from Shimonoseki, about an hour away; the coast guard is closer for anything at sea.

Hagi.name: Hagi
Hagi.basicInfo: The Sea of Japan coast of northern Yamaguchi Prefecture, from the hot-spring valleys of Nagato in the west to the old castle town of Hagi and the quiet farm town of Abu in the east, with the green karst plateau of Akiyoshidai rising at the southern edge. The northern part of the square is open sea scattered with small islands. Hagi sits on a delta between two branches of the Abu River, its grid of earthen walls, white-plastered storehouses and summer-orange trees hardly changed since it was the seat of the domain that helped bring down the shogunate; the castle ruins stand on a hill by the sea, and the small private academy that taught many Meiji leaders is now a shrine and museum. Its potters make Hagi ware, soft pale tea bowls that change color with use, and a pottery festival fills the town each May. Just north of town, little Kasayama is a tiny dormant volcano by the sea. To the west, Nagato has the fishing port of Senzaki, known for kamaboko and squid, the cliff island of Omijima with boat tours past its sea arches, the hot-spring towns of Yumoto and Tawarayama along mountain streams, and a taste for yakitori. Near the western edge, Motonosumi Shrine sends a tunnel of red torii down a headland to the waves. Akiyoshidai is a high grassland studded with white limestone pinnacles, burned each February to keep it open, above one of the largest limestone caves in Japan. Winters are gray and windy with snow on the plateau; summers are hot and green. The JR San'in Main Line follows the coast through Nagato and Higashi-Hagi, the Mine Line runs inland, and buses link Hagi to Shin-Yamaguchi on the Sanyo shinkansen in about an hour; from Musutafu the trip is about five hours, from Hakata under two. Hagi and Nagato each have a police station and a small hero office, and licensed heroes patrol the castle district at festivals and cover farm districts by car. Visitors bicycle through the samurai quarter, buy pottery, soak in onsen, walk the plateau and take ferries out to the islands.
Hagi.hiddenInfo: Hagi is aging fast, and empty samurai houses and closed kilns are a quiet worry; town talk is about who will keep the old quarter alive. Tourists crowd the torii shrine and Akiyoshidai on holidays, and some wander off into the karst fields or caves. Small crime is fake or stolen pottery sold as old Hagi ware, car break-ins at scenic stops and night poaching along the coast. Bigger hero help is in Yamaguchi city, about an hour south over the mountains.

Tsuwano.name: Tsuwano
Tsuwano.basicInfo: Tsuwano is the hill country of western Shimane where it meets northern Yamaguchi, a cell of forested ridges and clear river valleys that touches the Sea of Japan only in its northwest corner and along the north edge at Masuda. The Takatsu River, often called the clearest river in Japan, runs undammed from the Yoshika uplands in the east through gorges to the sea at Masuda, joined on the way by the Tsuwano River from the castle town of Tsuwano. Masuda, a small city near the north edge, has the stone gardens of a medieval painter-monk at Ikoen and Manpukuji, a large modern arts center, and Iwami Airport with flights to Haneda in about an hour and a half. In the narrow valley in the center, Tsuwano is called the Little Kyoto of San'in: white plaster walls and wooden samurai gates along Tonomachi street, canals full of fat carp, the tunnel of red torii climbing to Taikodani Inari Shrine, castle ruins reached by chairlift, and the heron dance at Yasaka Shrine in July. In the southeast the Chugoku Expressway passes the Yoshika towns of Muikaichi and Kakinoki, known for organic farming, and the south reaches into the hills north of Yamaguchi city. Winters are snowy inland and gray at the coast; summers are green and humid, and the rivers fill with ayu. People farm rice, raise beef, fish the rivers, make wasabi and sweets, and run inns for visitors. The Yamaguchi Line runs from Shin-Yamaguchi through Tsuwano to Masuda, served by the Super Oki limited express and on many weekends by a steam locomotive, and the San'in Main Line follows the coast from Masuda. From Fukuoka it is about two hours by shinkansen to Shin-Yamaguchi and the Super Oki; from Musutafu it is about five hours the same way, or a flight from Tokyo to Iwami. Visitors walk Tonomachi, climb to the shrine, ride the steam train, canoe the Takatsu and eat uzume-meshi, rice with the food hidden underneath. Police boxes sit in each town, a small hero office in Masuda covers the coast and the valleys, river guides with water Quirks help with rescues under permit, and sidekicks patrol the festival crowds.
Tsuwano.hiddenInfo: Masuda and the valleys are aging and losing people, and the tourist season is short. Small-time trouble is carp and ayu poaching, theft from unattended shrines and temples, drunk drivers on mountain roads, and Quirk-users poaching game or timber. Hero backup comes from Yamaguchi, Shin-Yamaguchi or Masuda's own small office; a serious incident needs heroes called in from Hiroshima or Fukuoka, an hour or more away.

Hiroshima.name: Hiroshima
Hiroshima.basicInfo: Hiroshima is the city and its bay at the western end of the Sanyo coast, where the Ota River spreads into a delta of six channels and the Inland Sea opens to the south. The city fills the delta in the middle of the cell, its suburbs climb the hills north and east, and Hiroshima Bay lies to the south, crowded with green islands and oyster rafts; the land rises into the forested Chugoku Mountains toward the north edge. Hiroshima is a big city of over a million, home to Hiroshima Castle, the Shukkeien garden, busy shopping arcades, streetcars and a red-clad pro baseball team adored across the region. Okonomiyaki layered with noodles and cabbage, oysters and momiji manju are everywhere. Southwest across a short ferry lies Miyajima, the sacred island of Itsukushima Shrine with its great vermilion torii standing in the sea at high tide, tame deer and a ropeway up Mount Misen. In the southeast corner, the naval port of Kure has shipyards, a big naval base and museums of ships and submarines. Fuchu, east of the city, is home to a major car plant, and Kumano in the hills makes most of Japan's calligraphy and makeup brushes. North and west lie Akiota and the Sandankyo gorge, the hot springs of Yuki and ski slopes in the snowy mountains. The climate is mild Setouchi: hot, humid summers, a rainy season in June, and calm winters with snow only in the hills. Hiroshima Station is a Nozomi stop on the Sanyo shinkansen, about three and a half hours from Musutafu and an hour from Fukuoka; the Sanyo Main Line, Kure Line, Geibi Line and Kabe Line radiate out, the Astram Line runs north, and the Sanyo and Chugoku expressways cross the region. From Ujina port ferries and high-speed boats go to Etajima, Kure and Matsuyama, and boats run to Miyajima from the city and Miyajimaguchi. Hiroshima has many hero agencies, police stations in every ward, Quirk-adapted streetcar crews and delivery riders, and sidekicks working the festivals and the baseball crowds, while maritime heroes and the coast guard watch the bay.
Hiroshima.hiddenInfo: A big city with big-city problems: purse snatchers and Quirk-using shoplifters in the arcades, nightlife brawls and touts in Nagarekawa, drug dealing, and bosozoku-style bike gangs on the bypasses. On the bay, oyster rafts get raided at night and smuggling slips through busy shipping lanes. Hero coverage is dense in the center and thin in the northern hills. Miyajima has its own pressures: crowds, overtourism and people feeding the deer.

Onomichi.name: Onomichi
Onomichi.basicInfo: Onomichi is the central Hiroshima coast and its islands, from the Saijo plateau in the west to the old port of Onomichi on the eastern edge, with the inland hills reaching north toward Akitakata and the Geiyo Islands of the Inland Sea filling the south. The land rises from a narrow coastal strip into rolling plateaus of rice fields and pine; south of the coast, the islands of Mukaishima, Innoshima, Ikuchijima and the northern half of Omishima are linked by the bridges of the Shimanami Kaido, and Osakikamijima and the rabbit island of Okunoshima sit to the southwest. Onomichi is a slope town of narrow lanes, temples, cats and views over a narrow channel full of shipyard cranes and small ferries; a ropeway climbs to Senkoji Park, and Onomichi ramen, soy broth with pork-fat flakes, is famous. Mihara, a castle port, is known for octopus and its summer Yassa dance festival; Takehara keeps an old merchant district of sake and salt; Higashihiroshima's Saijo is a sake town of brewery chimneys and white walls, with a big national campus nearby, and fills for its October sake festival. Inland, Akitakata dances Aki kagura and Sera grows flowers on its plateau. On the islands, lemons and mikan cover the slopes, Setoda has the colorful Kosanji temple, Innoshima holds a sea lords festival remembering the medieval pirate clans of these straits, and Omishima's Oyamazumi Shrine holds old armor and swords. The climate is sunny Setouchi, mild winters and hot summers, with calm seas and evening light over the islands. The Sanyo shinkansen stops at Higashi-Hiroshima, Mihara and Shin-Onomichi, the Sanyo Main Line and Kure Line follow the coast, the Onomichi Expressway runs north to Miyoshi, and Hiroshima Airport, near Mihara, has flights to Haneda. Cyclists ride the Shimanami Kaido south to Imabari, about seventy kilometers. From Musutafu it is about three and a half hours by shinkansen. Visitors cycle the islands, walk the temple path, tour breweries and eat octopus and ramen. Each town has police boxes and a small hero agency, and island shipyard workers with strength or heat-resistant Quirks work under licenses while sidekicks patrol festival nights.
Onomichi.hiddenInfo: The islands are aging and the shipyards ride boom and bust. Small-time trouble is bicycle theft along the Shimanami Kaido, drunk brawls at the sake festival, citrus theft from groves, and Quirk-users stealing scrap from shipyards. Smuggling through busy shipping lanes is a quiet concern. Hiroshima's heroes are about an hour away; local agencies and the coast guard handle the islands, and ferries are the only way to some places.

Kurashiki.name: Kurashiki
Kurashiki.basicInfo: Kurashiki is the coast of eastern Hiroshima and western Okayama, from Fukuyama in the west to Kurashiki on the eastern edge, with the low hills of the Kibi plateau to the north and the Hiuchi-nada sea to the south. A broad plain of rice fields, reclaimed land and factory zones runs along the coast, rivers such as the Takahashi and Ashida come down from the hills, and offshore the Kasaoka islands lie scattered across the sea; nearly half the cell is water, the Inland Sea filling the south. Fukuyama, a steel city of over four hundred thousand, has a castle right next to the shinkansen platforms, rose gardens and a May rose festival, and one of the country's largest steelworks on the shore; south of it, the old port of Tomonoura has stone lanterns, wooden warehouses, a famous sea bream net-fishing show in May and a sweet herbal liqueur. Kurashiki, another big city, is known for the Bikan Historical Quarter, where white-walled storehouses and willows line a canal, a fine Western art museum, ivy-covered brick mills and denim shops; its Mizushima coast is a huge petrochemical and steel complex lit up at night. Between them lie Kasaoka, a port with horseshoe crabs on its tidal flats, Ibara, a denim town, Yakage's old post town and Soja, with the five-story pagoda of Bitchu Kokubunji standing in fields. The climate is sunny Setouchi, mild winters and hot summers. The Sanyo shinkansen stops at Fukuyama, a Nozomi stop about three hours from Musutafu, and at Shin-Kurashiki; the Sanyo Main Line runs along the plain, the Hakubi Line goes north from Kurashiki, the Fukuen Line from Fukuyama, and small lines serve Ibara and Mizushima. The Sanyo Expressway crosses the region and the Seto-Chuo Expressway turns south toward the Seto Ohashi bridges just east of the cell. Okayama is fifteen minutes east of Kurashiki. Visitors punt on the Bikan canal, buy jeans, eat sea bream at Tomonoura and ferry out to the islands. Both cities have hero agencies and police stations, factory crews with heat or strength Quirks work under license, and sidekicks patrol the festival crowds and the canal district.
Kurashiki.hiddenInfo: Industrial cities with industrial tensions: night shifts, foreign workers, and labor disputes at the big plants. Small-time trouble is copper and scrap theft from factory zones, shoplifting and pickpockets among tourists in the Bikan quarter, bike gangs on the coast roads, and Quirk-users doing unlicensed work. Industrial accidents are a constant risk. Hero coverage is solid in Fukuyama and Kurashiki but thinner on the islands and in the hills.

Okayama.name: Okayama
Okayama.basicInfo: Okayama is where Honshu and Shikoku face each other across the narrowest part of the Inland Sea: the city of Okayama and its plain in the north, the Kagawa coast with Takamatsu and Marugame in the south, and between them the islands of the Bisan-seto and the big island of Shodoshima to the east. About half of the cell is water, calm and blue, crossed by ferries and freighters. Okayama, a big city of seven hundred thousand, has the black Crow Castle and Korakuen, one of Japan's three great gardens, the folktale of Momotaro, born from a peach, as its emblem, kibi dango sweets, white peaches and Muscat grapes; the Kibi plain to the west has old shrines and a cycling road among burial mounds. South of the city, the Seto Ohashi bridges carry road and rail from Kojima across the islands to Sakaide in Kagawa. Takamatsu, Kagawa's capital, is the udon capital of Japan, with hundreds of noodle shops; the Ritsurin garden, the flat-topped Yashima plateau and a modern port are its landmarks. Marugame has a castle with high stone walls and makes most of Japan's round paper fans. Kagawa's plain is dotted with irrigation ponds and cone-shaped hills, and pilgrims in white walk to temples of the Shikoku eighty-eight. Out in the sea lie the art islands of Naoshima, Teshima and Megijima, and Shodoshima, with olive groves, soy sauce breweries, somen noodles and the Kankakei gorge; Ushimado on the Okayama coast has olive groves too. The climate is the sunniest Setouchi: mild winters, hot dry summers. Okayama Station is a Nozomi stop, about two and three-quarter hours from Musutafu, and the hub for Shikoku: the Marine Liner reaches Takamatsu in about an hour across the bridge, and limited expresses go on to Matsuyama and Kochi. Ferries run from Okayama, Uno and Takamatsu to the islands. Visitors eat udon, cycle the islands and see the art festival held every three years. Both cities have hero agencies and police, ferry crews with water Quirks work under license, and maritime heroes patrol the straits with the coast guard.
Okayama.hiddenInfo: The art islands draw crowds, and the locals are aging and tired of them. Small-time trouble is theft from art installations, pickpockets on ferries, bike theft, and Quirk-users stealing olives and citrus. Shipping lanes in the Bisan-seto are busy and accidents happen. Hero coverage is dense in Okayama and Takamatsu, but on the small islands a ferry ride is the only way to help.

Awaji Island.name: Awaji Island
Awaji Island.basicInfo: The western shore of Awaji Island and the open Harima-nada around it, at the eastern end of the Seto Inland Sea's island country. Only about a sixth of the cell is land. Along the east edge runs Awaji's quiet west coast: long sandy beaches at Goshiki and Keino Matsubara, with pine groves, fishing harbors and sunset viewpoints over the water, and inland the island's onion fields and rice terraces climbing toward the central ridge, where the old Izanagi Shrine at Taga sits among cedars as the place where the creator god retired. At the southwest corner, the harbor of Fukura is home to Awaji's traditional puppet theater and to the boats that run out under the Onaruto Bridge to watch the Naruto whirlpools churning in the strait, with the Shikoku shore just across the water to the south. In the northwest, the Ieshima islands are a cluster of granite and fishing islands, reached by ferry from Himeji, where quarries cut stone and fishing crews work the strait. The eastern headlands of Shodoshima touch the western edge. The water of the Harima-nada is shallow, green and tidal, crossed by freighters and fishing boats, with nori seaweed rafts in winter and sand-eel fishing in spring. Winters are mild and dry, summers hot. Food is Awaji onions, sea bream, conger eel, sand eels simmered in soy, and Awaji beef. The Kobe-Awaji-Naruto Expressway runs down the island's spine just to the east, with expressway buses from Sannomiya and Osaka to Fukura and on into Tokushima; Fukura is about an hour and a half from Shin-Kobe, so Musutafu is about four hours away. Ferries from Himeji reach Ieshima in about half an hour. Awaji has a small hero agency in Sumoto and police boxes in the towns; a single licensed hero might cover half the island, and fishing crews with water Quirks are often the first to reach a capsized boat.
Awaji Island.hiddenInfo: Island life is slow and close-knit, and newcomers from Kobe who buy beach houses cause gossip. Problems are boating and fishing accidents, illegal sand and shellfish taking, and drunk drivers on the coast road. The Naruto strait's currents are deadly to swimmers. Help from Kobe or Tokushima is an hour away by road; local heroes and fishing crews handle most things.

Osaka Bay.name: Osaka Bay
Osaka Bay.basicInfo: The western half of Osaka Bay and its shores: the Akashi and south Kobe waterfront on the north, the eastern coast of Awaji Island on the west, the Senshu coast of southern Osaka with Kansai International Airport on the east, and the Kitan Strait leading out toward the Pacific in the south. About a third of the cell is land. The water is a shallow, busy inland sea, green-gray and full of ships: container vessels, car ferries to Shikoku and Kyushu, fishing boats and the fast boats that link Kobe Airport with Kansai Airport. In the northwest the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, one of the longest suspension bridges in the world, spans the strait to Awaji. Akashi itself is a cheerful fishing city famous for octopus, sea bream and its Uontana fish market, and for sitting on Japan's time meridian, marked by an observatory tower. East of it, the beaches of Maiko and Suma lead to Kobe's harborfront: Harborland, Meriken Park, the man-made Port Island and Kobe Airport. Across the bay, Awaji's east coast runs from Iwaya past the Yumebutai garden complex to Sumoto, a castle and hot-spring town on the island's main bay. On the southeast shore, Kishiwada's castle town holds the Danjiri Festival each September, with huge wooden floats hauled at a run around street corners; south of it Kaizuka, Izumisano and Rinku Town face the airport island across a long bridge, and the coast tapers to the fishing towns of Misaki and, across the Wakayama line, Kada, where the Tomogashima islands guard the strait. Winters are mild, summers humid. Food is Akashi-yaki egg dumplings, octopus, Awaji onions and Senshu water eggplant. The Sanyo Shinkansen stops at Nishi-Akashi, about two and a half hours from Musutafu; the JR Hanwa and Nankai lines serve the Senshu coast and the airport, and expressways cross both bridges. Akashi, Kobe and Kishiwada have hero agencies and busy police boxes; at the danjiri festival, sidekicks with strength Quirks walk beside the floats.
Osaka Bay.hiddenInfo: This is heavily used water, so trouble is maritime: freighter collisions in the straits, smuggling through Kobe's and the airport's cargo docks, and theft from containers. Kishiwada's festival is joyful and dangerous, with crush injuries and fights every year. Kansai Airport has its own security, police and contracted heroes. Osaka's agencies are close; nothing here is far from help.

Osaka South.name: Osaka South
Osaka South.basicInfo: Osaka South is downtown Osaka and the southern half of the metropolis, west of Musutafu: a sprawling river-delta city of canals, covered shopping arcades, neon signs and elevated highways, with port districts on the bay and older neighborhoods spreading south and east to the green hills of Nara. Downtown Osaka, at the north of the region, is the commercial heart, where Dotonbori's canal stays loud and bright past midnight, takoyaki stands line the arcades and Shin-Osaka Station lies about 8 km north, just over the line in Osaka North. The bay shore is a long line of container cranes, warehouses, factories and ferry piers; south along it run the industrial city of Sakai with its ancient keyhole tombs, and inland the old capital of Nara, its temples and its deer park about 30 km east. One old yakuza house still keeps a walled compound in a quiet district about 11 km southeast of downtown, on the southeastern outskirts. Summers are hot and humid, with a rainy season at the start and typhoons near the end; winters are short and mild; spring fills every riverbank with cherry-blossom parties. Kansai people talk fast, joke hard, haggle by habit and speak their own dialect, and they expect a hero to be approachable: a pro who will not banter with a shopkeeper or stop for a photo gets heckled, and a slow one gets heckled louder. The economy runs on trade, food and small business: wholesalers, bay-side factories, family shops in the arcades and a restaurant on every corner. Established local agencies work the streets with the Osaka police: agencies split the patrol districts, police boxes stand at the big crossings, and the arcade shopkeepers' associations keep a close eye on who protects them. People get around by subway, by the private lines that fan out south and east from the big terminals, by bicycle on every sidewalk and by taxi after the last train; the shinkansen from Shin-Osaka runs east to Musutafu in about 2 hours and Tokyo in about 2.5, and west to Fukuoka in about 2.5. Students of Shiketsu Academy, U.A.'s closest rival, are a common sight downtown in their peaked caps. A visitor can eat through the canal stalls, shop the arcades, work a kitchen or a market stall, walk with Nara's deer, patrol with a local agency, or go looking for trouble in the back streets.
Osaka South.hiddenInfo: Trigger, the Quirk-boosting street drug, has been trickling back into Osaka's nightlife districts since winter, sold in small doses by dealers too frightened to name a supplier, and the money runs upward to the old yakuza house on the southeastern outskirts. Fat Gum's agency and the prefectural police drug squad both work the case and share little, and Sir Nighteye's agency is quietly watching the same house. Underworld brokers meet clients in back-street bars and bay-side warehouses and pay well for quiet work.

Nabari.name: Nabari
Nabari.basicInfo: The forested upland on the border of Nara and Mie where the Kii Mountains begin: the Nabari and Uda highlands, the Murou and Soni plateaus, the upper valleys of the Kumozu, Kushida and Miya rivers, and, in the southwest, the source country of the Yoshino River in Higashiyoshino and Kawakami. About three quarters of the cell is steep wooded mountain, the rest small basins and valleys. Nabari, in the north, is a commuter town of hillside housing estates for Osaka workers, with the Akame Forty-Eight Waterfalls in a gorge just south, a trail of cascades once used, the story goes, for ninja training. West of it, Murou-ji is a mountain temple with a slender five-story pagoda among cedars, long known as the temple that welcomed women when Mount Koya did not. The Soni plateau's pampas grass turns the hills silver-gold in autumn, and the pointed peak of Mount Takami stands on the Nara-Mie line. East, in Mie, the Kintetsu line threads the Aoyama tunnels down to Sakakibara Onsen, a centuries-old spring, and the junction town of Ise-Nakagawa, while the slow JR Meisho line runs up the Kumozu valley from Matsusaka to Ise-Okutsu, an old pilgrim-road post town. Matsusaka's cattle farms, raising one of Japan's most famous beefs, spread up the valleys at the eastern edge. The south is deep cedar forest and dam lakes with few roads; Kawakami village keeps some of the oldest planted cedar forests in Japan. Summers are humid, winters cold and occasionally snowy. People commute, farm, grow tea, raise cattle and log cedar and cypress. The Kintetsu Osaka line connects Nabari to Osaka-Uehommachi in about an hour and Ise-Nakagawa to Nagoya in about an hour; Musutafu is two and a half to three hours away by way of Nagoya. Nabari has a small hero agency and police boxes; licensed heroes cover the vast mountain districts by car, and a forester's Quirk that senses unstable slopes is prized after heavy rain.
Nabari.hiddenInfo: The hills are emptying fast and the commuter estates are aging. Problems are illegal dumping on forest roads, theft of cattle and farm machinery, poaching, and hikers lost in the gorges. Landslides after typhoon rain are the real emergency. Hero help from Osaka, Nara or Tsu is one to two hours away by road; the local heroes cover the rest.

Ise-Shima.name: Ise-Shima
Ise-Shima.basicInfo: The Shima Peninsula and the southwestern shore of Ise Bay in Mie Prefecture, from Matsusaka on the western edge through Ise and Toba to the drowned inlets of Shima in the south. Ise Bay lies to the north, the Kumano Sea to the south, and the Irago Channel to the east. The north is a flat rice plain cut by the Kushida and Miya rivers; south of Ise, the forested hills of Ise-Shima National Park rise to Mt. Asama, and beyond them the coast breaks into rias: Ago Bay and Matoya Bay, crowded with pearl and oyster rafts. Winters are mild and bright, summers hot and humid, and typhoons come in from the south in late summer. Ise is a pilgrimage city built around Ise Jingu, Japan's most revered Shinto shrine: the Outer Shrine stands near Iseshi Station, and the Inner Shrine lies in deep cedar forest beside the clear Isuzu River, reached over the wooden Uji Bridge. Outside it, the old streets of Oharai-machi and Okage Yokocho sell red-bean mochi, Ise udon in thick dark sauce, tekone-zushi of marinated bonito and grilled shellfish. East at Futami, two wedded rocks joined by a sacred rope stand in the surf. Toba is a harbor town of hotels, a large aquarium and a pearl island, with ferries to the fishing islands of Toshijima, Sugashima and Kamishima. Ama divers still work the rocks for abalone, turban shell and seaweed out of Osatsu, and visitors eat the grilled catch beside the fire in their diving huts. Shima is resort and fishing country: pearl farms on Ago Bay, hotels at Kashikojima, lighthouses on Daiozaki and Anorisaki and the white beach at Goza. Matsusaka, a merchant town of old storehouses and castle walls, is famous for its marbled beef. Kintetsu limited expresses run from Nagoya and Osaka to Matsusaka, Ise, Toba and Kashikojima, JR lines and the Ise Expressway serve the north, and a car ferry crosses from Toba to Irago in about 55 minutes. From Musutafu the trip is about 2.5 hours by shinkansen to Nagoya and Kintetsu onward; from Osaka it is about two hours. Local hero offices in Ise and Toba keep the shrine approaches orderly, sidekicks work the New Year crowds, and a police box stands by the Uji Bridge.
Ise-Shima.hiddenInfo: The shrine crowds draw the small-time trade every pilgrim town has: pickpockets on the approach, sellers of fake charms, rental scams at the inns, and quarrels at the busiest festivals. Out on the bays, pearl harvests have been poor and rafts have been stripped at night, and the ama villages are aging with few new divers to replace them. Divers who use a Quirk to work deeper than the co-op allows are a sore point. Hero help is local in Ise and Toba; the larger agencies of Tsu and Nagoya are an hour or more away.

Cape Irago.name: Cape Irago
Cape Irago.basicInfo: The southern half of the Atsumi Peninsula in Aichi Prefecture, a long, low arm of land reaching west between Mikawa Bay and the open Pacific to end at Cape Irago, where the Irago Channel separates it from Toba and the Shima Peninsula. Most of the region is sea: the Pacific to the south and the busy shipping channel to the west. The peninsula is flat to gently rolling farmland on a low plateau. Its south shore, Omotehama, is a straight run of sand beach and low cliffs open to the ocean, where surfers ride the swell near Akabane and Hiroo and loggerhead turtles come ashore to nest in early summer. The region's northern edge touches the Mikawa Bay shore by Tahara, where a large car plant and wind turbines stand on reclaimed land. The climate is mild and sunny, with hard, dry northwest winds in winter. Tahara and its villages are rich farm country: greenhouses run in ranks across the fields, cabbage and broccoli fill the open ground in winter, melons and tomatoes grow under glass, and chrysanthemums are grown under electric lights so that at night whole valleys of greenhouses glow in rows across the dark land. In late winter the cape is covered in yellow rape blossoms, and in autumn hawks gather over it before crossing south. At the tip, Irago's white lighthouse stands on the rocks, the long sand beach of Koijigahama curves north, and a car ferry crosses to Toba in about 55 minutes. Fishing harbors at Akabane and Fukue land whitebait, octopus and the winter tiger puffer served in hot pot. The Atsumi Line commuter railway runs from Toyohashi to Mikawa-Tahara in about 35 minutes, and buses continue along Route 259 to the cape in about an hour. From Musutafu it is about an hour by shinkansen to Toyohashi, so most visitors reach the cape in under three hours. Visitors surf, cycle the flat coast roads, eat puffer and watch the hawks or the flower fields. Police boxes stand in Tahara and the larger villages, a small hero office in Tahara covers the whole peninsula, and at harvest a farmer whose Quirk reads ripeness by touch moves down the melon rows twice as fast as the crew.
Cape Irago.hiddenInfo: The peninsula is wealthy but thin on people: farmers are aging, field hands come and go on seasonal contracts, and the long roads between villages are dark and empty at night. Theft from greenhouses and packing sheds, melons and tools gone by morning, is the common crime, along with fights and drownings on the surf beaches. The single local hero office covers the whole peninsula; real backup comes from Toyohashi, forty minutes or more away by road.

Omaezaki.name: Omaezaki
Omaezaki.basicInfo: The Enshu coast of western Shizuoka, a narrow strip of shore running from the southern edge of Hamamatsu east past Iwata, Fukuroi and Kakegawa to the city of Omaezaki, whose cape at the region's eastern edge marks where Suruga Bay opens to the Pacific. Nearly all of the region is the open Enshu-nada sea; the land is a band of beach, dune and farmland along its northern edge. The shore is one long, nearly straight run of sand beaten by heavy surf, backed by belts of windbreak pine, fields and low towns. In southern Hamamatsu the Nakatajima dunes roll down to the sea, and every May the Hamamatsu Festival's giant kites fight over the sand. The broad gravel mouth of the Tenryu River opens between Hamamatsu and Iwata. Fukude's small port lands whitebait; Fukuroi grows crown muskmelons in glass houses, one fruit to a vine; tea fields reach down toward the coast in Kakegawa. Omaezaki is a fishing and surf town around a bonito and whitebait harbor, with windsurfers on its beaches year round, the cape lighthouse just past the region's eastern edge. The climate is sunny and mild, but the dry northwest wind of winter blasts down the coast for weeks, and summer brings typhoons and big swell. The coast also lives with the threat of a great Nankai Trough earthquake: tsunami towers, raised evacuation mounds and a long new seawall line the shore, and drills are taken seriously. Route 150 follows the coast the whole way; the Tokaido shinkansen and Tokaido Main Line run a few kilometers inland, with stations at Hamamatsu, Iwata, Fukuroi and Kakegawa, and local buses run down to the beaches and to Omaezaki. From Musutafu it is about an hour by shinkansen to Hamamatsu or 45 minutes to Kakegawa, then an hour by bus to Omaezaki. Visitors surf and windsurf, fly kites on the dunes, eat whitebait bowls and melon, and walk the beaches. Police boxes stand in every coastal town, small hero offices in Omaezaki and southern Hamamatsu cover long stretches of coast, and a lifeguard with a sonar Quirk works the summer beaches under a municipal permit.
Omaezaki.hiddenInfo: The coast's quiet worry is the sea itself: everyone knows the next great earthquake could send a tsunami over the dunes within minutes, and the drills make old residents tense. Day to day the trouble is ordinary: night races on Route 150 by riders with speed Quirks, drownings on the surf beaches, and theft from melon houses and fishing gear sheds. The local hero offices are spread thin over long coastline; bigger agencies in Hamamatsu can reach the beaches in twenty to forty minutes.

Mouth of Suruga Bay.name: Mouth of Suruga Bay
Mouth of Suruga Bay.basicInfo: The open mouth of Suruga Bay, Japan's deepest bay, where the water between Cape Omaezaki on the west and the cliffs of the western Izu Peninsula on the east falls away into the Suruga Trough, more than 2,000 m deep a short way offshore. The water is dark blue and cold below, warmed at the surface by branches of the Kuroshio current curling in from the south. On clear days Mt. Fuji stands over the head of the bay to the north, white from autumn to spring, and the Omaezaki lighthouse marks the western shore. Freighters and container ships run in and out to the port of Shimizu, deep-sea tuna boats head out from Yaizu, and small boats from the Shizuoka coast fish for bonito and horse mackerel, while the pink sakura shrimp fleets work the inner bay farther north. Winter brings strong westerlies, early summer brings fog, and typhoons come late summer and autumn. Coast guard patrol boats from Shimizu and Shimoda keep watch, and a few maritime heroes with water or flight Quirks work the bay. Far off to the southeast, beyond the peninsula's tip, police boats patrol the restricted exclusion zone around the prison island, and local boats keep well clear. A party could be out here on a fishing boat from Omaezaki, a charter, a passing freighter, or carried by a flying hero.
Mouth of Suruga Bay.hiddenInfo: The bay drops so deep so fast that anything lost here is gone for good, and some people rely on that. Small boats run cash cargo along the coast at night, and fishermen complain of nets cut by strangers. Hero help is a coast guard cutter or a maritime hero from the bay ports, thirty minutes to an hour out.

Sea off Toshima.name: Sea off Toshima
Sea off Toshima.basicInfo: Open sea in the northern Izu Islands, south of Izu Oshima and east of the Izu Peninsula's tip, where the small round island of Toshima rises on the western edge of the region: a single steep volcanic cone under 3 km across, covered in camellia groves, with one village of a few hundred people above a tiny harbor and no beach at all. The water is deep, clear and cobalt blue, carried northeast by the Kuroshio current. Oshima's volcano shows to the north, Niijima's long white shore to the southwest, and open Pacific to the east. The night ferry from Tokyo's Takeshiba pier and the jetfoils call at Toshima on the way south to Niijima, Shikinejima and Kozushima, though landings are often cancelled in heavy swell. Wild dolphins live around Toshima, and visitors swim with them in summer. Fishing boats from Oshima and Toshima work the grounds for alfonsino, bonito, flying fish and spiny lobster. Coast guard patrol boats pass on their rounds. Far to the southwest, beyond Niijima, police boats patrol the restricted exclusion zone around the prison island, and the ferries keep to their charted routes. A party could be out here on a ferry or jetfoil, a fishing or dolphin boat, a private yacht, or carried by a flying hero.
Sea off Toshima.hiddenInfo: Toshima lives by the boats: when the swell cancels landings for a week, food runs short and tempers with it. Visiting divers and anglers sometimes take lobster out of season, and dolphin boats compete for the same pods. The nearest hero help is on Oshima or the Izu mainland, an hour or more away even in good weather.

Pacific south of Boso.name: Pacific south of Boso
Pacific south of Boso.basicInfo: The open Pacific south of the Boso Peninsula's tip, from about twenty-five to seventy-five kilometers off Nojimazaki, where the sea opens out between the peninsula and the northern Izu Islands. The water is deep, well over a kilometer in most of the cell, and a vivid blue where the Kuroshio runs east through it, warm and fast; when the current swings south, cooler, greener water takes its place. Weather turns quickly here: summer squalls, typhoons in autumn, and strong westerly winds in winter. Boats from Shirahama, Chikura and Tateyama fish bonito, mackerel and flying fish, and sportfishers come for marlin and yellowtail. Big ships bound for Tokyo Bay pass through on their way to the Uraga channel to the northwest. To the north lies the low green tip of Boso; westward, on clear days, the volcanic islands of Izu Oshima, Toshima and Niijima show on the horizon. The coast guard patrols out of Tateyama and the Izu Islands, and maritime heroes take shifts covering the shipping lanes. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a charter, a passing ship, or carried by a flying hero.
Pacific south of Boso.hiddenInfo: This is empty water between busy lanes. The danger is weather and collision, and sportfishing boats sometimes ignore warnings. Help is the coast guard, an hour or more out. Petty villainy: ship-to-ship smuggling at night, illegal dumping, and breaking fishing rules.

Iki.name: Iki
Iki.basicInfo: The Genkai-nada around the north half of Iki, a low, rolling island between Kyushu and Tsushima. Most of this square is open water, but the island's north end lies inside it: the fishing town of Katsumoto with its morning market, the ferry port of Ashibe on the east coast, the hot-spring village of Yunomoto on the west, and Saruiwa, a sea stack shaped like a monkey's head in profile. Off Katsumoto lie a few small inhabited islets and uninhabited Tatsunoshima, whose white beaches and glassy water draw summer boat trips. Iki is gentle farmland of rice, barley and black cattle, dotted with small shrines, and it calls itself the birthplace of barley shochu; sea urchin rice bowls are the summer food. The water is a clear blue-green near shore and deep blue beyond, with the Tsushima Current setting northeast; winter northwesterlies make crossings rough. Jetfoils and ferries from Hakata reach Ashibe in about an hour and continue north to Tsushima, whose mountains show on the northwestern horizon. The coast guard patrols from Iki, and the island has a small police presence and a licensed hero or two for sea rescues. A party is out here by ferry, fishing boat or with a flying hero.
Iki.hiddenInfo: Iki is quiet; its problems are an aging population, drift trash on the north shore and fishermen worried about thinning squid. Small trouble is drunken fights at the port, theft from boats and poaching around the islets. Help from Fukuoka is an hour away by fast boat in good weather.

Genkai Sea.name: Genkai Sea
Genkai Sea.basicInfo: The Genkai-nada directly north of Fukuoka, the open water between Iki in the west and the Munakata coast in the east. The square is almost all sea; the only land is Oshima, Munakata's island of about seven square kilometers with a fishing harbor, hillside fields and a shrine where prayers are offered toward distant Okinoshima, and little Jinoshima near the eastern edge, known for wild camellias. Boats from Konominato on the Munakata coast reach Oshima in about twenty minutes. The water is a clear blue-green over sand and rock near the islands and a deeper blue offshore, mostly under a hundred meters deep, with the warm Tsushima Current setting northeast. Summers bring calm seas and squid boats at night; from November the northwest monsoon makes the Genkai-nada famous for rough, cold, gray water. This is the main approach to Hakata Port: ferries and jetfoils to Iki, Tsushima and Busan, fishing boats and cargo ships cross it every day, and Genkaijima and the hills of Itoshima show to the south. Boats from Oshima, Kanezaki and Fukuoka fish for sea bream, yellowtail, squid and Spanish mackerel. The coast guard and maritime heroes from Fukuoka are within half an hour. A party is out here aboard a ferry, a fishing or sightseeing boat, or with a flying hero.
Genkai Sea.hiddenInfo: Traffic is heavy near Hakata, so small collisions, drunk pleasure-boaters and stolen personal watercraft keep the harbor police busy in summer. Small-time smuggling moves through fishing boats and the Busan routes. Oshima's worry is losing its young people. Hero help is close by island standards, with Fukuoka half an hour away.

Kanmon Strait.name: Kanmon Strait
Kanmon Strait.basicInfo: The narrow Kanmon Strait and the cities on both shores, where Honshu meets Kyushu: Shimonoseki on the northern and eastern bank, Kitakyushu on the southern, and the coast west toward Munakata. The strait joins the Sea of Japan, open to the northwest as the Hibiki-nada, with the Inland Sea's Suo-nada to the southeast; at its tightest point, between Mekari and Dan-no-ura, it is only about seven hundred meters wide, with tidal currents near ten knots and hundreds of ships a day. The Kanmon Bridge carries the expressway over it, rail and road tunnels run under it, and a pedestrian tunnel lets people walk beneath the sea across the prefectural line in about fifteen minutes. Shimonoseki is a fish-market port: Karato market sells fugu, called fuku here, and sea urchin, vermilion Akama Shrine faces the waters of a great medieval sea battle, and the islet of a famous swordsmen's duel sits in the channel. Kitakyushu, a city of nearly a million, grew from five old towns: Moji's harbor of brick Meiji buildings and baked curry, Kokura's castle, covered Tanga market, nightlife and yaki udon, Yahata's steelworks and the night view from Mount Sarakura, and Wakamatsu and Tobata joined by a red suspension bridge. Farther west, the Onga River meets the sea at Ashiya and Munakata Taisha's main shrine stands in farmland near the edge. Summers are hot and humid, winters cool and windy. Kokura and Shin-Shimonoseki are on the Sanyo shinkansen: Hakata is about fifteen minutes away, Shin-Osaka a little over two hours, Musutafu about four. A monorail, the Kagoshima and Nippo lines and Kitakyushu Airport on its offshore island link the area, and overnight ferries sail from Shin-Moji to Osaka and Kobe and from Shimonoseki to Busan. Several hero agencies work both cities, police from two prefectures meet in the strait, and heat-tolerant and mutant-type workers are common in the mills and docks. Visitors eat fugu, walk the tunnel and watch Kokura's Gion drum festival in July.
Kanmon Strait.hiddenInfo: The busiest stretch of this coast for crime and rescue alike: collisions in the strait, people swept off seawalls by the current, smuggling through the container ports and ferry terminals, and the remnants of old gang families, much reduced in the hero era, running small rackets around Kokura's nightlife. The prefectural line through the strait leaves jurisdiction gaps that small-time villains try to use. Hero help is never far; the agencies here are busy and well equipped.

Yamaguchi.name: Yamaguchi
Yamaguchi.basicInfo: The southwest of Yamaguchi Prefecture between the Chugoku mountains and the Inland Sea: the prefectural capital Yamaguchi in its inland basin, the industrial port city of Ube, Hofu on the coast to the east, and the calm Suo-nada filling the southern part of the square. Northward the land climbs through rice valleys and forested hills toward the limestone country of Mine and the Akiyoshidai plateau. Yamaguchi is a quiet capital that once modeled itself on Kyoto: Rurikoji's five-story pagoda stands in a hillside park, old temples and a famous Zen dry garden sit on the city's edge, the Gion festival brings a heron dance in July, and the Tanabata lantern festival in August hangs thousands of red paper lanterns over the streets. Yuda Onsen, a hot-spring district inside the city, is said to have been found by a white fox. Shin-Yamaguchi, in the Ogori district, is the shinkansen stop and travel hub. Ube grew on coal and now runs cement and chemical plants along its waterfront, with a lakeside park full of outdoor sculpture and an airport with flights to Tokyo; Ube ramen is a rich pork and soy broth. Hofu has one of the three great Tenmangu shrines, old salt-farming flats and a naked festival in late autumn. Along the coast are tidal flats and small fishing ports; the sea beyond is shallow, sheltered and green-gray. The climate is the mild, sunny Inland Sea kind, with fog on winter mornings in the inland basin. The Sanyo shinkansen stops at Shin-Yamaguchi and Asa; Hakata is about thirty-five minutes away, Shin-Osaka about two hours, Musutafu about four. The Yamaguchi Line, which runs a steam train on some weekends, the Ube Line and Sanyo Line connect the towns, and the Sanyo and Chugoku expressways meet here. Police stations and small hero agencies cover each town, licensed heroes back up fire crews at Ube's plants, and workers with strength Quirks lift steel on construction sites under permit. Visitors soak at Yuda, see the pagoda, eat fugu and uiro sweets and ride the steam train north.
Yamaguchi.hiddenInfo: Ube's aging chemical and cement plants are a background worry; a leak or fire there draws heroes from across the prefecture. The capital is calm and a little sleepy, with road contracts and land deals as local gossip. Small crime is theft along the bypass roads, phone scams aimed at elderly farmers and copper theft from idle plants. Larger hero agencies are in Kitakyushu, about an hour west.

Shunan.name: Shunan
Shunan.basicInfo: Shunan is the Suo coast of southeastern Yamaguchi Prefecture, from the eastern edge of Hofu to Yanai, with the forested hills of the Chugoku Mountains behind and the Suo-nada sea in front; nearly half of the cell is water, the Inland Sea filling the south, with the Kaminoseki peninsula reaching out to the southeast. Shunan, the city formed around Tokuyama, is a port of petrochemical plants and refineries whose lights at night are a famous view, with a zoo, a shopping street and ferries to Kyushu. Kudamatsu next door builds shinkansen cars at its railcar works, Hikari has long pine-lined beaches at Murozumi, and Yanai is an old merchant town of white walls and red goldfish lanterns, whose August lantern festival fills the streets. Kaminoseki, at the tip of the peninsula, is a quiet fishing town of old houses facing small islands. Off Tokuyama, small islands such as Otsushima are reached by ferry, and inland the hills of rice terraces and cedar climb north to the upper Nishiki River valley. The climate is mild Setouchi, calm seas and sunny winters. The Sanyo shinkansen stops at Tokuyama, about forty-five minutes from Fukuoka and about four hours from Musutafu; the Sanyo Main Line runs along the coast and the Gantoku Line through the hills to Iwakuni, and the Sanyo Expressway crosses the region. Ferries run from Tokuyama to the Kunisaki Peninsula in Kyushu in about two hours, and from Yanai to Matsuyama. Visitors watch the factory lights, swim at Murozumi, buy goldfish lanterns and eat fugu and seafood. Each town has police and small hero agencies, plant crews with heat-resistant Quirks work under license, and sidekicks patrol the lantern festival.
Shunan.hiddenInfo: Industrial towns with shift workers, aging fishing villages. Small-time trouble is scrap and copper theft from industrial zones, bike gangs on coastal roads, and Quirk-users poaching shellfish. Hero coverage comes from Shunan's agencies; serious backup is from Hiroshima or Fukuoka, about an hour away by shinkansen.

Iwakuni.name: Iwakuni
Iwakuni.basicInfo: Iwakuni is the western mouth of Hiroshima Bay and the island-strewn waters south of it, a cell that is mostly Inland Sea: the land is the Iwakuni coast and its hills in the northwest corner, the big island of Suo-Oshima in the west, the southern half of Etajima and the Kurahashi island group in the northeast, and the Kutsuna islands of Ehime in the southeast, with the Iyo-nada sea opening to the south and the Aki-nada to the east. Iwakuni, a city of over a hundred thousand on the Nishiki River delta, is known for the Kintaikyo, a wooden bridge of five steep arches over the river, with a reconstructed castle on the wooded hill above, cormorant fishing on summer nights, rare white snakes kept as a natural monument, pressed Iwakuni sushi and lotus fields along the shore; a small airport on the shore has flights to Haneda. Suo-Oshima, joined to the mainland by a bridge from Yanai, is an island of mikan orange terraces, quiet beaches and fishing ports with old family ties to Hawaii. Across the water, Etajima keeps the red-brick halls of the naval officer school, and Kurahashi and Shimokamagari, Kure's islands, are linked by bridges and known for shipbuilding history, beaches and citrus. Small inhabited islands such as Hashirajima, Okikamuro and Heigunjima dot the sea, and Nakajima in the Kutsuna group grows mikan within sight of Matsuyama. The climate is mild Setouchi, calm and sunny, with summer typhoons and winter sea fog. Shin-Iwakuni and Iwakuni stations are about four hours from Musutafu by shinkansen and Sanyo Main Line, and about an hour from Fukuoka; a small single-track line follows the Nishiki River up into the hills. The Akinada Tobishima Kaido bridges hop between Kure's islands, ferries and high-speed boats from Hiroshima and Kure to Matsuyama cross the eastern waters, and small ferries reach the outer islands. Visitors walk the bridge, swim at island beaches and pick oranges. Iwakuni has police stations and a small hero agency, island police boxes are few, and ferry crews and fishers with water Quirks often help with rescues under permit.
Iwakuni.hiddenInfo: The islands are aging fast and many run on a single ferry. Small-time trouble is citrus theft, Quirk-assisted poaching of octopus and shellfish, bike theft at the bridge, and fights in the bars near the station. Jet noise from the base is an old local complaint. Hero help comes from Iwakuni or Hiroshima, but on the islands a boat or a flying hero is the only fast way in, and the coast guard does most sea rescues.

Matsuyama.name: Matsuyama
Matsuyama.basicInfo: Matsuyama is the northwest corner of Shikoku, the Ehime coast from Matsuyama city in the southwest to Imabari and Saijo in the east, facing the island-filled Inland Sea to the north and west; about half of the cell is water, the Iyo-nada to the west, the Aki-nada to the north and the Hiuchi-nada to the northeast. The Takanawa Peninsula's hills rise between Matsuyama and Imabari, and in the south the land climbs toward the Ishizuchi range on the southern edge. Matsuyama, Shikoku's largest city at about half a million, is a city of streetcars, citrus and hot springs: its castle stands on a hill in the center, reached by ropeway, and Dogo Onsen, one of Japan's oldest hot springs, keeps a wooden bathhouse at the end of the tram line; mikan juice, sea bream rice and literary history are its pride. Imabari, at the north tip, makes most of Japan's towels and builds ships in the country's largest shipbuilding cluster; its castle has a seawater moat, and it is the Shikoku end of the Shimanami Kaido bridges that hop north across Oshima, Hakatajima and the Kurushima Strait, one of the fastest tidal races in Japan. Saijo, in the east, is a town of spring water that wells up from the ground, with autumn festivals of floats and portable shrines, a railway museum and the ropeway up toward the sacred Mount Ishizuchi. The Hojo coast between Matsuyama and Imabari has beaches and Kikuma's roof-tile kilns. The climate is mild Setouchi: hot summers, mild winters, little snow. The JR Yosan Line links Matsuyama to Imabari and Saijo, and the Shiokaze limited express reaches Okayama in under three hours; Matsuyama Airport has flights to Haneda, and high-speed boats run to Hiroshima in about an hour and a quarter. From Musutafu it is about five and a half hours by shinkansen to Okayama and the Shiokaze. Visitors soak at Dogo, climb the castle, cycle the Shimanami Kaido and eat taimeshi. Matsuyama has several hero agencies and police stations, Imabari and Saijo have their own, shipyard crews with strength Quirks work under license, and sidekicks patrol the autumn festivals.
Matsuyama.hiddenInfo: A comfortable city and a working coast: shipyard booms and busts, labor disputes, and shipyard crews of many nationalities. Small-time trouble is bike theft, drunk brawls at the autumn festivals, Quirk-users stealing scrap or towels from factories, and pickpockets in Dogo. The Kurushima Strait's currents take careless boaters and swimmers every year. Hero coverage is solid in Matsuyama; Imabari and the islands lean on smaller agencies and the coast guard.

Niihama.name: Niihama
Niihama.basicInfo: Niihama is the eastern Ehime coast and the western tip of Kagawa, a strip of plain under steep mountains facing the Hiuchi-nada sea; about two fifths of the cell is water, the Inland Sea filling the north, and the land runs from Niihama in the west to Kanonji in the northeast, with the Shikoku Mountains rising sharply to the south. Niihama grew up around the Besshi copper mine, whose ruins high in the mountains, terraced stone buildings in the forest, are a heritage park; the city is still a metals and chemicals town. It is famous for its October drum-float festival, when huge Taiko-dai floats carried by teams of over a hundred clash in the streets. East of it, Shikokuchuo is Japan's paper city, its mills turning out tissue and paper products under the hills, with tea from the hamlet of Shingu. Kanonji, in Kagawa, has a giant coin-shaped sand drawing on its beach, two pilgrimage temples on one hill and the dried-sardine island of Ibukijima offshore, and Mitoyo's Chichibugahama beach turns into a mirror at low tide at sunset. The mountains behind rise into the Ishizuchi range and over the ridge into Kochi Prefecture on the southern edge, a quiet land of steep cedar slopes and gorges. The climate is mild Setouchi on the coast, with snow in the mountains. The JR Yosan Line follows the coast, with the Shiokaze and Ishizuchi limited expresses linking Okayama, Takamatsu and Matsuyama, and at Kawanoe the expressways from Matsuyama, Takamatsu, Kochi and Tokushima meet. From Musutafu it is about four to four and a half hours by shinkansen to Okayama and the Shiokaze. Visitors see the drum-float festival, walk the mine ruins, take photos at Chichibugahama and eat udon. Each town has police boxes and a small hero agency, mill and plant workers with heat or strength Quirks work under license, and sidekicks patrol the festivals.
Niihama.hiddenInfo: The drum-float festival is famous for clashes between neighborhood teams, and every year police and heroes break up fights and keep crowds back. Small-time trouble is metal theft, illegal dumping, and Quirk-users poaching game in the mountains. Hero help comes from Niihama and Matsuyama, about an hour away; in the mountains, a car and a long walk are the only way in.

Iya Valley.name: Iya Valley
Iya Valley.basicInfo: Iya Valley is the mountain heart of Shikoku, from the Kagawa plain at Zentsuji and Kotohira in the north, over the Sanuki Mountains, down to the Yoshino River and Awa-Ikeda, and south into the steep gorges of Iya and up to Mount Tsurugi; it is all land, mountains and valleys. In the north, Kotohira is the shrine town of Konpira-san, the sea god's shrine reached by 785 stone steps lined with shops, with Japan's oldest kabuki theater at its foot; nearby Zentsuji is the birthplace temple of the pilgrimage's founder, and the Manno reservoir is Japan's largest irrigation pond. In the middle, the Yoshino River runs east past Awa-Ikeda, a crossroads town, and the white-walled merchant street of Wakimachi with its firewall gables. South of Ikeda, the Iya Valley cuts deep into the mountains: vine bridges of woven wisteria hang over green water, hamlets cling to slopes, and in Oku-Iya the scarecrow village of Nagoro and the double vine bridges sit beneath Mount Tsurugi, Shikoku's second-highest peak, with a chairlift and a shrine near the summit. The climate is cool in the mountains, with snow in winter, and the Iya is said to be where defeated Heike warriors hid. People grow buckwheat, potatoes and tea, raise cattle and run inns. The JR Dosan Line runs from Kotohira over the mountains to Awa-Ikeda and the Oboke gorge on the western edge, served by the Nanpu limited express from Okayama, and the Tokushima Line follows the Yoshino; the Tokushima Expressway follows the Yoshino past Ikeda. Takamatsu Airport in the north has flights to Haneda. From Musutafu it is about four and a half hours by shinkansen to Okayama and the Nanpu, then a bus into Iya. Visitors climb Konpira, cross vine bridges, hike Tsurugi, raft the Yoshino and eat Iya soba. Each town has police boxes and a licensed hero covers the mountains, pilgrims walk the roads, and rafting guides with water Quirks help with rescues.
Iya Valley.hiddenInfo: The Iya Valley is emptying, many hamlets are nearly abandoned, and roads close in landslides and snow. Small-time trouble is theft from shrines and pilgrims, illegal logging, and Quirk-users poaching game. Kotohira's crowds bring pickpockets. Hero help comes from Takamatsu or Tokushima, about an hour or more away, and deep in the valley it can take several hours.

Tokushima.name: Tokushima
Tokushima.basicInfo: The eastern lowland of Tokushima Prefecture in Shikoku: the Naruto coast at the mouth of the strait, the delta of the Yoshino River with Tokushima city, the Anan coast to the south and the steep forested Katsuura and Kamikatsu valleys inland. The eastern part of the cell is the Kii Channel, the open water between Shikoku and the Kii Peninsula. At the north edge, the Onaruto Bridge crosses to Awaji above the Naruto whirlpools, and Naruto is a mix of fishing harbors, sandy sweet-potato fields and a huge ceramic-tile art museum on a hill. The Yoshino River, broad and braided, runs east into a plain of lotus fields, old indigo-dyeing towns and Tokushima city, the capital, which sits around Mount Bizan, a green hill with a ropeway. Each August the city's streets fill for four nights with the Awa Odori, hundreds of dance troupes moving to shamisen and drum before more than a million visitors, with sidekicks and police working every block. North of the river, the Shikoku eighty-eight-temple pilgrimage begins at Ryozen-ji, and pilgrims in white walk the roads here year-round. South, Komatsushima and Anan are port and factory towns, and inland Kamikatsu is a mountain village known for zero-waste living and for selling decorative leaves to fine restaurants, while a ropeway climbs to the mountaintop temple of Tairyu-ji. The climate is warm and humid, with typhoons in late summer. Food is sudachi citrus squeezed on everything, Naruto wakame and sweet potatoes, Tokushima ramen with sweet pork and raw egg, and Awa beef. The JR Kotoku, Naruto, Tokushima and Mugi lines run from Tokushima station; expressway buses cross the bridges to Kobe in about two hours and to Osaka in about two and a half; a ferry crosses to Wakayama, and the airport has flights to Tokyo. Musutafu is about four and a half hours away. Tokushima has a small hero agency and police boxes; licensed heroes cover the valleys by car, and a lotus farmer whose Quirk lets her breathe mud-water digs roots faster than any machine.
Tokushima.hiddenInfo: Tokushima is peaceful and proud. Trouble peaks at Awa Odori: crowd crushes, drunken fights and pickpockets, with every hero on eastern Shikoku on duty. Otherwise it is depopulating valleys, pilgrims who get lost or fall ill, and small smuggling through the ports. Big-city help comes from Kobe or Osaka across the bridges, about two hours away.

Wakayama.name: Wakayama
Wakayama.basicInfo: The western coast of the Kii Peninsula in Wakayama Prefecture, from the city of Wakayama at the mouth of the Kino River south along a coast of bays, orange-terraced hills and fishing towns to the cape at Hinomisaki, with the Kii Channel filling the western half of the cell. Wakayama city is a prefectural capital of modest size, centered on the white keep of Wakayama Castle on its wooded hill, which sits right at the northern edge. South of it lie the scenic bay of Wakanoura and the hillside temple of Kimii-dera, then the lacquerware and factory town of Kainan and a resort on a reclaimed island. Beyond, the coast turns rugged: Arida's valley is terraced into mikan orange groves that turn the hillsides orange in late autumn; Yuasa, a small town of lattice-fronted breweries, claims to be the birthplace of Japanese soy sauce; and Yura's Kokoku-ji is the temple of the wandering bamboo-flute monks and the origin of kinzanji miso. Gobo, on the Hidaka River, keeps Dojo-ji temple and its legend of the woman who became a serpent. Hinomisaki, the westernmost point of the peninsula, has cliffs, a lighthouse and a view across the channel toward Shikoku. Inland, steep orange and plum orchards climb into the mountains. The climate is warm and sunny, wet in typhoon season. Food is Wakayama ramen in soy-and-pork broth, mikan, pickled ume, whitebait and sea bream. The JR Kisei line runs along the coast, with the Kuroshio limited express reaching Wakayama from Shin-Osaka in about an hour and Gobo in under two; the Nankai line reaches Wakayama from Namba, the little Kishigawa line keeps a cat stationmaster at Kishi, and the Hanwa Expressway runs south. A ferry links Wakayama port with Tokushima. Musutafu is about three hours from Wakayama city. Wakayama has hero agencies and police boxes; licensed heroes cover the coast towns, and orchard workers with climbing or long-reach Quirks are in demand at harvest.
Wakayama.hiddenInfo: The coast is easygoing, but the prefecture is aging and the fishing towns are shrinking. Trouble is theft from orchards at harvest, illegal fishing and drunk driving on the coast road. Typhoon floods and landslides are the real emergencies, and the expected Nankai Trough earthquake is always on people's minds. Osaka's agencies are an hour north; the southern towns rely on a few local heroes.

Koyasan.name: Koyasan
Koyasan.basicInfo: The heart of the Kii Mountains: the monastery town of Koyasan in the north, the Ryujin and Totsukawa river gorges, and the Kumano Hongu country in the south, a cell almost entirely of steep forested ridges and deep valleys. Koyasan sits in a high basin ringed by eight peaks, a town of more than a hundred temples founded by Kobo Daishi; visitors sleep in temple lodgings, eat vegetarian monk's cuisine and sesame tofu, and walk at dusk through Okunoin, a two-kilometer cemetery path among giant cedars and mossy tombs leading to the founder's mausoleum. From there the mountains run south in endless cedar ridges. The Koya-Ryujin Skyline road follows the crests to Ryujin Onsen, a valley hot spring famous for smoothing skin, past Mount Gomadan, the prefecture's highest peak. To the east, Totsukawa, one of Japan's largest villages by area, strings its hamlets along the Totsu River gorge, with the swaying Tanize suspension bridge, riverside hot springs and an old summer bon dance. In the south, Kumano Hongu Taisha, head of the three Kumano grand shrines, stands in cedar woods above the river, and nearby an enormous torii at Oyunohara marks its original site on a sandbank. Hot spring villages cluster around it: Yunomine, with one of Japan's oldest public baths; Kawayu, where people dig their own pools in the riverbed; and Watarase. The Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trails cross the cell, the Kohechi from Koyasan to Hongu over three high passes and the Nakahechi from Tanabe through Chikatsuyu. It is among the rainiest country in Japan, misty and lush, with typhoons in late summer and snow on the high ridges. There is no railway except the cable car up to Koyasan from the north; long local buses follow the gorge roads, including the route from Yamato-Yagi in Nara through Totsukawa to Shingu, the longest local bus run in the country. Koyasan is about two hours from Shin-Osaka and four and a half from Musutafu; Hongu is most of a day. Police boxes and a handful of licensed heroes cover huge districts, and a mail carrier with a mutant mountain-goat build still delivers to hamlets the roads do not reach.
Koyasan.hiddenInfo: The mountains are sacred and quiet, but vast. Lost hikers on the Kohechi and landslides that cut off villages are the main emergencies, and help can be hours away. Koyasan's tourist crowds draw pickpockets and a few con artists dressed as pilgrims or monks. Wildlife poaching and illegal logging happen in remote valleys. The nearest real hero force is in Wakayama, Nara or Osaka, two hours or more by road.

Owase.name: Owase
Owase.basicInfo: The Higashi-Kishu coast of southern Mie and the mountains behind it: the ria coast around Owase, the long beach at Kumano, and the high Odaigahara plateau on the Nara border, with the open Kumano Sea filling the southeastern half of the cell. The coast is steep and deeply indented, with small harbors tucked into drowned valleys and cypress plantations climbing straight up from the water. Owase is a compact fishing and forestry town on its own deep bay, with a large fish market, yellowtail and tuna pens in the inlets, a plant drawing up deep-sea water and fine hinoki cypress timber; its shrine holds a rowdy Ya-Ya Festival each February, and the town gets some of the heaviest rain in Japan. North along the coast, Kihoku's hamlets and the stone-paved passes of the old Iseji pilgrim route, Magose among them, wind through the cedars. South, Kumano city faces Shichiri-mihama, a beach of rounded pebbles running more than twenty kilometers toward Shingu, beside the wave-carved rocks of Onigajo and Hana-no-Iwaya Shrine, a sacred cliff hung with a long rope from its summit. The Kumano fireworks each August are launched from boats and from the cliffs, and the Maruyama rice terraces climb a hillside inland. West and up, Odaigahara is a misty high plateau of moss, spruce and deer, with the sheer Daijagura cliff above the Osugi gorge, one of the rainiest places in the country. Summers are hot and stormy, winters mild on the coast and snowy on the heights. Food is bonito, saury pressed into sushi, yellowtail, mehari-zushi rice balls wrapped in pickled greens, and Kumano mikan. The JR Kisei line runs down the coast with the Nanki limited express from Nagoya, about three hours to Owase, and the Kisei Expressway now reaches Kumano; Musutafu is about four and a half hours away. Owase and Kumano have police boxes and a small hero agency, and a few licensed heroes cover the long coast; a pearl diver whose Quirk lets her hold her breath for an hour is the harbor's unofficial rescue swimmer.
Owase.hiddenInfo: Owase and Kumano are shrinking, and the coast is a long way from anywhere. Typhoon storm surges, landslides on the coast road and floods are the real dangers. Small crime is theft of fish and timber and poaching on the plateau. The nearest larger hero agencies are in Tsu and Ise, an hour or two away; heroes from Nagoya take most of a morning.

Kumano Sea.name: Kumano Sea
Kumano Sea.basicInfo: The open Kumano Sea, the stretch of Pacific south of the Shima Peninsula, with the rocky southern shore of Minami-Ise just past the region's northern edge and the long ria coast of Kihoku and Owase to the west. Close to shore the water is green over reefs and kelp; farther out it turns deep blue and falls away toward the Nankai Trough, thousands of meters down. The warm Kuroshio runs offshore, and the coast behind it is one of the rainiest in Japan, with heavy summer downpours and typhoons that often come ashore here in late summer. Coastal freighters and tankers rounding the Kii Peninsula between the Tokyo and Osaka ports pass through in a steady line, their lights strung across the dark at night. Fishing boats from Nakiri, Gokasho, Nishiki and Owase work the grounds for bonito and tuna, mackerel and sardine, and spiny lobster nets are set near the rocks. There are no islands and no ferries; the open horizon is broken only by ships and, on clear days, the hills of the Shima coast. Coast guard boats from Toba and Owase patrol the area, and maritime heroes come out mostly for storms and sinkings. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a coastal freighter, a yacht rounding the Kii Peninsula, or carried by a flying hero.
Kumano Sea.hiddenInfo: Rough water and few witnesses: small boats sometimes meet freighters offshore to pass cargo that never shows on a manifest, and fishermen argue over grounds and nets. Help is a coast guard cutter or a hero flying out from Toba or Owase, most of an hour away.

Sea off Irago.name: Sea off Irago
Sea off Irago.basicInfo: Open Pacific south of the Atsumi Peninsula and the Irago Channel, where the shipping approaches to Ise Bay and Mikawa Bay meet the ocean. Beyond sight of the beaches the water is deep blue and heaves with long swells, sloping down toward the Nankai Trough, while the warm Kuroshio runs farther out. This is one of the busiest sea lanes in Japan: tankers, container ships and bulk carriers bound for Nagoya and Yokkaichi, and huge car carriers sailing from Mikawa Bay, all funnel toward the channel, and pilot boats meet them off the cape. The long-distance car ferry from Nagoya to Sendai and Hokkaido heads out through here and turns east. Fishing boats from Atsumi and Shima work the grounds for bonito, horse mackerel and puffer, keeping clear of the big ships. On clear days the Irago lighthouse and the hills of Shima show to the north, and nothing else but sea to the south. Winter westerlies, summer southerly swell and late-summer typhoons can close the lane. Coast guard patrol boats keep traffic in order, and maritime heroes are called out for collisions and fires at sea. A party could be out here on the ferry, a freighter, a fishing boat, or carried by a flying hero.
Sea off Irago.hiddenInfo: Heavy traffic means near-misses and the occasional collision, and crews on long voyages sometimes slip goods to small boats that meet them off the cape. Help comes from the coast guard or maritime heroes out of Toba and Nagoya, an hour or more away.

Enshu-nada.name: Enshu-nada
Enshu-nada.basicInfo: The open Enshu-nada, the stretch of Pacific off the long sand coast of western Shizuoka, known to sailors for generations as rough water. Here, well offshore, the water is deep blue and heavy with swell, falling away toward the Nankai Trough, and the warm Kuroshio current runs to the south. In winter the dry northwest wind races down from the mountains and whips the sea white; in summer, long southerly swells roll toward the beaches, and typhoons can turn it violent from late summer into autumn. The coastal shipping route between Tokyo Bay and the ports of Nagoya and Osaka passes through, and at night the freighters' lights move in a slow line. Fishing boats from Maisaka, Fukude and Omaezaki come out for bonito and mackerel, while the whitebait boats stay near the beaches. On a clear winter day the coastal hills and, far beyond, the snow of the Southern Alps can show to the north, and to the northeast the cape at Omaezaki. Coast guard patrol boats and the occasional maritime hero cover the area. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a coastal freighter, a yacht, or carried by a flying hero.
Enshu-nada.hiddenInfo: The sea itself is the danger: small boats caught by the winter wind, and pleasure craft that set out on a calm morning and do not come back. Rescue is a coast guard cutter or a maritime hero from Hamamatsu or Omaezaki, most of an hour away.

Pacific off Omaezaki.name: Pacific off Omaezaki
Pacific off Omaezaki.basicInfo: Open Pacific south of Cape Omaezaki and the mouth of Suruga Bay, where the Suruga Trough runs out to meet the Nankai Trough in deep, dark blue water. The Kuroshio current flows east to the south, sometimes swinging close enough to warm the surface and push ships along. The busy coastal shipping route between Tokyo Bay and the ports of Nagoya, Osaka and Kobe rounds the Izu and Omaezaki capes here, and freighters, tankers and car carriers pass in a steady line day and night. Tuna and bonito boats out of Omaezaki and Yaizu work the open water, and sport fishing boats chase marlin in late summer. On clear days the Omaezaki lighthouse shows to the north and the Izu Peninsula's mountains to the northeast. To the east, police boats patrol the restricted exclusion zone around the prison island, and ships give it a wide berth. Weather is open-ocean weather: strong winter westerlies, fog in early summer and typhoons from late summer into autumn. Coast guard cutters patrol the route, and maritime heroes come out for sinkings and fires at sea. A party could be out here on a freighter, a fishing boat, a yacht, or carried by a flying hero.
Pacific off Omaezaki.hiddenInfo: Fishermen grumble that the exclusion zone to the east has cost them good grounds, and a few push closer to its edge than they should. Help is a coast guard cutter or a maritime hero from the Shizuoka coast, an hour or more away.

Miyakejima.name: Miyakejima
Miyakejima.basicInfo: Two islands of the central Izu Islands in the open Pacific, about 180 km south of Tokyo: round, volcanic Miyakejima in the north of the region and steep, forested Mikurajima about 20 km to its south. Both belong to Tokyo. All around is deep blue sea carried east by the Kuroshio current, with Kozushima's flat-topped mountain on the western horizon. Miyakejima is about 8 km across, a single volcano, Mt. Oyama, whose summit collapsed into a wide crater in its last great eruption; the whole island was evacuated for years, and people still live with volcanic gas: monitors stand at the village halls, sirens are tested, and a few high roads stay closed. Black lava fields from past eruptions run down to the sea, and on the south side lava that buried a village and half a school is now crossed by a walkway. Around the cones, laurel forest and black pine shelter so many birds that the island is a favorite of birdwatchers, and Tairo-ike, a quiet crater lake in the southeast forest, rings with them. Its five villages sit along a ring road of about 30 km, where islanders fish, grow ashitaba, run small inns and dive shops and guide birders. Ferries dock at whichever of three piers the wind allows, and a small airport takes planes from Chofu in under an hour. Mikurajima is a cliff-walled island with one village of a few hundred people above a single exposed pier where the ferry often cannot land. Its old forest of giant chinquapin and boxwood may be entered only with a licensed guide, shearwaters nest in burrows across the slopes, and wild dolphins live all around it, so swimming tours fill the summer. Visitor numbers are limited and lodging must be booked ahead. The night ferry from Tokyo's Takeshiba pier reaches Miyakejima at dawn after about six and a half hours and continues to Mikurajima and Hachijojima, and an inter-island helicopter links the islands. From Musutafu, a trip here means a train to Tokyo and an overnight ferry, most of a day. Winter winds cancel ferries, and typhoons come in late summer. A police box stands on each island, a small hero office in Ako covers both, and a volcano watcher with a gas-sensing Quirk works under a disaster office permit.
Miyakejima.hiddenInfo: Life here depends on the volcano and the weather: a gas alert or a week of cancelled ferries can empty the shop shelves. The islands are aging and quiet, and the one local hero office covers both; real help comes from Tokyo by air, an hour or more away, and not at all in a typhoon. Trouble is small: anglers fishing out of season, tourists slipping into Mikura's forest without a guide, and fishermen who grumble that the exclusion zone to the west has closed off old grounds.

Pacific east of Miyakejima.name: Pacific east of Miyakejima
Pacific east of Miyakejima.basicInfo: The open Pacific east of Miyakejima and Mikurajima, a wide reach of empty, deep-blue ocean beside the middle of the Izu Islands chain, about two hundred kilometers south of Tokyo. There is no land in the cell itself. Miyakejima's volcano shows to the west on clear days, a broad dark cone that sometimes trails steam, with the steep green dome of Mikurajima to its south. The bottom lies a kilometer or two down, and the Kuroshio usually flows east through this water in a warm, fast band, though in some years it loops far to the south. The weather is nearly subtropical: warm, humid summers, typhoons from late summer, and gusty westerly winters. Bonito, flying fish, yellowtail and marlin follow the current, boats out of the islands fish its edges, and wild dolphins swim near Mikurajima.
