The big ferry from Tokyo to the southern Izu Islands passes to the west by night, and cargo ships sometimes cross. The coast guard watches by aircraft and patrol boat, and maritime heroes cover the islands on long rotations. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a yacht, a passing ship, or carried by a flying hero.
Pacific east of Miyakejima.hiddenInfo: Very little happens here. The risk is weather and distance: a sick passenger or a disabled boat may wait hours for help. Help is the coast guard, by aircraft from the mainland or the islands. Small villainy: illegal fishing by unlicensed boats and the occasional smuggling transfer at sea.

Hirado.name: Hirado
Hirado.basicInfo: The far northwest of Kyushu and the islands off it: the southern half of Iki at the top of the square, the open channel south of it, the Higashi-Matsuura peninsula of Saga Prefecture on the east side, Takashima and the mouth of Imari Bay in the middle, and Hirado and Ikitsuki islands at the southwest corner, in Nagasaki Prefecture. More than three quarters of it is sea. Southern Iki is rolling farmland and small harbors around Gonoura, its main port, with the moated Yayoi-era village of Haranotsuji rebuilt on the plain, a small airport and long sandy beaches. On the peninsula, Yobuko is famous for squid served still translucent, a morning market and the bridge to Kabeshima; nearby are the stone ramparts of the castle from which the 1590s invasion of Korea was launched and the windy cape of Hadomisaki. Takashima, linked by bridge, is where a Mongol fleet sank in a typhoon in 1281, and archaeologists still map wrecks offshore. Hirado, joined to the mainland by a red suspension bridge, was one of Japan's first ports open to Europeans: a white stone warehouse rebuilt from the Dutch trading post stands by the harbor under the castle, and hidden Christian villages, terraced rice fields and small churches sit on the island's western slopes. Ikitsuki beyond, an old whaling island, is linked by another long bridge. The climate is mild, rainy in June and July and battered by northwesterlies in winter. People fish, farm rice and cattle, dive for abalone and sea urchin and run inns. Jetfoils from Hakata reach Gonoura in about an hour, ferries also sail from Karatsu, buses and the Chikuhi Line reach Karatsu and Yobuko from Fukuoka in about an hour and a half, and the Matsuura Railway's coastal diesel cars stop at Tabira-Hiradoguchi, the westernmost station on Japan's main-island railways. From Musutafu, allow most of a day. Licensed heroes cover these coasts by car and boat, police boxes stand in every harbor town, and sidekicks patrol summer festivals and squid markets. Visitors eat squid, drive the bridges, tour churches and take boats to the islets.
Hirado.hiddenInfo: Fishing towns worry about thinning squid and the price of fuel. Unlicensed divers go after Mongol relics off Takashima, a protected site, and abalone poaching is steady. Real hero help is spread thin: Karatsu and Sasebo have small agencies, and Fukuoka is an hour and a half away. Small crime is theft from boats and churches and drunken trouble at harbor festivals.

Iizuka.name: Iizuka
Iizuka.basicInfo: The inland country east and southeast of Fukuoka: the Chikushi plain with Dazaifu and Chikushino, the old coal-mining Chikuho basin around Iizuka, Nogata and Tagawa, the Asakura farmland on the north bank of the Chikugo River, the sacred peak of Mount Hiko in the east, and the Buzen coast at Yukuhashi in the northeast corner. Tosu, the rail and expressway crossroads of Kyushu, sits on the western edge. Dazaifu was the ancient government seat of Kyushu, and its Tenmangu shrine to the god of learning draws students before exams and millions of visitors who eat grilled umegae mochi along the approach; Futsukaichi Onsen is next door. Over the hills, Sasaguri has a huge bronze reclining Buddha, and Mount Homan rises above old shrines with sweeping views. The Chikuho basin once fed Japan's furnaces with coal; its slag heaps are green hills now, Tagawa keeps two brick chimneys and a winding tower as a monument, Iizuka has an old wooden kabuki playhouse, and the towns are known for sweets from the days when the Nagasaki road carried sugar through. Akizuki, a tiny castle town in the hills, is famous for cherry blossom and autumn color; Asakura has triple waterwheels, persimmon and pear orchards and the riverside hot springs of Harazuru, where cormorant fishing is done in summer. Koishiwara potters work in the hills, and Mount Hiko's mountain-ascetic trails climb through cedar to nearly twelve hundred meters. Summers are hot and humid, with heavy rains in early July that sometimes flood the valleys; winters are cool, with occasional snow on the mountains. Nishitetsu trains run to Dazaifu, JR lines link Hakata with Iizuka in about forty minutes, the Heisei Chikuho Railway runs through the basin, and the Kyushu and Oita expressways meet at Tosu. From Musutafu, about five hours. Each town has police and small hero agencies; heroes manage exam-season crowds at Dazaifu and flood rescues in the rainy season, and Tosu's warehouses hire strength-type workers. Visitors pray for exam luck, soak at Futsukaichi, walk Akizuki and hike Mount Hiko.
Iizuka.hiddenInfo: Chikuho still carries the hard reputation of its coal days: shuttered shopping streets, old mine shafts that cave in under fields, and a few old gang families, much reduced since heroes rose, running small rackets in Tagawa and Iizuka. Asakura's hill farms dread the July rains. Dazaifu's crowds draw pickpockets and fake charm sellers, and Tosu's warehouses see cargo theft. Fukuoka's agencies are thirty minutes to an hour away.

Nakatsu.name: Nakatsu
Nakatsu.basicInfo: The Buzen coast of northern Oita Prefecture and the hills behind it: Nakatsu and Buzen on the shallow Suo-nada, Usa and its great shrine on the plain to the east, Bungo-Takada at the western foot of the Kunisaki peninsula, the Yabakei gorge country in the southwest, and the north shore of Beppu Bay at Hiji in the southeast corner. The northern part of the square is sea, wide tidal flats at low water where horseshoe crabs still breed and fishermen catch pike conger. Nakatsu is a castle town whose castle stands at the river mouth with seawater in its moat, and it calls itself the capital of karaage, with dozens of shops frying garlic-and-soy chicken; its summer Gion festival parades floats through the old streets, and a big car assembly plant nearby gives the town its factory shifts. Usa Jingu, head of all the Hachiman shrines in Japan, sits in a forest of camphor and cedar with vermilion halls and a lotus pond, and Usa's farms grow rice, barley for shochu and grapes for the Ajimu wineries in the hills, where farm stays are common. Bungo-Takada has a shopping street restored to look the way it did in the 1950s, and in the hills toward Kunisaki are great Buddhas carved into rock faces and Fukiji, the oldest wooden building in Kyushu. Yabakei is a land of strange volcanic rock pillars and gorges: a tunnel dug by hand through a cliff over decades, a temple of hundreds of stone arhats in a cave, and blazing color each November. The Innai valley has dozens of old stone arch bridges. Summers are hot, winters mild on the coast and cold in the gorges. Limited expresses on the JR Nippo Line run from Hakata via Kokura to Nakatsu in about an hour and a quarter and on through Usa toward Beppu, and the Higashi-Kyushu Expressway follows the coast. From Musutafu, about five hours. Each town has a police station; small hero agencies in Nakatsu and Usa cover the countryside, and sidekicks direct the New Year crowds at the shrine. Visitors eat karaage, pray at Usa, drive the gorges and taste local wine.
Nakatsu.hiddenInfo: The Buzen coast is a quiet, working region where factory jobs keep the towns alive while farm villages empty out. Small crime is theft of shrine offerings, car theft, joyriding on the gorge roads and the odd brawl at shift change. Flash floods and rockfalls in Yabakei are the bigger danger. Larger hero help comes from Kitakyushu, about an hour north, or from Oita.

Kunisaki.name: Kunisaki
Kunisaki.basicInfo: The Kunisaki Peninsula and the water around it: a round, knuckled thumb of old volcanic land pushing east from northern Oita into the western Seto Inland Sea, with the long, thin tip of Ehime's Sadamisaki Peninsula reaching toward it from the east. Most of this cell is open water. The Kunisaki side lies in the west and northwest; the Iyo-nada sea fills the middle; Sadamisaki's last few kilometers enter at the southeast corner, its tip facing Kyushu across the Hayasui Strait just south of the edge. Kunisaki is a wheel of steep ridges and narrow valleys running down from the extinct cone of Mount Futago at its center to a ring of small fishing and farming coasts. The valleys hold the Rokugo Manzan temples, a thousand-year-old mountain Buddhist culture of stone guardian statues, moss-grown steps, cave shrines and ridge-walking ascetic trails. Kitsuki, on the southwest shore facing Beppu Bay, is a compact castle town split between two hills of samurai lanes with a merchant street in the hollow between, where visitors rent kimono to walk the slopes. The town of Kunisaki and the villages of Aki and Musashi line the east coast; Oita Airport sits on reclaimed land on that shore, with a long airport bus run down to Beppu and Oita. Off the north coast, little Himeshima is reached by car ferry from Imi and is known for farmed kuruma prawns and its fox dance at Bon. Sadamisaki is a narrow ridge of a peninsula lined with wind turbines; its tip village of Misaki is a ferry port with a car ferry across the strait to Saganoseki in about seventy minutes, and the strait's fierce tides make its line-caught horse mackerel and mackerel some of the most prized fish in Japan. Winters are mild and dry, summers hot. The JR Nippo Main Line and the Higashi-Kyushu Expressway cross the peninsula's base at Kitsuki. From Musutafu, it is about four hours by shinkansen to Kokura and another hour on a limited express, or a flight from Haneda into Oita Airport; from Hakata, a limited express reaches Kitsuki in under two hours. Small hero offices in Kitsuki and Kunisaki cover the whole peninsula, police boxes sit at the ferry ports, and the summer festivals draw sidekicks on loan from Oita.
Kunisaki.hiddenInfo: Kunisaki is aging fast: many valley hamlets are down to a handful of households, empty temple lodgings need minding, and wild boar and deer raid the paddies. Hero coverage is thin; the nearest large agencies are in Oita and Beppu, about an hour away by road, so airport security and the coast guard often reach trouble first. Small-time crime is ordinary: poaching from the prawn farms, thefts from unattended temple halls and roadside stands, unlicensed Quirk use by fishermen working the strait's currents. Fog over the Iyo-nada can close the ferries.

Yawatahama.name: Yawatahama
Yawatahama.basicInfo: The western shoulder of Ehime where the Sadamisaki Peninsula leaves Shikoku: the root of that long ridge, the port city of Yawatahama, the old castle town of Ozu on the Hiji River, the merchant town of Uchiko, and the hills of Seiyo around Unomachi. The western third of the cell is sea, the Iyo-nada north of the Sadamisaki ridge and the Uwa Sea and Bungo Channel south of it; the rest is steep, folded hill country running east into higher mountains. Terraced mandarin orchards on stone walls climb nearly every slope that faces the sea, and the coastal road from Iyo-Nagahama past Shimonada runs right along the water. Ikata, on the peninsula's north side, is a wind-swept fishing and orchard town. Yawatahama is a working fishing port with a big wholesale fish market, a market hall for visitors and its own champon noodle soup; car ferries leave here for Beppu in under three hours and for Usuki in a little over two. Ozu sits in a basin on the Hiji River with a rebuilt wooden castle keep above the water, a riverside villa and tea house on the bluffs, cormorant fishing by lantern light from June through September, and riverbank taro-stew gatherings in autumn. From late autumn to early spring, cold morning air drains down the Hiji and pours out its mouth at Nagahama as a fast river of fog under the red iron bascule bridge. Uchiko preserves a street of wax merchants' houses and a restored kabuki theater from the Taisho years. Unomachi in Seiyo has old merchant lanes and the terraced rice paddies of the Uwa hills. The JR Yosan Line limited express runs from Matsuyama to Uchiko, Ozu, Yawatahama and Unomachi on its way to Uwajima, and the Matsuyama Expressway follows the same inland line. From Musutafu, it is most of a day by train through Okayama and Matsuyama, or a flight to Matsuyama and under an hour on the train; from Osaka, about five hours. Small hero agencies in Ozu and Yawatahama cover the district, with patrols doubled in cormorant season and at the autumn festivals, and orchard workers with climbing or lifting Quirks are hired by the season.
Yawatahama.hiddenInfo: The orchard terraces depend on an aging workforce and seasonal hires, and labor disputes and pay theft among pickers simmer quietly at harvest. Fishermen and the Yawatahama market watch for poachers in the Uwa Sea and for theft of catch and gear from the piers. Real hero muscle comes from Matsuyama, about an hour away; at night, one small office often handles calls for the whole district.

Mount Ishizuchi.name: Mount Ishizuchi
Mount Ishizuchi.basicInfo: The mountain spine of western Shikoku: from the summit ridge of Mount Ishizuchi near the northern edge, at 1,982 meters the highest peak in western Japan, south across the Kumakogen highlands and the Shikoku Karst to the upper Shimanto and Niyodo watersheds. Almost all of it is land, steep and forested, with cedar and cypress plantations below and beech, fir and dwarf bamboo on the ridges. Ishizuchi is a sacred mountain of mountain ascetics; its rock summit, Tengudake, is reached along a knife-edge ridge, and the old pilgrim route climbs long chains bolted into the cliffs, with easier detours for the less brave. The Ishizuchi Skyline road climbs from Omogo Gorge, a deep green canyon famous for autumn color, to the trailhead at Tsuchigoya, and the UFO Line, a ridge-top road, runs along the Kochi side above a sea of clouds. Kumakogen is a cool highland town of farms and two pilgrimage temples, one built against a sheer cliff, on Route 33 between Matsuyama and Kochi; Tobe, in the northern foothills, makes heavy white porcelain painted in indigo. South, the Shikoku Karst is a long limestone plateau with grazing cattle, white rock pinnacles and wind turbines along the prefectural line, with views to the Pacific on clear days. Below it, Tsuno town holds the source of the Shimanto River on Mount Irazu, and Yusuhara is a cloud-high town of terraced paddies and striking modern timber buildings. Niyodogawa town lines the clear, startlingly blue upper Niyodo River. Winters bring hard frost and real snow to the high roads, which close on Ishizuchi from December; summers are cool above 1,000 meters and wet everywhere. There is no railway. Local buses run Route 33 from Matsuyama to Kumakogen and on toward Kochi, and Routes 194, 197 and 439 thread the valleys. From Musutafu it is most of a day; Matsuyama is a little over an hour by bus or car from Kumakogen. Hikers file plans at police boxes, rural rescue heroes with flight or climbing Quirks are on call for the peaks, and the July mountain-opening festival brings crowds of white-clad pilgrims and extra patrols.
Mount Ishizuchi.hiddenInfo: This is the emptiest country in the corridor: villages of a few elderly households, schools long closed, and forest roads that wash out in every heavy rain. Search and rescue is the real hero work here, for lost hikers, pilgrims and drivers caught by landslides or snow, and the nearest real agencies are in Matsuyama and Kochi, one to two hours off by road. Small-time trouble means illegal logging, poaching, theft from unlocked farmhouses and shrines, and people who come up to the karst or the gorge to drop out of sight for a while.

Kochi.name: Kochi
Kochi.basicInfo: The heart of Kochi Prefecture: Kochi city on its bay, the plain of Nankoku and Kami to the east, the Niyodo River valley at Ino to the west, and the coast running southwest past Tosa city to the port of Susaki. The southern third of the cell is the open water of Tosa Bay; the northern half is steep green mountain. Kochi city sits where its rivers meet Urado Bay, around one of the few castles in Japan with its original keep, a city of trams, covered arcades and a famously loud food hall where strangers share tables over katsuo no tataki, bonito seared over a straw fire. A Sunday market has run down the avenue below the castle for three centuries. Katsurahama, a curving beach with a rocky point and a bronze statue of the city's most famous Bakumatsu-era son, faces the Pacific at the mouth of Urado Bay, and Godaisan hill above the bay holds a pilgrimage temple and a botanical garden. In August the Yosakoi Festival fills every street with dance teams in wild costume clacking wooden naruko clappers. East, the Nankoku plain is greenhouse country of eggplant, peppers and ginger, with Kochi Ryoma Airport near the shore and the limestone cave of Ryugado in the hills of Kami. West, Ino makes Tosa washi paper beside the Niyodo, a river so clear its blue has its own name, and the Yokonami Peninsula carries a skyline road between Tosa Bay and a long inlet. Susaki, at the western edge, is a fishing and limestone port known for nabeyaki ramen served in clay pots. The climate is warm, sunny and very wet, and typhoons often make landfall here. The JR Dosan Line limited express runs from Okayama in about two and a half hours and continues west to Susaki; the trams run the city east to west; the Kochi Expressway climbs north over the mountains. From Musutafu, it is about five and a half hours by shinkansen and limited express through Okayama, or a little over three by air through Tokyo; from Osaka, about three and a half hours. Kochi city keeps several modest hero agencies and a full prefectural police headquarters, and the Yosakoi nights are the busiest patrol of the year.
Kochi.hiddenInfo: Kochi people are proud, blunt and slow to trust outsiders, and the city's drinking culture keeps police boxes busy with brawls and late-night Quirk flare-ups. The real worries are the expected Nankai Trough earthquake and tsunami, drilled for constantly, and flood season. Kochi has its own heroes but no large agency; serious villain trouble means calling help from Osaka or Okayama, hours away. Petty crime is pickpockets in the Yosakoi crowds, greenhouse theft, and small gangs running unlicensed fights and gambling in the nightlife streets.

Aki.name: Aki
Aki.basicInfo: The eastern Kochi coast and the mountains behind it: a long, nearly straight shore running southeast along Tosa Bay from Geisei through the small city of Aki, Tano and Nahari toward Cape Muroto, then around the peninsula's eastern side up the Pacific coast to Kannoura and Shishikui at the Tokushima border. The cape's tip lies just south of the edge. Inland, most of the cell is steep forest country cut by the Nahari, Yasuda and Monobe rivers, rising to ridges well over 1,000 meters. The coast is a narrow shelf of fields and greenhouses squeezed between the mountains and a pebble shore pounded by Pacific swell, with seawalls, tsunami towers and evacuation signs everywhere. Aki has samurai houses, eggplant greenhouses and boats that net baby sardines; Tano makes sea salt; Kiragawa in northern Muroto keeps a lane of old merchant houses with plaster walls set with rows of tiles against the storms, and binchotan charcoal is still burned in the hills behind it. Up the valleys, Umaji is a mountain village built almost entirely on yuzu citrus, Kitagawa has a large public garden modeled on a French painter's water-lily pond, and the old Yanase cedar logging railway survives in stone bridges and tunnels. Higher in the Monobe valley, hamlets keep an old folk religion of their own. On the eastern side, Toyo town's Kannoura and Ikumi beaches draw surfers all year. The Tosa Kuroshio Railway's elevated Gomen-Nahari Line runs along the coast from Gomen near Kochi to Nahari, its stations dressed with cartoon mascots; from there, Route 55 buses continue around the cape, and the road-rail bus from Tokushima's coast reaches Kannoura. Kochi Ryoma Airport is about forty minutes west. From Musutafu, it is most of a day by train through Okayama and Kochi; from Osaka, about four and a half hours. Two tiny hero offices, in Aki and Kannoura, cover the whole coast, and the November yuzu harvest brings pickers with handy Quirks into the hills.
Aki.hiddenInfo: The Aki coast is losing people fast, and the expected Nankai earthquake hangs over every seaside hamlet; tsunami drills are a fact of life, and upland villages can be cut off for days when roads slide. The nearest serious hero support is in Kochi city, an hour or more away, so local police and volunteer fire crews do most of the work. Trouble is small: yuzu and greenhouse theft, illegal lobster and abalone diving, speeding on Route 55, and the odd drifter sleeping rough on the surf beaches.

Kaiyo Coast.name: Kaiyo Coast
Kaiyo Coast.basicInfo: The southernmost coast of Tokushima, where Shikoku's eastern shore bends south toward Cape Muroto, and the wide open water beyond it at the mouth of the Kii Channel. Only the northwest corner is land: a ria coast of small coves, headlands and river mouths from Hiwasa in Minami town through Mugi to the Kaiyo towns of Asakawa, Kainan and Kaifu. Everything east and south of that is sea, with the mountains of Wakayama's coast a faint line far to the east on clear days. Behind the coast, the Shikoku mountains crowd close, forested and wet. Hiwasa is a pilgrimage town grown up around Yakuo-ji, the temple where travelers in an unlucky year come to have their misfortune lifted, its steps scattered with offered coins; below it, Ohama beach is a loggerhead turtle nesting ground watched over from May to August, with a sea turtle museum beside it. In October, the town's shrine festival drives heavy drum floats into the sea. Mugi is a small fishing port of lobster pots and drying nets on a sheltered bay. Kaiyo, at the mouth of the Kaifu River, has some of the best surf in western Japan, and surfers drive down from Osaka and Kobe before dawn. The towns are small, quiet and old, and life follows the boats, the tides and the citrus harvest. The JR Mugi Line runs local trains, and a limited express as far as Mugi, down the coast from Tokushima; at Awa-Kainan, the Asa Kaigan Railway's road-rail bus climbs from the street onto the rails, runs the line to Kannoura and drives off onto Route 55 toward Muroto. Tokushima city is about two hours north by local train. From Osaka, it is about four and a half hours by expressway bus and train; from Musutafu, most of a day. Small coast guard patrol boats and the occasional sea-adapted hero work the water. One small hero office in Hiwasa covers the coast, with extra sidekicks sent down for turtle season and the summer surf crowds.
Kaiyo Coast.hiddenInfo: Southern Tokushima is quiet and aging, and the expected Nankai earthquake shapes everything: tsunami towers, hilltop shelters, drills. Hero help is thin; the nearest real agency is in Tokushima city, around two hours off, and the coast guard covers the water. Ordinary trouble is poaching of lobster and abalone, surf-spot turf fights between locals and weekend visitors, vandalism of turtle nests, and theft of coin offerings from the temple steps.

Shirahama.name: Shirahama
Shirahama.basicInfo: The southwest coast of the Kii Peninsula around Tanabe Bay, and the broad stretch of open water west of it. Only a thin strip in the northeast corner is land: Minabe, Tanabe city, the hot-spring resort of Shirahama on its hooked headland, and the coast just south toward Tsubaki. The rest of the cell is the Kii Channel opening into the Pacific, with Shikoku out of sight far to the west. Shirahama is one of Japan's oldest hot-spring towns, a resort of big hotels and seaside baths whose landmarks lie in a row along its west shore: the bright white sand of Shirarahama beach, the Sakinoyu bath cut into the sea rocks, the flat tilted sandstone shelves of Senjojiki, the sheer cliffs of Sandanbeki with a sea cave below, and Engetsu, a small island with a round hole that frames the sunset near the equinoxes. The resort also has an airport, a large safari-style animal park, an aquarium and a busy fish market. Across the bay, Tanabe is a working city of fishing boats and plum merchants and the gateway to the Kumano Kodo pilgrim trails inland; its Tokei Shrine festival in late July brings out tall floats. Minabe, just north, is the plum capital of Japan: every hill is an orchard, white with blossom in February, and its umeboshi pickled plums are sold all year, while binchotan charcoal makers still work the same hills. Winters are mild, summers hot and humid, with heavy rain and typhoons in late summer. The JR Kisei Main Line brings the Kuroshio limited express from Shin-Osaka in about two and a half hours, the Kisei Expressway runs south past Tanabe, and Nanki-Shirahama Airport has flights from Haneda in a little over an hour. From Musutafu, it is about four and a half hours by shinkansen and limited express, or a short flight from Tokyo. Shirahama keeps a small resort hero office, and lifeguards with water Quirks work the beaches; Tanabe has its own police station and hero office, and sidekicks fill the summer fireworks nights on Shirarahama.
Shirahama.hiddenInfo: Shirahama lives on tourism and has the quiet problems of a resort: summer crowds, drownings and rip currents off the rocks, drunk visitors, and pickpockets in the onsen streets. The sea cliffs along the west shore are dangerous in a swell, and police patrol the lookouts. Hero help beyond the resort office comes from Wakayama city, about an hour and a half north. Ordinary villainy is plum theft at harvest, thieves working hotel parking lots, and small-time fraud aimed at older pilgrims.

Kushimoto.name: Kushimoto
Kushimoto.basicInfo: The southern tip of the Kii Peninsula and the deep south of Kumano: the rocky coast from Susami east around Cape Shionomisaki, the southernmost point of Honshu, to Kushimoto, Taiji and Nachikatsuura, and the steep forested mountains rising behind them toward Nachi and the Ogumotori pass. Shingu lies just past the eastern edge and Hongu just past the northern one. About half the cell is land, the rest the Pacific and the Kumano-nada. Kushimoto is a fishing and resort town on a sandbar between the cape and Kii-Oshima, an island reached by a high bridge with a looping approach; the jagged line of the Hashiguiiwa rocks marches out toward the island, and the warm Kuroshio feeds coral reefs and a marine park with an underwater observatory. Oshima's Kashinozaki lighthouse overlooks the reef where an Ottoman frigate was wrecked in 1890, and the island keeps a museum and memorial to the friendship with Turkey that followed. The Kozagawa River runs down a gorge past a vast single rock face to the sea. Taiji is a small, old whaling town with a whale museum. Nachikatsuura is a hot-spring town and Japan's biggest port for fresh tuna, with dawn auctions; above it, Kumano Nachi Taisha and its vermilion pagoda stand beside Nachi Falls, a single drop of 133 meters, and the stone-paved Daimonzaka slope of the Kumano Kodo climbs through giant cedars. On July 14, the Nachi Fire Festival carries huge burning torches down the shrine steps. The climate is among the warmest on Honshu, with palms and subtropical plants on the coast and some of Japan's heaviest rain in the mountains. The JR Kisei Main Line follows the coast: the Kuroshio limited express from Shin-Osaka takes about three and a half hours to Kushimoto, and the Nanki from Nagoya a little longer to Kii-Katsuura. Route 42 hugs the shore, and the Kisei Expressway reaches Susami. From Musutafu, it is about five hours either way around the peninsula. Small hero offices in Kushimoto and Katsuura cover the coast, the coast guard and maritime heroes watch the cape, and sidekicks with heat resistance guard the fire festival.
Kushimoto.hiddenInfo: The far south of Kii is remote and aging; Route 42 runs long empty stretches between towns, and landslides in the Kumano mountains can cut off whole valleys after a typhoon. The nearest large hero agencies are in Wakayama city and Tsu, three or more hours away, so locals rely on the coast guard and their own small offices. Small crime is tuna and gear theft at the ports, fraud aimed at pilgrims, and coin thefts from shrines.

Sea off Shingu.name: Sea off Shingu
Sea off Shingu.basicInfo: The Kumano-nada off the mouth of the Kumano River, a deep, open stretch of the Pacific east of the Kii Peninsula's southern corner. Only a thin edge of land touches the northwest: the city of Shingu on the Wakayama bank of the river mouth and, across the river on the Mie bank, the start of the long pebble beach of Shichiri Mihama running north. The water is deep blue and shelves quickly to depths of over a thousand meters; the warm Kuroshio sweeps along offshore to the south, bringing heavy swell, sea fog in early summer, and typhoons in late summer and autumn. Purse seiners and line boats from Katsuura, Shingu and Kumano work for bonito, tuna, mackerel and the slim autumn saury used in the local pressed sushi. There are no islands in view and no ferries cross here. From the water, the dark Kumano mountains stand behind Shingu. A party out here is on a fishing boat, a coast guard cutter from Owase or Kushimoto, or carried by a flying or swimming hero. Shingu is about four hours from Nagoya by the Nanki limited express.
Sea off Shingu.hiddenInfo: Open, empty water. Weather is the danger: sudden swells, fog and typhoons catch small boats, and the coast guard does most rescues. Small-time trouble is illegal fishing, the occasional smuggling run along the coast, and boaters using water Quirks without a license. The nearest hero agency large enough to help is hours away in Tsu or Wakayama.

Open Pacific south of Izu.name: Open Pacific south of Izu
Open Pacific south of Izu.basicInfo: Empty open ocean south of the northern Izu Islands, out of sight of land in most weather. The water is deep, over 1,000 m, and a clear, intense blue, and the Kuroshio current runs east through here as a warm, fast stream that can push a small boat miles off course in an afternoon. Long swells roll in from the south, winter westerlies raise steep seas, and typhoons cross from late summer into autumn. On clear days the peaks of Mikurajima and Miyakejima show to the northeast and Kozushima to the north. Coastal freighters bound between Tokyo and the southwestern ports pass to the north, and the night ferry to Hachijojima runs to the east. Tuna long-liners and sport fishing boats come out for tuna and marlin, and whales and dolphins travel the current. To the north, police boats patrol the restricted exclusion zone around the prison island, and boats heading that way are hailed and turned back. Coast guard cutters and the occasional maritime hero cover this water on long patrols. A party could be out here on a fishing boat, a yacht, a coast guard cutter, or carried by a flying hero.
Open Pacific south of Izu.hiddenInfo: This is the emptiest water on the map; a disabled boat can drift for a day before anyone notices. Help is a coast guard helicopter or a flying hero from the islands, an hour or more away.

Waters off Mikurajima.name: Waters off Mikurajima
Waters off Mikurajima.basicInfo: Open sea south of Mikurajima on the line of the Izu Islands, where the Kuroshio current pours through the gap between Mikurajima and Hachijojima in a fast, warm stream that old sailors called the Black Current River. The water is deep and a rich, clear blue, and crossing it in a small boat means fighting the current. The only land is Inambajima, a lone, steep rock tower in the western part of the region, uninhabited and white with seabirds, famous among divers and anglers for the big fish that gather around it. Mikurajima's cliffs show to the north and Hachijojima's twin peaks to the south on clear days. The night ferry from Tokyo passes through on its way to Hachijojima after calling at Miyakejima and Mikurajima, and small planes fly overhead. Fishing boats from Hachijojima and Miyakejima work the grounds for alfonsino, bonito, yellowtail and tuna. Winter winds and typhoon swell can stop the ferry for days. Coast guard patrols and maritime heroes come out mostly for rescues. A party could be out here on the ferry, a fishing or dive boat, or carried by a flying hero.
Waters off Mikurajima.hiddenInfo: The current here is strong enough to carry a stalled boat far off its course, and divers at Inambajima are sometimes swept away. Help is a coast guard cutter or a hero flying out from Hachijojima or Miyakejima, an hour or more away.

Imari.name: Imari
Imari.basicInfo: The northwest of Kyushu where Saga meets Nagasaki: the porcelain towns of Imari, Arita and Hasami, the naval port city of Sasebo, the island-studded Kujukushima coast, the southern half of Hirado Island, and the northern arm of Omura Bay with its narrow Hario Strait. About half the square is sea and drowned coast. Arita is where Japanese porcelain began four centuries ago, and its long main street of kilns and shops holds a pottery fair every Golden Week that draws crowds by the hundred thousand; Imari's port shipped that porcelain to the world, and in the hills above it Okawachiyama is a misty village of chimneys where the lords' kilns were once kept secret. Hasami and Mikawachi make everyday and fine wares too. Sasebo is a city of about a quarter million around a deep natural harbor and naval base, with a long covered shopping arcade, big hamburgers sold since the base days, and the Kujukushima islands, more than two hundred green islets scattered across bright water, seen from hilltop lookouts and cruise boats. South of the city, Huis Ten Bosch, a resort built as a Dutch town of canals and windmills, glows with light shows at night, and the Saikai bridges cross Hario Strait above swirling tidal currents. The climate is warm and wet, rainy in June and July, with typhoons in late summer. Limited expresses on the JR Sasebo Line link Arita and Sasebo with Hakata in under two hours, another runs to the resort, the Matsuura Railway follows the coast through Imari, and the Nishi-Kyushu Expressway runs from Takeo to Sasebo. From Musutafu, allow most of a day. Sasebo has several hero agencies and harbor police, smaller towns have police boxes, licensed heroes help manage the crowds at Arita's fair, and kiln workers with heat-resistant Quirks fire the kilns under permit. Visitors buy porcelain, cruise the islands, eat Sasebo burgers and Imari beef and stay at the resort.
Imari.hiddenInfo: Sasebo's nightlife near the naval port sees bar fights and the occasional sailor in trouble, handled by police and shore patrols. The porcelain trade has quiet problems with counterfeit antique ware and theft from kilns. The Hario Strait currents drown the careless. Small crime is pickpocketing at the pottery fair and the resort and scams aimed at tourists. Sasebo's agencies are the nearest real hero help; Fukuoka is two hours away.

Saga.name: Saga
Saga.basicInfo: The Saga plain and the head of the Ariake Sea: the prefectural capital Saga, the canal town of Yanagawa and the old coal city of Omuta across the Chikugo River on the eastern side, the hot-spring towns of Takeo and Ureshino in the west, and the Tara mountains and Ariake shore in the southwest. The Ariake Sea has the biggest tides in Japan, about six meters, and at low water the shore turns into kilometers of gleaming gray mud where mudskippers hop and fishermen slide out on boards; in winter it becomes a grid of poles and nets for nori, and Saga leads the country in seaweed. The plain behind is flat rice and barley land crossed by creeks and old reclaimed dikes. Saga is a calm, low-rise capital around its castle moat, and every autumn the Saga International Balloon Fiesta fills the sky over the Kase River with hundreds of hot-air balloons. Yoshinogari, a reconstructed Yayoi-era moated village, lies in the north. Yanagawa is laced with moats where boatmen pole flat boats under willows, and it serves eel steamed over rice; Okawa makes furniture, and Omuta has World Heritage coal pits and port works. Takeo has a vermilion gate over its baths and a giant camphor tree said to be three thousand years old; Ureshino grows green tea and simmers tofu in its spring water. Kashima's Yutoku Inari Shrine climbs a cliff in vermilion, and at Tara a torii stands in the sea, reachable on foot at low tide. Summers are hot and humid, winters mild. The Nagasaki Main Line and Nishi-Kyushu shinkansen serve the west, the Kagoshima Line, Kyushu shinkansen and Nishitetsu trains the east; Hakata to Saga takes about forty minutes and to Yanagawa a little under an hour. From Musutafu, about five and a half hours. Each town has police and small hero agencies; heroes are on duty at the balloon fiesta, where unlicensed flight is banned, and farmers use earth and water Quirks under permit at planting time. Visitors ride Yanagawa's canals, soak at Takeo and Ureshino and walk the mudflats.
Saga.hiddenInfo: The Ariake shore carries an old quarrel between fishing cooperatives and farmers over the sea wall that closed off Isahaya Bay, blamed for poor nori harvests. The mudflats drown people who misjudge the tide. Omuta and the old coal towns have empty shopping streets and some rough edges. Small crime is nori and crop theft, scams on the elderly and drunken trouble at festivals. Fukuoka's agencies are about an hour away.

Kurume.name: Kurume
Kurume.basicInfo: The upper Chikugo country and northern Kumamoto: Kurume on the river at the northwest corner, the tea hills of Yame, the Tsue and Shaka mountains across the middle, the old timber town of Hita in its basin at the northern edge, and the Kikuchi and Yamaga plains of Kumamoto Prefecture in the south, reaching the rim of the Aso caldera in the southeast. Nearly all of it is land. Kurume is a solid working city known as the birthplace of pork-bone ramen, for indigo kasuri cloth, rubber footwear and azaleas, and its Suitengu shrine is the head of that faith. Yame grows some of Japan's finest green tea and shaded gyokuro on misty hillside terraces, especially around Hoshino village, known for its starry skies; Yame also has the largest burial mound in northern Kyushu and makes paper lanterns. In the mountains, cedar forests, dams and narrow gorges hide small hot springs. Hita, ringed by cedar plantations, keeps a merchant quarter of white-walled houses and soy sauce breweries, cormorant fishing on the Mikuma River in summer, and riverside inns at Amagase. In the south, Yamaga holds a lantern festival each August where dancers wear gilded paper lanterns on their heads, and its old wooden theater still stages plays; Kikuchi has a cool gorge of waterfalls and rich rice paddies, and the farms around Tamana grow watermelons and strawberries. Summers are hot and humid, with July downpours that flood mountain valleys; winters are cold in the hills. The Kyushu shinkansen stops at Kurume, Chikugo-Funagoya and Shin-Tamana; Hakata to Kurume is about twenty minutes, and Kumamoto lies just south. The Kyudai Line and the Oita Expressway climb east from Kurume to Hita in about an hour and on toward Yufuin, and the Kyushu Expressway runs north and south. From Musutafu, about five hours. Each town has police and small hero agencies; licensed heroes cover mountain districts and flood rescues, and tea farmers with plant Quirks work the harvest under permit. Visitors eat ramen, sip tea in Yame, stroll Hita's old quarter and soak in mountain springs.
Kurume.hiddenInfo: The July rains are the region's real fear; hill villages around Hita and Yame have been cut off before, and every hero and firefighter is called out when the rivers rise. Mountain villages are emptying, and the dams left old resentments. Small crime is theft of tea and fruit, scams targeting the elderly and street racing on mountain roads. Kurume and Kumamoto have the nearest sizable agencies.

Beppu.name: Beppu
Beppu.basicInfo: The volcanic heart of northern Kyushu: Beppu's steaming hot-spring city on Beppu Bay at the eastern edge, Yufuin in its basin under Mount Yufu, the high Kuju mountains, the castle town of Taketa, and the northern half of Aso's great caldera at the southwest corner, crossing from Oita into Kumamoto Prefecture. Beppu has more hot-spring vents than anywhere else in Japan; white steam rises from hundreds of chimneys across its hillsides, and its eight onsen districts offer sand baths, mud baths and old public bathhouses. The Hells, boiling ponds of cobalt blue and blood red, draw tour buses, and in Kannawa food is steamed over the vents. A ropeway climbs Mount Tsurumi behind the city. Over the pass, Yufuin is a quieter resort of small inns, galleries and a lake that steams on cold mornings under twin-peaked Mount Yufu. To the southwest the Kuju mountains, the highest on Kyushu's mainland at nearly eighteen hundred meters, rise above highland meadows, wetlands and pink azaleas in June; the Yamanami Highway crosses the grasslands toward Aso, past Japan's tallest pedestrian suspension bridge at Kokonoe and the riverside baths of Kurokawa. Aso's caldera is one of the largest in the world, a green bowl of farms and towns where red cattle graze and the grass is burned each spring; its active crater, Naka-dake, steams at the southern edge and closes to visitors when the gas is bad. Taketa has castle ruins on a cliff and fizzing carbonated springs at Nagayu. Summers are cool in the highlands, winters snowy on the passes. Limited expresses from Hakata reach Beppu by way of Kokura in about two hours, a sightseeing train reaches Yufuin by way of Kurume and Hita in a little over two, the Hohi Line and Route 57 cross through Aso to Kumamoto, and overnight ferries sail from Beppu to Osaka. From Musutafu, about five and a half hours. Beppu has several hero agencies; the highlands are covered by licensed heroes on long patrols alongside park rangers and volcano watchers. Visitors bathe, hike Kuju, ride horses on Aso's grasslands and eat steamed food and toriten.
Beppu.hiddenInfo: Aso and Kuju are live volcanic country; gas alerts, closed roads and hikers lost in fog on the Kuju ridges are routine work for rangers and heroes. Beppu's older entertainment streets keep a seedy edge, and illegal hot-spring drilling and fake spring water are local grievances. Yufuin worries about crowds. Small crime is bag snatching in tourist streets and unlicensed Quirk massage parlors. Beppu and Oita have the nearest agencies; the highlands are an hour from any.

Oita.name: Oita
Oita.basicInfo: The eastern coast of Oita Prefecture from the capital south to the Saiki rias, facing the Bungo Channel: Oita city on the southern shore of Beppu Bay at the western edge, the Saganoseki Peninsula pointing east toward Shikoku, then the castle town of Usuki, the quarry town of Tsukumi and the port of Saiki, with forested mountains behind and the open channel beyond. Beppu's hot springs lie just west of the edge. A little under half the cell is land; the east is the Bungo Channel, with Shikoku's coast on the far side. Oita is a mid-sized industrial city, with a downtown of arcades around the old castle moat and a waterfront of steelworks, refineries and petrochemical plants on reclaimed land east of the river mouths. Saganoseki is a fishing town under the tall chimney of a copper smelter; its line-caught horse mackerel and mackerel from the fast Hayasui Strait are luxury brands, and a car ferry crosses to Sadamisaki in about seventy minutes. Usuki is a quiet castle town of soy sauce and miso breweries, famous for fugu, for the Usuki stone Buddhas carved into a soft cliff in a valley outside town, and for a November festival of bamboo lanterns. Tsukumi lives on limestone and citrus. Saiki, the largest city in Kyushu by area, is a fishing port proud of its sushi, at the head of a ria coast of fish farms and small islands. Oita food is chicken tempura, karaage, flat-noodle dango-jiru soup, marinated fish ryukyu, dried shiitake, and kabosu citrus squeezed over everything. The climate is mild, drier in the north and wetter in the southern rias, with typhoons in late summer. The JR Nippo Main Line's Sonic limited express reaches Oita from Hakata in about two hours, and the Nichirin runs south to Saiki and Miyazaki; the Oita and Higashi-Kyushu expressways cross the area, ferries leave Usuki for Yawatahama, and overnight ferries from Oita and Beppu reach Kobe and Osaka. From Musutafu, it is about five and a half hours by shinkansen to Kokura and the Sonic, or a flight from Haneda. Oita city has several established hero agencies and the prefectural police headquarters, and its steelworks hire Quirk-assisted crews.
Oita.hiddenInfo: Oita is a solid regional city with its own hero scene, but the coast south of Usuki empties out fast, and help there can be an hour or more away. The steel and petrochemical complex brings labor tension, industrial accidents, and a steady trickle of theft from shipping yards. The fishing towns quarrel over catch limits and the poaching of the prized Saganoseki fish. Petty crime downtown is the ordinary sort: bar fights, unlicensed Quirk use by night crowds, and small gangs skimming from the docks and pachinko halls.

Uwajima.name: Uwajima
Uwajima.basicInfo: The southwest corner of Ehime and the Uwa Sea: a deeply indented ria coast of drowned valleys, narrow peninsulas and small islands running south from Yoshida through the castle city of Uwajima to the fishing towns of Ainan, with the Bungo Channel open to the west. Only about a third of the cell is land; the western half is water, the Uwa Sea grading into the channel, with Kyushu's coast low on the horizon on clear days. Behind the coast, the Onigajo mountains rise steeply, and rice and mandarin terraces climb wherever a slope faces the sun. Uwajima is a small castle city whose hilltop keep is one of the twelve original castle towers left in Japan, with a wisteria garden and a covered market street below. It is known for bull sumo, a traditional sport in which two huge bulls push horn to horn in a ring several times a year, and for its July festival, when giant demon-bull ushi-oni floats charge through town. The bays are covered with pearl rafts and the pens of farmed red sea bream; tai-meshi, raw bream over rice with egg and sauce, and fried jakoten fish cake are the local foods. Yoshida, to the north, is mandarin country. Along the coast south of Uwajima, the terraced potato fields of Yusumizugaura climb a whole headland in stone steps, the hamlet of Sotodomari is walled in high stone against typhoon winds, and Ainan has Kanjizai-ji, the pilgrimage temple farthest from the first. Winters are mild, summers hot, and typhoons strike in late summer. The JR Yosan Line limited express runs from Matsuyama in about an hour and a half, and the Yodo Line, a slow single-track line, runs east up the Shimanto River to Kubokawa; the Matsuyama Expressway reaches Uwajima's southern edge. From Musutafu, it is most of a day by shinkansen to Okayama and limited express through Matsuyama, or a flight to Matsuyama and a train south. Uwajima keeps a small hero agency and a police station, the coast guard and a few maritime sidekicks watch the pearl and fish farms, and farmhands with strength Quirks are hired at harvest.
Uwajima.hiddenInfo: The pearl and fish farms are big money in a poor district, and quiet disputes over water rights, red tide losses and theft from the rafts run under the surface. Outlying hamlets and islands are aging and some are close to empty. Beyond Uwajima's one agency, the nearest real hero muscle is in Matsuyama, about ninety minutes away. Small crime is pearl and catch theft, illegal betting around bull sumo, and poachers working other people's rafts at night.

Shimanto.name: Shimanto
Shimanto.basicInfo: The southwest of Kochi Prefecture: the middle and lower Shimanto River, the Kuroshio coast along the western edge of Tosa Bay, and the inland hills along the Ehime border, from Kubokawa and Kihoku in the north to Shimanto city near the river mouth and Sukumo on its bay in the southwest. Most of it is land, rolling forest and narrow river valleys; the southeast corner is Tosa Bay. The Shimanto is called the last clear river in Japan, barely dammed along its length: it loops west from its source in the mountains to the north, past Kubokawa and Toka toward the Ehime line, then south through deep green gorges to the sea below Nakamura. It is crossed by low concrete chinkabashi, sinking bridges without railings built to let floods pour over them. People fish it for ayu sweetfish, river shrimp and eel, gather green aonori laver at its mouth in winter, and paddle canoes and roofed river boats in summer. Kubokawa is a farming and rail junction town with a pilgrimage temple whose ceiling is painted in hundreds of panels. Nakamura, the old center of Shimanto city, is a quiet town laid out on a grid in imitation of Kyoto. In the Ehime hills, Matsuno has the cool stone gorge of Nametoko. On the coast, the Kuroshio town ports of Saga and Ogata catch bonito by pole and line, run whale-watching boats, and hold a beach art show of printed T-shirts strung over the sand each May. Sukumo, in the southwest corner, is a fishing and fish-farming port on a sheltered bay. Summers are among the hottest in Japan, and typhoons and flash floods are regular. The Tosa Kuroshio Railway runs from Kubokawa to Nakamura and Sukumo, with limited expresses from Kochi in under two hours, and the JR Yodo Line follows the river west to Uwajima; the Kochi Expressway reaches the Kubokawa area. From Musutafu, it is most of a day by train through Okayama and Kochi, or a flight to Kochi and two hours on the train; from Osaka, about five hours. Small hero offices in Shimanto city and Sukumo cover an enormous rural district, and river rescue in flood season is their real work.
Shimanto.hiddenInfo: This is deep rural Japan: aging villages, empty schools, wild boar and deer in the fields, and long drives between anything. Floods are the real enemy, and the sinking bridges make a dangerous road in heavy rain. The nearest sizable hero agencies are in Kochi city, two hours away. Small crime is eel and ayu poaching, illegal gravel digging, theft from empty houses, and the occasional fugitive hiding in the hills on the bet that no one will come looking soon.

Tosa Bay.name: Tosa Bay
Tosa Bay.basicInfo: The open middle of Tosa Bay, the wide arc of the Pacific between Cape Muroto in the east and Cape Ashizuri in the west, south of Kochi city. The water is a deep, clear blue, the shelf dropping quickly to great depth toward the trough far offshore. The warm Kuroshio runs past to the south and keeps the bay mild all year; Pacific swell is near constant, and the bay is a regular path for typhoons in late summer and autumn. From here the Kochi coast is a low green line to the north with the mountains of Shikoku behind it, and the capes at either end are faint on clear days. There are no islands in view and no ferries cross the bay. Fishing boats from Kochi, Usa, Susaki, Kure and Saga work it for skipjack bonito by pole and line in spring and autumn, along with mackerel, whitebait close inshore, and deep-water fish, and whale-watching boats go out after the Bryde's whales that live in the bay year round. A party out here is on a fishing or whale-watching boat, a coast guard cutter from Kochi, or the back of a flying or swimming hero.
Tosa Bay.hiddenInfo: Open water with little going on beneath it: the dangers are weather, swell and fishing traffic. Coast guard boats from Kochi handle most rescues, and the only heroes who reach the bay quickly are flyers or swimmers out of Kochi city. Small trouble is illegal fishing, boaters showing off with water Quirks, and the odd stolen boat.

Cape Muroto.name: Cape Muroto
Cape Muroto.basicInfo: The Pacific around Cape Muroto, the southeastern tip of Shikoku, where Tosa Bay ends and the open approach to the Kii Channel begins. A little land in the north is the cape itself: the town of Muroto with its fishing port at Murotsu, the uplifted wave-cut terraces and black rock shelves of a geopark, the white Muroto Misaki lighthouse on the bluff, a pilgrimage temple on the hill above, and the sea caves where the founder of the Shikoku pilgrimage is said to have meditated. Muroto pumps cold, clean water from deep below the sea and sells it, and its boats bring in golden-eyed alfonsino from deep water off the cape. The weather station here is famous for record typhoon winds; the cape takes the full force of storms, and the sea is often rough, with swell from the south and the Kuroshio running close offshore, deep blue and warm. West of the cape lies Tosa Bay, east the open Pacific toward the Kii Channel, and the seafloor drops away steeply to the south. No ferries cross. A party here might be on a fishing boat out of Murotsu, a coast guard cutter, or carried by a flying or swimming hero, and Route 55 buses reach the cape from Nahari and Kannoura.
Cape Muroto.hiddenInfo: Muroto is remote, aging and exposed: typhoons and the expected Nankai earthquake are the worries, and help from Kochi city is about two hours away by road. The coast guard does the rescues offshore. Small trouble is illegal diving for lobster and abalone, gear theft at the port, and boaters ignoring storm warnings.

Southern Kii Channel.name: Southern Kii Channel
Southern Kii Channel.basicInfo: Open Pacific between Cape Muroto and the Kii Peninsula, the southern approach to the Kii Channel and the sea lane into Osaka Bay. No land lies inside; on clear days the dark headland of Muroto shows to the northwest and the mountains of Wakayama's coast to the northeast, each tens of kilometers off. The water is deep, open and blue, the seafloor falling southward toward the Nankai Trough, and the warm Kuroshio runs along the south, setting ships eastward. Swell is near constant; fog forms in early summer and typhoons pass through in late summer and autumn. This is one of Japan's busiest shipping approaches: container ships, tankers, car carriers and bulk ships bound to and from Osaka, Kobe and Wakayama pass in long lines, and overnight long-distance ferries between the Osaka Bay ports and southern Kyushu cross it, lit up at night. Fishing boats from Muroto, Kaiyo and Tanabe come out after bonito and tuna. A party out here would be on a ferry deck or a fishing boat, aboard a coast guard patrol, or carried by a flying or swimming hero.
Southern Kii Channel.hiddenInfo: Big-ship traffic is the main risk: collisions, fires and crew lost overboard far from shore. The coast guard handles nearly everything, and the nearest heroes able to reach the open channel are flyers or maritime specialists from Wakayama, Tokushima or Kochi. Small trouble is smuggling aboard freighters and illegal fishing.

Pacific off Shirahama.name: Pacific off Shirahama
Pacific off Shirahama.basicInfo: Open Pacific southwest of the Kii Peninsula, off Shirahama, Susami and the coast toward Cape Shionomisaki. No land lies inside the cell; the Kii coast is a dark wooded line a few dozen kilometers to the north, with Shirahama's hotels and headland visible on clear days, and open ocean everywhere else. The water is deep and a strong cobalt blue. The Kuroshio, Japan's great warm current, runs fast along the south of the cell and swings close to land near Cape Shionomisaki to the east, often at several knots, carrying warm water, flying fish and the occasional sea turtle. Swell is constant; typhoons pass in late summer and autumn, and winter brings strong northwest winds off the land. Ships bound to and from the Kii Channel cross the area, and long-distance overnight ferries from Osaka and Kobe pass at night. Fishing boats from Susami troll for bonito, and boats from Tanabe and Shirahama go out for tuna, mackerel and deep-water fish. A party here is on a fishing or charter boat out of Shirahama or Susami, a coast guard patrol from Tanabe, or carried by a flying or swimming hero.
Pacific off Shirahama.hiddenInfo: Open water: weather and the Kuroshio's strong current are the danger, sweeping disabled boats and swimmers far offshore quickly. Coast guard boats from Tanabe and Kushimoto handle rescues, and only flying or maritime heroes from the Shirahama area can reach far out. Small trouble is illegal fishing and charter skippers cutting corners.

Pacific off Kushimoto.name: Pacific off Kushimoto
Pacific off Kushimoto.basicInfo: Open Pacific south of Cape Shionomisaki, the southernmost tip of Honshu, which rises just beyond the northern edge with its white lighthouse and grassy bluff; Kii-Oshima and the Kashinozaki lighthouse lie to the northeast. The Kuroshio passes closer to land here than almost anywhere on Honshu's coast, a fast warm river within the ocean running east at several knots, deep blue, clear and full of life, and it feeds the coral and tropical fish of Kushimoto's reefs just north. The seafloor drops quickly to great depths. Swell is constant, the cape is a notorious meeting place of wind and current, rough in winter, and it sits on a regular typhoon track in late summer. Coastal shipping between Tokyo Bay and Osaka Bay rounds the cape here, so lines of freighters, tankers and car carriers pass day and night. Fishing boats from Kushimoto and Katsuura work for tuna, bonito and longtooth grouper, and the bluefin tuna farm pens in the sheltered bays behind Oshima lie just north. A party here is on a fishing boat, a diving charter out of Kushimoto, a coast guard patrol, or carried by a flying or swimming hero.
Pacific off Kushimoto.hiddenInfo: Shipping traffic and the current make this a busy rescue sea; the coast guard station at Kushimoto handles most calls, and maritime heroes on loan from Wakayama cover the cape in typhoon season. Small trouble is illegal fishing, theft from the tuna pens, and divers poaching the reefs.
